- `record CpuTimes(user_us: i64, system_us: i64, idle_us: i64, waiting_us: i64, stolen_us: i64)`: What `cpu_times` answers: the time every processor of the machine has spent since it started, summed over the processors, in microseconds, read at one moment.
- `record ProcessUsage(resident_bytes: i64, virtual_bytes: i64, user_ns: i64, system_ns: i64)`: What `process_usage` answers: what a process holds and has spent, read at one moment.
- `record Owner(id: AccountId, name: str?)`: The user that owns a process, as `processes` tells it.
- `record Process(id: i64, parent_id: i64, name: str, started_unix_ms: i64, owner: Owner?, usage: ProcessUsage?)`: What `processes` answers for one process of the machine, read at one moment.
- `record NetworkCounters(name: str, bytes_received: i64, bytes_sent: i64, packets_received: i64, packets_sent: i64, errors_received: i64, errors_sent: i64, dropped_received: i64, dropped_sent: i64)`: What `network_counters` answers for one network interface: what it has carried since the machine started, every count at or above 0.
- `function cpu_times() -> CpuTimes?`, called `os.cpu_times()`: The time every processor of the machine has spent since it started, summed, in microseconds, in one reading. Fails `unsupported`.
- `function cpu_usage(before: CpuTimes, after: CpuTimes) -> f64?`, called `os.cpu_usage(before: before, after: after)`: The share of the machine's processors' time that was busy between two readings, in percent, from 0.0 to 100.0, as psutil's `cpu_percent` answers. Fails `invalid`.
- `function process_usage(id: i64) -> ProcessUsage?`, called `os.process_usage(id)`: What the process `id` holds and has spent, read at one moment: its resident and virtual memory, and its time in its own code and the system's. Fails `invalid`, `not_found`, `permission`, `unsupported`.
- `function network_counters() -> [NetworkCounters]?`, called `os.network_counters()`: The counters of every network interface of the machine, in the system's order, each since the machine started. Fails `unsupported`, `not_text`.
- `function processes() -> [Process]?`, called `os.processes()`: Every process of the machine this program may read, in ascending order of id, at one moment: a monitor's table, with no `ps`. Fails `unsupported`.
- `function user_named(name: str) -> User?`, called `os.user_named(name)`: The user named `name`: its id, home and primary group, as the system's record of users holds them, which a directory service may be the source of. Fails `invalid`, `not_found`.
- `function user_identified(id: AccountId) -> User?`, called `os.user_identified(id)`: The user whose id is `id`, as `user_named` answers it. Fails `invalid`, `not_found`.
- `function group_named(name: str) -> Group?`, called `os.group_named(name)`: The group named `name`: its id. Fails `not_found`.
- `function group_identified(id: AccountId) -> Group?`, called `os.group_identified(id)`: The group whose id is `id`, as `group_named` answers it. Fails as `user_identified` does.
- `function groups_of(user: str) -> [Group]?`, called `os.groups_of(user)`: The groups the user named `user` belongs to, in the system's order, each once. Fails as `user_named` does.
- `function change_user(name: str) -> ()?`, called `os.change_user(name)`: Changes the user and the groups this process runs as to those of the user named `name`: its other groups, then its group, then its user, all of the real, effective and saved ids at once, every thread of the process changed, and the process unable to take back the user it was. Fails `invalid`, `not_found`, `permission`, `failed`, `unsupported`.
- `function random_bytes(count: i64) -> [u8]?`, called `os.random_bytes(count)`: `count` bytes from the system's generator for keys, fit for a unique name or a key. Fails `invalid`.
- `function terminal_size() -> TerminalSize?`, called `os.terminal_size()`: The size of the terminal the process's standard output is, in one reading. Fails `unsupported`.
- `function catch_stop() -> ()?`, called `os.catch_stop()`: Makes Ctrl-C and SIGTERM, on Windows Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Break and the console closing, ask the program's stop instead of ending it; a second one still ends it. Fails `invalid`, `failed`.
- `function ask_stop()`, called `os.ask_stop()`: Asks the program's own stop, from any thread: from this call every call that waits fails `stopped`, as after a signal `catch_stop` caught.
- `function is_stop_asked() -> bool`, called `os.is_stop_asked()`: Whether the stop was asked, by a signal after `catch_stop` or by `ask_stop`: a loop that works between its waits asks it between two pieces of work.
- `variant Signal = .hangup | .interrupt | .quit | .kill | .user1 | .user2 | .terminate | .child | .resume | .stop | .terminal_stop | .terminal_input | .terminal_output | .window_changed`: A signal, named the same on every platform, where each system numbers it its own way (`signal_number`).
- `function count_signal(signal: Signal) -> ()?`, called `os.count_signal(signal)`: Makes each `signal` the program receives counted, for `take_signals` to answer, instead of doing what it would: ending the program, stopping it, or nothing. Fails `invalid`, `unsupported`, `failed`.
- `function take_signals(signal: Signal) -> i64`, called `os.take_signals(signal)`: How many times `signal` came since the last call, the count set back to 0; 0 for a signal `count_signal` does not count.
- `function signal_number(signal: Signal) -> i64?`, called `os.signal_number(signal)`: The number this platform gives `signal`: the number `process.Status` holds for a signal that ended a child. Fails `unsupported`.
- `function signal_of(number: i64) -> Signal?`, called `os.signal_of(number)`: The signal this platform numbers `number`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function signal_name(signal: Signal) -> str`, called `os.signal_name(signal)`: The name POSIX gives `signal`, as a shell's `kill -l` writes it: `SIGINT` for `.interrupt`.


### hash

Layer 0, named `use <rebel>/hash`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/hash/).

Checksums and fast hashes that are not cryptographic, computed over bytes or over text, all at once or in steps: CRC-32 by the IEEE polynomial, by Castagnoli's or by one of the caller's; CRC-64 by ISO's polynomial, by ECMA's or by one of the caller's; Adler-32; FNV-1 and FNV-1a in 32 and 64 bits; and xxHash's XXH32 and XXH64, with a seed, the checksums of LZ4's and Zstandard's frames.

- `constant KOOPMAN: u32`, value `0xeb31d82e`: Koopman's polynomial for a CRC-32, its bits reversed as `crc32_poly`'s `poly` takes it: 0xeb31d82e, which is 0x741b8cd7 read from the other end.
- `function crc32(data: [u8]) -> u32`, called `hash.crc32(data)`: The CRC-32 of `data` by the IEEE polynomial, the one zlib, gzip, PNG and Ethernet check with, and Python's `zlib.crc32`.
- `function crc32_text(s: str) -> u32`, called `hash.crc32_text(s)`: The CRC-32 of the bytes of `s` by the IEEE polynomial, what `crc32` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function crc32c(data: [u8]) -> u32`, called `hash.crc32c(data)`: The CRC-32C of `data`, by Castagnoli's polynomial, the one iSCSI, ext4 and the instruction of SSE 4.2 check with.
- `function crc32c_text(s: str) -> u32`, called `hash.crc32c_text(s)`: The CRC-32C of the bytes of `s`, what `crc32c` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function crc32_combine(first: u32, second: u32, second_len: u64) -> u32`, called `hash.crc32_combine(first: first, second: second, second_len)`: The CRC-32 by the IEEE polynomial of two pieces one after the other, made from the CRC-32 of each and the length of the second, without their bytes.
- `function adler32(data: [u8]) -> u32`, called `hash.adler32(data)`: The Adler-32 of `data`, the checksum of zlib's streams (RFC 1950), and Python's `zlib.adler32`: faster than a CRC-32, and weaker over a few bytes.
- `function adler32_text(s: str) -> u32`, called `hash.adler32_text(s)`: The Adler-32 of the bytes of `s`, what `adler32` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function adler32_combine(first: u32, second: u32, second_len: u64) -> u32`, called `hash.adler32_combine(first: first, second: second, second_len)`: The Adler-32 of two pieces one after the other, made from the Adler-32 of each and the length of the second, without their bytes.
- `function fnv1_32(data: [u8]) -> u32`, called `hash.fnv1_32(data)`: The FNV-1 hash of `data` in 32 bits: from the offset 2166136261, each byte multiplies by the prime 16777619 and then mixes in by exclusive or.
- `function fnv1_32_text(s: str) -> u32`, called `hash.fnv1_32_text(s)`: The FNV-1 hash of the bytes of `s` in 32 bits, what `fnv1_32` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function fnv1a_32(data: [u8]) -> u32`, called `hash.fnv1a_32(data)`: The FNV-1a hash of `data` in 32 bits: from the offset 2166136261, each byte mixes in by exclusive or and then multiplies by the prime 16777619.
- `function fnv1a_32_text(s: str) -> u32`, called `hash.fnv1a_32_text(s)`: The FNV-1a hash of the bytes of `s` in 32 bits, what `fnv1a_32` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function fnv1_64(data: [u8]) -> u64`, called `hash.fnv1_64(data)`: The FNV-1 hash of `data` in 64 bits: from the offset 14695981039346656037, each byte multiplies by the prime 1099511628211 and then mixes in by exclusive or.
- `function fnv1_64_text(s: str) -> u64`, called `hash.fnv1_64_text(s)`: The FNV-1 hash of the bytes of `s` in 64 bits, what `fnv1_64` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function fnv1a_64(data: [u8]) -> u64`, called `hash.fnv1a_64(data)`: The FNV-1a hash of `data` in 64 bits: from the offset 14695981039346656037, each byte mixes in by exclusive or and then multiplies by the prime 1099511628211.
- `function fnv1a_64_text(s: str) -> u64`, called `hash.fnv1a_64_text(s)`: The FNV-1a hash of the bytes of `s` in 64 bits, what `fnv1a_64` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function crc64_iso(data: [u8]) -> u64`, called `hash.crc64_iso(data)`: The CRC-64 of `data` by ISO's polynomial, Go's `crc64.ISO`: the register starts and ends with every bit flipped, as Go's does.
- `function crc64_iso_text(s: str) -> u64`, called `hash.crc64_iso_text(s)`: The CRC-64 of the bytes of `s` by ISO's polynomial, what `crc64_iso` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function crc64_ecma(data: [u8]) -> u64`, called `hash.crc64_ecma(data)`: The CRC-64 of `data` by ECMA-182's polynomial, Go's `crc64.ECMA` and the check of the `xz` format.
- `function crc64_ecma_text(s: str) -> u64`, called `hash.crc64_ecma_text(s)`: The CRC-64 of the bytes of `s` by ECMA-182's polynomial, what `crc64_ecma` answers for its UTF-8.
- `variant Algorithm32 = .crc32 | .crc32c | .crc32_poly(poly: u32) | .adler32 | .fnv1_32 | .fnv1a_32`: Which checksum or hash of 32 bits a `State32` computes.
- `record State32(algorithm: Algorithm32, value: u32, table: [i64])`: A checksum or hash of 32 bits computed in steps: the caller holds it and feeds it piece by piece with `update32` and `update32_text`, and its `value` is at every moment what feeding all the pieces at once answers.
- `function start32(algorithm: Algorithm32) -> State32`, called `hash.start32(algorithm)`: A state of `algorithm` that has been fed nothing, its `value` the checksum or hash of no bytes.
- `function resume32(algorithm: Algorithm32, value: u32) -> State32`, called `hash.resume32(algorithm, value)`: A state of `algorithm` that goes on from `value`, the checksum or hash of bytes fed before: what Go's `crc32.Update` and Python's `zlib.crc32` and `zlib.adler32` take as the value to start from.
- `function update32(@state: State32, data: [u8])`, called `hash.update32(@state, data)`: Feeds `data` to `state`, whose `value` becomes the checksum or hash of what it was fed before and then `data`.
- `function update32_text(@state: State32, s: str)`, called `hash.update32_text(@state, s)`: Feeds the bytes of `s` to `state`, as `update32` feeds its UTF-8.
- `variant Algorithm64 = .crc64_iso | .crc64_ecma | .crc64_poly(poly: u64) | .fnv1_64 | .fnv1a_64`: Which checksum or hash of 64 bits a `State64` computes.
- `record State64(algorithm: Algorithm64, value: u64, table: [i64])`: A checksum or hash of 64 bits computed in steps: the caller holds it and feeds it piece by piece with `update64` and `update64_text`, and its `value` is at every moment what feeding all the pieces at once answers.
- `function start64(algorithm: Algorithm64) -> State64`, called `hash.start64(algorithm)`: A state of `algorithm` that has been fed nothing, its `value` the checksum or hash of no bytes.
- `function resume64(algorithm: Algorithm64, value: u64) -> State64`, called `hash.resume64(algorithm, value)`: A state of `algorithm` that goes on from `value`, the checksum or hash of bytes fed before: what Go's `crc64.Update` takes as the value to start from.
- `function update64(@state: State64, data: [u8])`, called `hash.update64(@state, data)`: Feeds `data` to `state`, whose `value` becomes the checksum or hash of what it was fed before and then `data`.
- `function update64_text(@state: State64, s: str)`, called `hash.update64_text(@state, s)`: Feeds the bytes of `s` to `state`, as `update64` feeds its UTF-8.
- `function xxh32(data: [u8], seed: u32) -> u32`, called `hash.xxh32(data, seed)`: xxHash's XXH32 of `data` with `seed`: a fast hash of 32 bits, the checksum of LZ4's frames, what Python's `xxhash.xxh32_intdigest` answers.
- `function xxh32_text(s: str, seed: u32) -> u32`, called `hash.xxh32_text(s, seed)`: The XXH32 of the bytes of `s` with `seed`, what `xxh32` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function xxh64(data: [u8], seed: u64) -> u64`, called `hash.xxh64(data, seed)`: xxHash's XXH64 of `data` with `seed`: a fast hash of 64 bits, whose low 32 bits are a Zstandard frame's checksum, what Python's `xxhash.xxh64_intdigest` answers.
- `function xxh64_text(s: str, seed: u64) -> u64`, called `hash.xxh64_text(s, seed)`: The XXH64 of the bytes of `s` with `seed`, what `xxh64` answers for its UTF-8.
- `record Xxh32(seed: u32, value: u32, lanes: [i64], held: [u8], fed: i64)`: An XXH32 computed in steps: the caller holds it and feeds it piece by piece with `update_xxh32` and `update_xxh32_text`, and its `value` is at every moment what `xxh32` answers for all the pieces at once.
- `function start_xxh32(seed: u32) -> Xxh32`, called `hash.start_xxh32(seed)`: An XXH32 with `seed` that has been fed nothing, its `value` the XXH32 of no bytes.
- `function update_xxh32(@state: Xxh32, data: [u8])`, called `hash.update_xxh32(@state, data)`: Feeds `data` to `state`, whose `value` becomes the XXH32 of what it was fed before and then `data`.
- `function update_xxh32_text(@state: Xxh32, s: str)`, called `hash.update_xxh32_text(@state, s)`: Feeds the bytes of `s` to `state`, as `update_xxh32` feeds its UTF-8.
- `record Xxh64(seed: u64, value: u64, lanes: [i64], held: [u8], fed: i64)`: An XXH64 computed in steps, as an `Xxh32` computes an XXH32: made by `start_xxh64`, fed by `update_xxh64` and `update_xxh64_text`, its `value` at every moment what `xxh64` answers for all the pieces at once.
- `function start_xxh64(seed: u64) -> Xxh64`, called `hash.start_xxh64(seed)`: An XXH64 with `seed` that has been fed nothing, its `value` the XXH64 of no bytes.
- `function update_xxh64(@state: Xxh64, data: [u8])`, called `hash.update_xxh64(@state, data)`: Feeds `data` to `state`, whose `value` becomes the XXH64 of what it was fed before and then `data`.
- `function update_xxh64_text(@state: Xxh64, s: str)`, called `hash.update_xxh64_text(@state, s)`: Feeds the bytes of `s` to `state`, as `update_xxh64` feeds its UTF-8.


### sets

Layer 0, named `use <rebel>/sets`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/sets/).

Sets of values, kept in a `{K: bool}`: the language has no set type, and a map's keys are already distinct and found by hashing, so a set is a map whose keys are its elements, each under `true`.

- `function from_list<K>(elements: [K]) -> {K: bool}`, called `sets.from_list(elements)`: A set of the elements of `elements`.
- `function contains<K>(s: {K: bool}, element: K) -> bool`, called `sets.contains(s, element)`: Whether `s` holds `element`.
- `function to_list<K>(s: {K: bool}) -> [K]`, called `sets.to_list(s)`: The elements of `s` as a list, in the order they were first added.
- `function add<K>(s: {K: bool}, element: K) -> {K: bool}`, called `sets.add(s, element)`: `s` with `element` added.
- `function add_all<K>(s: {K: bool}, elements: [K]) -> {K: bool}`, called `sets.add_all(s, elements)`: `s` with every element of `elements` added.
- `function remove<K>(s: {K: bool}, element: K) -> {K: bool}`, called `sets.remove(s, element)`: `s` without `element`.
- `function remove_all<K>(s: {K: bool}, elements: [K]) -> {K: bool}`, called `sets.remove_all(s, elements)`: `s` without any element of `elements`.
- `function keep_where<K>(s: {K: bool}, keeps: (function(K) -> bool)) -> {K: bool}`, called `sets.keep_where(s, keeps)`: The elements of `s` that `keeps` accepts.
- `function remove_where<K>(s: {K: bool}, removes: (function(K) -> bool)) -> {K: bool}`, called `sets.remove_where(s, removes)`: `s` without the elements `removes` accepts.
- `function union_of<K>(s: {K: bool}, other: {K: bool}) -> {K: bool}`, called `sets.union_of(s: s, other: other)`: The union of `s` and `other`: every element either holds.
- `function intersection<K>(s: {K: bool}, other: {K: bool}) -> {K: bool}`, called `sets.intersection(s: s, other: other)`: The intersection of `s` and `other`: the elements both hold.
- `function difference<K>(s: {K: bool}, other: {K: bool}) -> {K: bool}`, called `sets.difference(s: s, other: other)`: The difference of `s` and `other`: the elements of `s` that `other` does not hold.
- `function symmetric_difference<K>(s: {K: bool}, other: {K: bool}) -> {K: bool}`, called `sets.symmetric_difference(s: s, other: other)`: The symmetric difference of `s` and `other`: the elements one holds and the other does not.
- `function union_all<K>(s: {K: bool}, others: [{K: bool}]) -> {K: bool}`, called `sets.union_all(s, others)`: The union of `s` and every set of `others`: every element any of them holds.
- `function intersection_all<K>(s: {K: bool}, others: [{K: bool}]) -> {K: bool}`, called `sets.intersection_all(s, others)`: The intersection of `s` and every set of `others`: the elements all of them hold.
- `function difference_all<K>(s: {K: bool}, others: [{K: bool}]) -> {K: bool}`, called `sets.difference_all(s, others)`: The elements of `s` that no set of `others` holds.
- `function is_subset<K>(s: {K: bool}, other: {K: bool}) -> bool`, called `sets.is_subset(s: s, other: other)`: Whether every element of `s` is an element of `other`.
- `function is_superset<K>(s: {K: bool}, other: {K: bool}) -> bool`, called `sets.is_superset(s: s, other: other)`: Whether every element of `other` is an element of `s`.
- `function is_proper_subset<K>(s: {K: bool}, other: {K: bool}) -> bool`, called `sets.is_proper_subset(s: s, other: other)`: Whether `s` is a subset of `other` and `other` holds an element `s` does not.
- `function is_proper_superset<K>(s: {K: bool}, other: {K: bool}) -> bool`, called `sets.is_proper_superset(s: s, other: other)`: Whether `s` is a superset of `other` and holds an element `other` does not.
- `function is_disjoint<K>(s: {K: bool}, other: {K: bool}) -> bool`, called `sets.is_disjoint(s: s, other: other)`: Whether `s` and `other` share no element.


### errors

Layer 0, named `use <rebel>/errors`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/errors/).

Failures told well: words added to a failure as it travels up, its code kept; several failures joined into one; a failure told to a person, in one line or as an indented chain; and one dropped on purpose where it cannot matter.

- `function context<T>(r: T?, what: str) -> T?`, called `errors.context(r, what)`: `r` with `what` written before its message where it fails: the message becomes `what: <the old message>` and the code stays. Fails where `r` fails, with its code.
- `function context_by<T, A>(r: T?, describe: (function(A) -> str), subject: A) -> T?`, called `errors.context_by(r, describe, subject)`: `r` with the words `describe` makes of `subject` written before its message where it fails; where `r` holds a value `describe` is not called, so words that cost something to build are built only for a failure. Fails where `r` fails, with its code.
- `function with_code<T>(r: T?, code: str) -> T?`, called `errors.with_code(r, code)`: `r` with `code` in place of its code where it fails; the message stays. Fails where `r` fails, with `code`.
- `function combine<T>(results: [T?]) -> ()?`, called `errors.combine(results)`: The failures of `results` joined into one, or `ok()` where none fails. Fails where any result fails, as above.
- `function collect<T>(results: [T?]) -> [T]?`, called `errors.collect(results)`: Every value of `results` in order, where none fails; else their failures joined as `combine` joins them. Fails where any result fails: with that failure as it is where it is the only one, else with the joined failure `combine` answers.
- `function discard_value<T>(r: T?) -> ()?`, called `errors.discard_value(r)`: `r` with its value dropped: `ok()` where it holds one, the same failure where it fails. Fails where `r` fails, with its code and its message.
- `function ignore(r: ()?)`, called `errors.ignore(r)`: Nothing: the failure `r` may hold is dropped, for a failure that cannot change what the program does next.
- `function chain_of<T>(r: T?) -> [str]`, called `errors.chain_of(r)`: The links of the message of `r`, the outermost first: what each `context` wrote, then the message the failure began with.
- `function parts_of<T>(r: T?) -> [()?]`, called `errors.parts_of(r)`: The failures a joined failure holds, each with its own code and message; a failure that joins nothing is its own one part.
- `function has_code<T>(r: T?, code: str) -> bool`, called `errors.has_code(r, code)`: Whether `r` fails with `code`, or joins, at any depth, a failure that does.
- `function format_line<T>(r: T?) -> str`, called `errors.format_line(r)`: The failure of `r` told in one line as an abort tells it, `<code>: <message>`.
- `function format_chain<T>(r: T?) -> str`, called `errors.format_chain(r)`: The failure of `r` told as an indented chain, one link a line: its code and its outermost link first, then each link that caused it.


### threads

Layer 0, named `use <rebel>/threads`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/threads/).

A function run on another thread and waited for, through the language's own `spawn` and `t.wait()` (spec § 11), under names of this package's own and with a pool that bounds how many run at once.

- `constant LIMIT: str`, value `pool.LIMIT`: The code of a thread the system, or the runtime's bound of threads running at once, refused to start: `start`, `start_sized`, `start_text`, `run_all` and `run_all_text` fail with it.
- `record Thread(running: (thread i64))`: A thread `start` or `start_sized` started, which the program owes `wait`.
- `function start(body: (function(i64) -> i64), arg: i64) -> Thread?`, called `threads.start(body, arg)`: Starts `body` on `arg` on a thread of its own and answers it, running. Fails `limit`.
- `function start_sized(body: (function(i64) -> i64), arg: i64, stack: i64) -> Thread?`, called `threads.start_sized(body, arg: arg, stack: stack)`: Starts `body` on `arg` on a thread with a stack of at least `stack` bytes, and answers it, running. Fails `limit`.
- `function wait(@thread: Thread) -> i64`, called `threads.wait(@thread)`: Waits for `thread` to end and answers what its body returned.
- `record TextThread(running: (thread str))`: A thread `start_text` started, which the program owes `wait_text`.
- `function start_text(body: (function(str) -> str), arg: str) -> TextThread?`, called `threads.start_text(body, arg)`: Starts `body` on a copy of `arg` on a thread of its own and answers it, running. Fails `limit`.
- `function wait_text(@thread: TextThread) -> str`, called `threads.wait_text(@thread)`: Waits for `thread` to end and answers what its body returned.
- `function run_all(body: (function(i64) -> i64), values: [i64], workers: i64) -> [i64]?`, called `threads.run_all(body, values, workers)`: `body` of each of `values`, each run on a thread, the answers in the order of `values`. Fails `limit`.
- `function run_all_text(body: (function(str) -> str), values: [str], workers: i64) -> [str]?`, called `threads.run_all_text(body, values, workers)`: `body` of a copy of each of `values`, each run on a thread, the answers in the order of `values`. Fails `limit`.
- `function max_running() -> i64`, called `threads.max_running()`: How many threads the runtime runs at once, the program's started and not yet waited for among them: past it a start fails `limit`.


### containers/ordered

Layer 0, named `use <rebel>/containers/ordered`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/containers/ordered/).

An ordered map and an ordered set: keys kept in the order a function of the program gives, each found, added and taken out at a cost of the logarithm of the size, with the keys at or around a bound, a range walked in order, and the key of a rank and the rank of a key.

- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `codes.NOT_FOUND`: The code of a search that found nothing, which every function of this package whose `Fails` names `not_found` answers.
- `record Ordered(tree: tree.Tree)`: The shape of an ordered map or an ordered set: a binary search tree balanced by the sizes of its branches, whose nodes are the slots of the program's lists, a key at each slot of a key list and, for a map, its value at the same slot of a value list.
- `function new_map() -> Ordered`, called `ordered.new_map()`: An empty ordered map, whose program keeps an empty key list and an empty value list beside it.
- `function new_set() -> Ordered`, called `ordered.new_set()`: An empty ordered set, whose program keeps an empty key list beside it.
- `function size(ordered: Ordered) -> i64`, called `ordered.size(ordered)`: How many keys an ordered map or set holds.
- `function put<K, V>(@ordered: Ordered, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], key: K, value: V, less: (function(a: K, b: K) -> bool))`, called `ordered.put(@ordered, @key_list, @value_list, key, value, less)`: Puts `value` under `key` in an ordered map, replacing the value of a key it holds.
- `function get<K, V>(ordered: Ordered, key_list: [K] lent, value_list: [V] lent, key: K, less: (function(a: K, b: K) -> bool)) -> V?`, called `ordered.get(ordered, key_list, value_list, key, less)`: The value under `key` in an ordered map. Fails `not_found`.
- `function remove<K, V>(@ordered: Ordered, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], key: K, less: (function(a: K, b: K) -> bool)) -> V?`, called `ordered.remove(@ordered, @key_list, @value_list, key, less)`: Takes `key` and its value out of an ordered map, answering the value. Fails `not_found`.
- `function remove_at<K, V>(@ordered: Ordered, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], at: i64)`, called `ordered.remove_at(@ordered, @key_list, @value_list, at)`: Takes the entry at slot `at` out of an ordered map.
- `function add<K>(@ordered: Ordered, @key_list: [K], key: K, less: (function(a: K, b: K) -> bool)) -> bool`, called `ordered.add(@ordered, @key_list, key, less)`: Adds `key` to an ordered set, answering whether it was new.
- `function discard<K>(@ordered: Ordered, @key_list: [K], key: K, less: (function(a: K, b: K) -> bool)) -> bool`, called `ordered.discard(@ordered, @key_list, key, less)`: Takes `key` out of an ordered set, answering whether it was there.
- `function discard_at<K>(@ordered: Ordered, @key_list: [K], at: i64)`, called `ordered.discard_at(@ordered, @key_list, at)`: Takes the key at slot `at` out of an ordered set.
- `function contains<K>(ordered: Ordered, key_list: [K] lent, key: K, less: (function(a: K, b: K) -> bool)) -> bool`, called `ordered.contains(ordered, key_list, key, less)`: Whether an ordered map or set holds a key equal to `key`.
- `function slot_of<K>(ordered: Ordered, key_list: [K] lent, key: K, less: (function(a: K, b: K) -> bool)) -> i64?`, called `ordered.slot_of(ordered, key_list, key, less)`: The slot of the key equal to `key` in an ordered map or set. Fails `not_found`.
- `function floor_slot<K>(ordered: Ordered, key_list: [K] lent, key: K, less: (function(a: K, b: K) -> bool)) -> i64?`, called `ordered.floor_slot(ordered, key_list, key, less)`: The slot of the largest key at or before `key`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function ceiling_slot<K>(ordered: Ordered, key_list: [K] lent, key: K, less: (function(a: K, b: K) -> bool)) -> i64?`, called `ordered.ceiling_slot(ordered, key_list, key, less)`: The slot of the smallest key at or after `key`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function lower_slot<K>(ordered: Ordered, key_list: [K] lent, key: K, less: (function(a: K, b: K) -> bool)) -> i64?`, called `ordered.lower_slot(ordered, key_list, key, less)`: The slot of the largest key strictly before `key`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function higher_slot<K>(ordered: Ordered, key_list: [K] lent, key: K, less: (function(a: K, b: K) -> bool)) -> i64?`, called `ordered.higher_slot(ordered, key_list, key, less)`: The slot of the smallest key strictly after `key`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function rank_of<K>(ordered: Ordered, key_list: [K] lent, key: K, less: (function(a: K, b: K) -> bool)) -> i64`, called `ordered.rank_of(ordered, key_list, key, less)`: How many keys of an ordered map or set go before `key`: its rank, held or not.
- `function slot_at_rank(ordered: Ordered, rank: i64) -> i64?`, called `ordered.slot_at_rank(ordered, rank)`: The slot of the key with `rank` keys before it. Fails `not_found`.
- `function first_slot(ordered: Ordered) -> i64?`, called `ordered.first_slot(ordered)`: The slot of the smallest key. Fails `not_found`.
- `function last_slot(ordered: Ordered) -> i64?`, called `ordered.last_slot(ordered)`: The slot of the largest key. Fails `not_found`.
- `function next_slot(ordered: Ordered, at: i64) -> i64?`, called `ordered.next_slot(ordered, at)`: The slot of the key just after the one at `at`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function previous_slot(ordered: Ordered, at: i64) -> i64?`, called `ordered.previous_slot(ordered, at)`: The slot of the key just before the one at `at`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function slots(ordered: Ordered) -> [i64]`, called `ordered.slots(ordered)`: Every slot in the order of the keys.
- `function slots_between<K>(ordered: Ordered, key_list: [K] lent, from: K, to: K, less: (function(a: K, b: K) -> bool)) -> [i64]`, called `ordered.slots_between(ordered, key_list, from: from, to: to, less)`: The slots of the keys from `from` up to `to`, `to` left out, in order.
- `function keys_in_order<K>(ordered: Ordered, key_list: [K] lent) -> [K]`, called `ordered.keys_in_order(ordered, key_list)`: The keys of an ordered map or set in their order.
- `function clear<K, V>(@ordered: Ordered, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V])`, called `ordered.clear(@ordered, @key_list, @value_list)`: Empties an ordered map, every key and value let go.
- `function clear_set<K>(@ordered: Ordered, @key_list: [K])`, called `ordered.clear_set(@ordered, @key_list)`: Empties an ordered set, every key let go.


### containers/deque

Layer 0, named `use <rebel>/containers/deque`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/containers/deque/).

A double-ended queue: items put in and taken out at either end in constant time over many calls, read and written by their place from the front, and, where it is bounded, the oldest dropped as new ones come.

- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `codes.NOT_FOUND`: The code of a search that found nothing, which every function of this package whose `Fails` names `not_found` answers.
- `constant INVALID: str`, value `codes.INVALID`: The code of an item put into a full bounded deque, which `insert` answers.
- `record Deque(ring: ring.Ring)`: The shape of a double-ended queue: a ring over the slots of the program's item list, so an item goes in or comes out at either end without the others moving.
- `function new() -> Deque`, called `deque.new()`: An empty deque without a bound, whose program keeps an empty item list beside it.
- `function new_bounded(most: i64) -> Deque`, called `deque.new_bounded(most)`: An empty deque that holds at most `most` items, the last ones pushed.
- `function over<T>(items: [T] lent) -> Deque`, called `deque.over(items)`: The shape of a deque holding `items`, the first one at the front: the list the program has becomes the deque's item list.
- `function size(deque: Deque) -> i64`, called `deque.size(deque)`: How many items a deque holds.
- `function capacity(deque: Deque) -> i64?`, called `deque.capacity(deque)`: The most items a bounded deque holds. Fails `not_found`.
- `function push_back<T>(@deque: Deque, @items: [T], value: T)`, called `deque.push_back(@deque, @items, value)`: Adds `value` at the back of a deque.
- `function push_front<T>(@deque: Deque, @items: [T], value: T)`, called `deque.push_front(@deque, @items, value)`: Adds `value` at the front of a deque.
- `function pop_back<T>(@deque: Deque, @items: [T]) -> T?`, called `deque.pop_back(@deque, @items)`: Takes the back item out of a deque and answers it. Fails `not_found`.
- `function pop_front<T>(@deque: Deque, @items: [T]) -> T?`, called `deque.pop_front(@deque, @items)`: Takes the front item out of a deque and answers it. Fails `not_found`.
- `function first<T>(deque: Deque, items: [T] lent) -> T?`, called `deque.first(deque, items)`: The front item of a deque, left in. Fails `not_found`.
- `function last<T>(deque: Deque, items: [T] lent) -> T?`, called `deque.last(deque, items)`: The back item of a deque, left in. Fails `not_found`.
- `function get<T>(deque: Deque, items: [T] lent, at: i64) -> T?`, called `deque.get(deque, items, at)`: The item at place `at` of a deque, counted from the front. Fails `not_found`.
- `function put<T>(deque: Deque, @items: [T], at: i64, value: T)`, called `deque.put(deque, @items, at, value)`: Writes `value` over the item at place `at` of a deque, counted from the front.
- `function insert<T>(@deque: Deque, @items: [T], at: i64, value: T) -> ()?`, called `deque.insert(@deque, @items, at, value)`: Puts `value` at place `at` of a deque, counted from the front, the items from there on moving one place back. Fails `invalid`.
- `function remove_at<T>(@deque: Deque, @items: [T], at: i64) -> T`, called `deque.remove_at(@deque, @items, at)`: Takes out the item at place `at` of a deque, counted from the front, and answers it, the items after it moving one place forward.
- `function rotate_left<T>(@deque: Deque, @items: [T], by: i64)`, called `deque.rotate_left(@deque, @items, by)`: Moves the first `by` items of a deque to its back, in their order.
- `function rotate_right<T>(@deque: Deque, @items: [T], by: i64)`, called `deque.rotate_right(@deque, @items, by)`: Moves the last `by` items of a deque to its front, in their order: Python's `deque.rotate`.
- `function to_list<T>(deque: Deque, items: [T] lent) -> [T]`, called `deque.to_list(deque, items)`: The items of a deque, front to back.
- `function clear<T>(@deque: Deque, @items: [T])`, called `deque.clear(@deque, @items)`: Empties a deque, keeping its bound.


### containers/bits

Layer 0, named `use <rebel>/containers/bits`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/containers/bits/).

A set of bits of a fixed size: bits set, cleared and turned over one at a time or a run at a time, counted, combined with another set, scanned for the next set or clear one, and read and written as places, bytes, words or text.

- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `codes.NOT_FOUND`: The code of a search that found nothing, which every function of this package whose `Fails` names `not_found` answers.
- `constant INVALID: str`, value `codes.INVALID`: The code of a text that is not bits, which `parse` answers.
- `record Bits(words: bitwords.Words)`: A set of bits of a fixed size, numbered from 0, held 64 to a word.
- `function new(count: i64) -> Bits`, called `bits.new(count)`: A set of `count` bits, every one clear.
- `function size(bits: Bits) -> i64`, called `bits.size(bits)`: How many bits a set holds, set or clear.
- `function is_set(bits: Bits, at: i64) -> bool`, called `bits.is_set(bits, at)`: Whether bit `at` is set.
- `function set_bit(@bits: Bits, at: i64)`, called `bits.set_bit(@bits, at)`: Sets bit `at`.
- `function clear_bit(@bits: Bits, at: i64)`, called `bits.clear_bit(@bits, at)`: Clears bit `at`.
- `function flip_bit(@bits: Bits, at: i64)`, called `bits.flip_bit(@bits, at)`: Turns bit `at` over.
- `function put_bit(@bits: Bits, at: i64, value: bool)`, called `bits.put_bit(@bits, at, value)`: Sets bit `at` where `value` is true and clears it where false.
- `function set_range(@bits: Bits, from: i64, to: i64)`, called `bits.set_range(@bits, from: from, to: to)`: Sets the bits from `from` up to `to`, `to` left out.
- `function clear_range(@bits: Bits, from: i64, to: i64)`, called `bits.clear_range(@bits, from: from, to: to)`: Clears the bits from `from` up to `to`, `to` left out.
- `function flip_range(@bits: Bits, from: i64, to: i64)`, called `bits.flip_range(@bits, from: from, to: to)`: Turns over the bits from `from` up to `to`, `to` left out.
- `function count_ones(bits: Bits) -> i64`, called `bits.count_ones(bits)`: How many bits of a set are set.
- `function intersection(bits: Bits, other: Bits) -> Bits`, called `bits.intersection(bits: bits, other: other)`: The bits set in both sets: Java's `BitSet.and`, named as `sets` names it.
- `function union_of(bits: Bits, other: Bits) -> Bits`, called `bits.union_of(bits: bits, other: other)`: The bits set in either set: Java's `BitSet.or`, named as `sets` names it.
- `function symmetric_difference(bits: Bits, other: Bits) -> Bits`, called `bits.symmetric_difference(bits: bits, other: other)`: The bits set in one set and not the other: Java's `BitSet.xor`, named as `sets` names it.
- `function difference(bits: Bits, other: Bits) -> Bits`, called `bits.difference(bits: bits, other: other)`: The bits set in `bits` and clear in `other`: Java's `BitSet.andNot`, named as `sets` names it.
- `function complement(bits: Bits) -> Bits`, called `bits.complement(bits)`: Every bit of a set turned over, within its size: .NET's `BitArray.Not`, and Java's `BitSet.flip` over the whole size.
- `function is_disjoint(bits: Bits, other: Bits) -> bool`, called `bits.is_disjoint(bits: bits, other: other)`: Whether no bit is set in both sets.
- `function is_subset(bits: Bits, other: Bits) -> bool`, called `bits.is_subset(bits: bits, other: other)`: Whether every bit set in `bits` is set in `other`.
- `function is_clear(bits: Bits) -> bool`, called `bits.is_clear(bits)`: Whether no bit of a set is set.
- `function is_full(bits: Bits) -> bool`, called `bits.is_full(bits)`: Whether every bit of a set is set.
- `function next_set(bits: Bits, from: i64) -> i64?`, called `bits.next_set(bits, from)`: The first set bit at or after `from`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function next_clear(bits: Bits, from: i64) -> i64?`, called `bits.next_clear(bits, from)`: The first clear bit at or after `from`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function previous_set(bits: Bits, from: i64) -> i64?`, called `bits.previous_set(bits, from)`: The last set bit at or before `from`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function previous_clear(bits: Bits, from: i64) -> i64?`, called `bits.previous_clear(bits, from)`: The last clear bit at or before `from`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function to_indices(bits: Bits) -> [i64]`, called `bits.to_indices(bits)`: The set bits of a set, from the smallest.
- `function from_indices(count: i64, indices: [i64]) -> Bits`, called `bits.from_indices(count, indices)`: A set of `count` bits with the bits of `indices` set.
- `function to_bytes(bits: Bits) -> [u8]`, called `bits.to_bytes(bits)`: The bits of a set as bytes, bit `i` in byte `i / 8` at the place of value `2` to the power `i % 8`: the order of Java's `BitSet.toByteArray`.
- `function from_bytes(data: [u8]) -> Bits`, called `bits.from_bytes(data)`: The set of `data.len() * 8` bits whose bytes are `data`, in the order of `to_bytes`.
- `function to_words(bits: Bits) -> [i64]`, called `bits.to_words(bits)`: The words of a set, bit `i` at bit `i % 64` of word `i / 64`, the sign bit being bit 63: Java's `BitSet.toLongArray` order.
- `function from_words(count: i64, words: [i64]) -> Bits`, called `bits.from_words(count, words)`: A set of `count` bits read from `words` in the order of `to_words`.
- `function format(bits: Bits) -> str`, called `bits.format(bits)`: A set written as one character a bit, `0` or `1`, bit 0 first.
- `function parse(text: str) -> Bits?`, called `bits.parse(text)`: The set `text` writes, one character a bit, `0` or `1`, bit 0 first. Fails `invalid`.
- `function with_size(bits: Bits, count: i64) -> Bits`, called `bits.with_size(bits, count)`: A copy of a set made `count` bits long: bits added are clear, bits past the new size dropped.
- `function part(bits: Bits, from: i64, to: i64) -> Bits`, called `bits.part(bits, from: from, to: to)`: The bits from `from` up to `to`, `to` left out, as a set of their own whose bit 0 is bit `from`.
- `function shift_up(bits: Bits, by: i64) -> Bits`, called `bits.shift_up(bits, by)`: A copy of a set with each bit `i` moved to `i + by`, bits moved past the size dropped and the first `by` bits clear.
- `function shift_down(bits: Bits, by: i64) -> Bits`, called `bits.shift_down(bits, by)`: A copy of a set with each bit `i` moved to `i - by`, the first `by` bits dropped and the last `by` bits clear.


### containers/cache

Layer 0, named `use <rebel>/containers/cache`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/containers/cache/).

A cache of a capacity that forgets the entry used least recently to make room and, where it has a time to live, every entry written longer ago than that.

- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `codes.NOT_FOUND`: The code of a search that found nothing, which every function of this package whose `Fails` names `not_found` answers.
- `record Cache(entries: lru.Lru)`: The shape of a cache that holds at most its capacity of entries, forgetting the one used least recently to make room and, where it has a time to live, every entry written longer ago than that.
- `function new(most: i64) -> Cache`, called `cache.new(most)`: An empty cache of at most `most` entries whose entries never expire.
- `function new_with_ttl(most: i64, ttl: i64) -> Cache`, called `cache.new_with_ttl(most: most, ttl: ttl)`: An empty cache of at most `most` entries, each forgotten `ttl` after it was last written.
- `function size(cache: Cache) -> i64`, called `cache.size(cache)`: How many entries a cache holds, those expired since the last call that was given the time included.
- `function capacity(cache: Cache) -> i64`, called `cache.capacity(cache)`: The most entries a cache holds.
- `function put<K, V>(@cache: Cache, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], @lookup: {K: i64}, key: K, value: V, now: i64)`, called `cache.put(@cache, @key_list, @value_list, @lookup, key, value, now)`: Puts `value` under `key`, the entry becoming the one used last and, with a time to live, written at `now`.
- `function get<K, V>(@cache: Cache, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], @lookup: {K: i64}, key: K, now: i64) -> V?`, called `cache.get(@cache, @key_list, @value_list, @lookup, key, now)`: The value under `key`, the entry becoming the one used last. Fails `not_found`.
- `function peek<K, V>(cache: Cache, value_list: [V] lent, lookup: {K: i64} lent, key: K, now: i64) -> V?`, called `cache.peek(cache, value_list, lookup, key, now)`: The value under `key`, the cache left as it was: no use is counted and nothing is forgotten. Fails `not_found`.
- `function contains<K>(cache: Cache, lookup: {K: i64} lent, key: K, now: i64) -> bool`, called `cache.contains(cache, lookup, key, now)`: Whether a cache holds a live entry under `key`, counting no use.
- `function remove<K, V>(@cache: Cache, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], @lookup: {K: i64}, key: K) -> V?`, called `cache.remove(@cache, @key_list, @value_list, @lookup, key)`: Takes the entry under `key` out of a cache and answers its value. Fails `not_found`.
- `function expire<K, V>(@cache: Cache, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], @lookup: {K: i64}, now: i64)`, called `cache.expire(@cache, @key_list, @value_list, @lookup, now)`: Forgets every entry expired at `now`.
- `function slots(cache: Cache) -> [i64]`, called `cache.slots(cache)`: The slots of a cache's entries, the one used last first.
- `function oldest_slot(cache: Cache) -> i64?`, called `cache.oldest_slot(cache)`: The slot of the entry used least recently, the next one a full cache forgets. Fails `not_found`.
- `function clear<K, V>(@cache: Cache, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], @lookup: {K: i64})`, called `cache.clear(@cache, @key_list, @value_list, @lookup)`: Empties a cache, keeping its capacity and time to live.


### containers/indexed

Layer 0, named `use <rebel>/containers/indexed`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/containers/indexed/).

A map that keeps its keys in the order they were first put, each at a position from 0, as Rust's indexmap and Python's `dict` do: an entry found by its key or by its position, taken out by swapping the last one in or by shifting the rest, moved, swapped and sorted.

- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `codes.NOT_FOUND`: The code of a search that found nothing, which every function of this package whose `Fails` names `not_found` answers.
- `record Indexed(table: table.Table)`: The shape of a map that keeps its keys in the order they were first put, each at a position from 0, as Rust's indexmap and Python's `dict` do: a key at each position of the program's key list, its value at the same position of its value list, and the program's lookup map naming each key's position.
- `function new() -> Indexed`, called `indexed.new()`: An empty map that keeps its order, whose program keeps an empty key list, an empty value list and an empty lookup map beside it.
- `function size(indexed: Indexed) -> i64`, called `indexed.size(indexed)`: How many entries a map that keeps its order holds.
- `function put<K, V>(@indexed: Indexed, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], @lookup: {K: i64}, key: K, value: V) -> i64`, called `indexed.put(@indexed, @key_list, @value_list, @lookup, key, value)`: Puts `value` under `key` and answers its position: a new key goes last, a held one keeps its place and has its value replaced.
- `function get<K, V>(indexed: Indexed, value_list: [V] lent, lookup: {K: i64} lent, key: K) -> V?`, called `indexed.get(indexed, value_list, lookup, key)`: The value under `key`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function position_of<K>(indexed: Indexed, lookup: {K: i64} lent, key: K) -> i64?`, called `indexed.position_of(indexed, lookup, key)`: The position of `key`, from 0, in the order the keys were first put. Fails `not_found`.
- `function contains<K>(indexed: Indexed, lookup: {K: i64} lent, key: K) -> bool`, called `indexed.contains(indexed, lookup, key)`: Whether the map holds an entry under `key`.
- `function key_at<K>(indexed: Indexed, key_list: [K] lent, at: i64) -> K`, called `indexed.key_at(indexed, key_list, at)`: The key at position `at`.
- `function value_at<V>(indexed: Indexed, value_list: [V] lent, at: i64) -> V`, called `indexed.value_at(indexed, value_list, at)`: The value at position `at`.
- `function swap_remove<K, V>(@indexed: Indexed, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], @lookup: {K: i64}, key: K) -> V?`, called `indexed.swap_remove(@indexed, @key_list, @value_list, @lookup, key)`: Takes `key` out and answers its value, the last entry moving into its position: the order changes, and it costs a constant. Fails `not_found`.
- `function shift_remove<K, V>(@indexed: Indexed, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], @lookup: {K: i64}, key: K) -> V?`, called `indexed.shift_remove(@indexed, @key_list, @value_list, @lookup, key)`: Takes `key` out and answers its value, every entry after it moving one position forward: the order is kept, at the cost of the entries moved. Fails `not_found`.
- `function swap_remove_at<K, V>(@indexed: Indexed, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], @lookup: {K: i64}, at: i64)`, called `indexed.swap_remove_at(@indexed, @key_list, @value_list, @lookup, at)`: Takes the entry at position `at` out, the last entry moving into it.
- `function shift_remove_at<K, V>(@indexed: Indexed, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], @lookup: {K: i64}, at: i64)`, called `indexed.shift_remove_at(@indexed, @key_list, @value_list, @lookup, at)`: Takes the entry at position `at` out, every entry after it moving one position forward.
- `function move<K, V>(indexed: Indexed, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], @lookup: {K: i64}, from: i64, to: i64)`, called `indexed.move(indexed, @key_list, @value_list, @lookup, from: from, to: to)`: Moves the entry at position `from` to position `to`, the entries between moving one position to make room.
- `function swap<K, V>(indexed: Indexed, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], @lookup: {K: i64}, at: i64, with: i64)`, called `indexed.swap(indexed, @key_list, @value_list, @lookup, at: at, with: with)`: Swaps the entries at positions `at` and `with`.
- `function sort_by_key<K, V>(@indexed: Indexed, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], @lookup: {K: i64}, less: (function(a: K, b: K) -> bool))`, called `indexed.sort_by_key(@indexed, @key_list, @value_list, @lookup, less)`: Puts the entries in the order of their keys by `less`, entries of equal keys keeping their order.
- `function keys_in_order<K>(indexed: Indexed, key_list: [K] lent) -> [K]`, called `indexed.keys_in_order(indexed, key_list)`: The keys in their order.
- `function values<V>(indexed: Indexed, value_list: [V] lent) -> [V]`, called `indexed.values(indexed, value_list)`: The values in the order of their keys.
- `function clear<K, V>(@indexed: Indexed, @key_list: [K], @value_list: [V], @lookup: {K: i64})`, called `indexed.clear(@indexed, @key_list, @value_list, @lookup)`: Empties a map that keeps its order.


### containers/heap

Layer 0, named `use <rebel>/containers/heap`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/containers/heap/).

A heap, the priority queue: a plain `[T]` the program owns, kept so that its element at 0 is one nothing goes before by the program's order, an element going in or coming out at a cost of the logarithm of the length.

- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `codes.NOT_FOUND`: The code of an empty heap asked for an element, which `pop` and `peek` answer.
- `function heapify<T>(@xs: [T], less: (function(a: T, b: T) -> bool))`, called `heap.heapify(@xs, less)`: Arranges `xs` as a heap by `less`, in its own place.
- `function add<T>(@heap: [T], value: T, less: (function(a: T, b: T) -> bool))`, called `heap.add(@heap, value, less)`: Adds `value` to `heap`, which stays a heap by `less`.
- `function pop<T>(@heap: [T], less: (function(a: T, b: T) -> bool)) -> T?`, called `heap.pop(@heap, less)`: Takes out of `heap` and answers its first element, one that nothing in it goes before by `less`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function peek<T>(heap: [T]) -> T?`, called `heap.peek(heap)`: The first element of `heap`, the one `pop` would take, leaving it in. Fails `not_found`.
- `function fix<T>(@heap: [T], at: i64, less: (function(a: T, b: T) -> bool))`, called `heap.fix(@heap, at, less)`: Puts the element at `at` of `heap` back in its place after the program changed it, so the list is a heap again.
- `function remove_at<T>(@heap: [T], at: i64, less: (function(a: T, b: T) -> bool)) -> T`, called `heap.remove_at(@heap, at, less)`: Takes out of `heap` and answers its element at `at`, the heap staying one.
- `function sort_in_place_by<T>(@xs: [T], less: (function(a: T, b: T) -> bool))`, called `heap.sort_in_place_by(@xs, less)`: Sorts `xs` by `less` in its own place, with no second list.


### graphs

Layer 0, named `use <rebel>/graphs`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/graphs/).

The orders and the paths of a graph: a topological order, all at once or handed out in stages, the cycle that forbids one, the strongly connected components, the nodes a node reaches, and the paths of least weight.

- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `codes.NOT_FOUND`: The code of a search that found nothing, which every function of this package whose `Fails` names `not_found` answers.
- `constant INVALID: str`, value `codes.INVALID`: The code of an input the function does not read: a graph with a cycle, where `topological_order` and `new_sorter` answer it; a weight below zero, infinite or not a number, where `shortest_path` and `distances_from` do; a node handed back that was not handed out, where `done` does.
- `function nodes_of<K>(graph: {K: [K]}) -> [K]`, called `graphs.nodes_of(graph)`: Every node of `graph` once: each key, followed by the nodes of its list not met before, in the order the graph gives them.
- `function topological_order<K>(graph: {K: [K]}) -> [K]?`, called `graphs.topological_order(graph)`: Every node of `graph`, each after every node it points to: a node's dependencies before it. Fails `invalid`.
- `function cycle_of<K>(graph: {K: [K]}) -> [K]?`, called `graphs.cycle_of(graph)`: A cycle of `graph`: nodes each pointed to by the one after it, the first node standing at the end again. Fails `not_found`.
- `function strong_components<K>(graph: {K: [K]}) -> [[K]]`, called `graphs.strong_components(graph)`: The strongly connected components of `graph`: the largest groups of nodes each reaching every other one of its group.
- `function reachable_from<K>(graph: {K: [K]}, from: K) -> [K]?`, called `graphs.reachable_from(graph, from)`: Every node `from` reaches by the edges of `graph`, `from` first, then the nearer before the farther. Fails `not_found`.
- `function shortest_path<K>(graph: {K: {K: f64}}, from: K, to: K) -> [K]?`, called `graphs.shortest_path(graph, from: from, to: to)`: The nodes of a path from `from` to `to` of the least total weight, both ends included. Fails `not_found`, `invalid`.
- `function distances_from<K>(graph: {K: {K: f64}}, from: K) -> {K: f64}?`, called `graphs.distances_from(graph, from)`: The least total weight of a path from `from` to every node it reaches. Fails `not_found`, `invalid`.
- `record Sorter(stages: stages.Stages)`: A topological order handed out in stages, for work done in parallel: the nodes ready are handed out together, and a node becomes ready once every node it points to is done.
- `function new_sorter<K>(graph: {K: [K]}) -> Sorter?`, called `graphs.new_sorter(graph)`: A sorter of `graph`'s nodes, none handed out yet. Fails `invalid`.
- `function ready(@sorter: Sorter) -> [i64]`, called `graphs.ready(@sorter)`: The nodes become ready since the last call, now handed out: Python's `get_ready`.
- `function done(@sorter: Sorter, node: i64) -> ()?`, called `graphs.done(@sorter, node)`: Marks `node` done, so the nodes that wait on it alone become ready: Python's `done`. Fails `invalid`, `not_found`.
- `function is_active(sorter: Sorter) -> bool`, called `graphs.is_active(sorter)`: Whether a sorter has more to hand out or nodes handed out and not done: Python's `is_active`.


### qr

Layer 0, named `use <rebel>/qr`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/qr/).

QR codes made by ISO/IEC 18004: a text or bytes written in numeric, alphanumeric, byte and kanji segments, every version from 1 to 40 and every level of error correction, the mask chosen by the standard's penalty rules, and the symbol written as a matrix of modules, as SVG text, as text for a terminal, or as pixels a program hands to `image` and `image/png`.

- `constant INVALID: str`, value `codes.INVALID`: The code of an input the function does not read: a character a segment's mode cannot write, a version outside 1 to 40, a mask outside 0 to 7, a colour SVG cannot hold, a count of codes outside 1 to 16.
- `constant UNSUPPORTED: str`, value `codes.UNSUPPORTED`: The code of data that no symbol of the versions allowed holds at the level asked, which `make`, `make_bytes`, `make_segments` and `make_sequence` answer.
- `variant Level = .low | .medium | .quartile | .high`: How much of a symbol can be lost or misread and still be restored: the four levels of error correction, each spending more of the symbol on it.
- `variant Mode = .numeric | .alphanumeric | .byte | .kanji`: How the characters of a segment are written, which decides how many bits each costs.
- `constant LEVELS: [Level]`, value `[.low, .medium, .quartile, .high]`: The four levels, weakest first: L, M, Q and H.
- `constant MODES: [Mode]`, value `[.numeric, .alphanumeric, .byte, .kanji]`: The four modes, in the order of the standard's tables.
- `function letter_of(level: Level) -> str`, called `qr.letter_of(level)`: The letter the standard names `level` by: "L", "M", "Q" or "H".
- `variant Segment = .numeric(digits: str) | .alphanumeric(text: str) | .byte(data: [u8]) | .kanji(sjis: [u8]) | .eci(assignment: i64)`: A piece of a symbol's data written in one mode, or a declaration that changes how the bytes after it are read.
- `record Options(level: Level, min_version: i64, max_version: i64, boost: bool)`: How `make_segments` chooses a symbol.
- `function default_options(level: Level) -> Options`, called `qr.default_options(level)`: The options that make the smallest symbol at `level`: every version from 1 to 40 tried, and the level kept as asked.
- `record Code(version: i64, level: Level, mask: i64, size: i64, modules: [[bool]])`: A QR code made: its version, its level, its mask and its modules.
- `function make(text: str, level: Level) -> Code?`, called `qr.make(text, level)`: The smallest QR code of `text` at `level`, its characters split into numeric, alphanumeric and byte segments so that it is shortest, the mask chosen by the standard's penalty rules. Fails `unsupported`.
- `function make_bytes(data: [u8], level: Level) -> Code?`, called `qr.make_bytes(data, level)`: The smallest QR code of `data` at `level`, one byte segment. Fails `unsupported`.
- `function make_segments(segments: [Segment], options: Options) -> Code?`, called `qr.make_segments(segments, options)`: The QR code of `segments` in their order, the smallest version `options` allows, the mask chosen by the penalty rules. Fails `invalid`, `unsupported`.
- `function segments_of(text: str, version: i64) -> [Segment]`, called `qr.segments_of(text, version)`: The segments that write `text` in the fewest bits for a version of `version`'s group, each character's mode chosen so: numeric for runs of digits, alphanumeric for runs of its set, byte for the rest.
- `function make_sequence(text: str, level: Level, count: i64) -> [Code]?`, called `qr.make_sequence(text, level, count)`: The codes of a structured append: `text` spread over `count` symbols of one version, which a reader joins back in order. Fails `invalid`, `unsupported`.
- `function capacity_of(version: i64, level: Level, mode: Mode) -> i64?`, called `qr.capacity_of(version, level, mode)`: How many characters of `mode` a symbol of `version` holds at `level`, in one segment. Fails `invalid`.
- `function with_mask(code: Code, mask: i64) -> Code?`, called `qr.with_mask(code, mask)`: `code` with its data masked by `mask` instead, its format information written again. Fails `invalid`.
- `function penalty_of(code: Code) -> i64`, called `qr.penalty_of(code)`: The penalty score of `code` by the standard's four rules: runs of five or more alike, blocks of two by two alike, patterns that look like a finder, and dark modules far from half.
- `variant Region = .finder | .timing | .alignment | .format | .version | .dark_module | .data`: Which pattern of a symbol a module belongs to, for a program that draws the patterns apart.
- `function region_of(code: Code, x: i64, y: i64) -> Region`, called `qr.region_of(code, x: x, y: y)`: The pattern the module at column `x` and row `y` of `code` belongs to.
- `function designator_of(code: Code) -> str`, called `qr.designator_of(code)`: The name of `code`'s symbol, its version and its level's letter: "1-M", "40-H".
- `function to_text(code: Code, border: i64, invert: bool) -> str`, called `qr.to_text(code, border, invert)`: `code` as text of block characters, each module two characters wide and each row a line, the quiet zone around it.
- `function to_compact_text(code: Code, border: i64, invert: bool) -> str`, called `qr.to_compact_text(code, border, invert)`: `code` as text half as tall: each character holds two rows of one module, by the half blocks U+2580 and U+2584 and the full block U+2588.
- `function to_terminal(code: Code, border: i64) -> str`, called `qr.to_terminal(code, border)`: `code` drawn in a terminal by colours: each module two spaces on a black or a white ground, so it reads alike whatever the terminal's own colours.
- `record SvgOptions(scale: i64, border: i64, dark: str, light: str)`: How `to_svg` draws a code.
- `function default_svg_options() -> SvgOptions`, called `qr.default_svg_options()`: The SVG options of an ordinary code: one pixel a module, four modules of quiet zone, black on white.
- `function to_svg(code: Code, options: SvgOptions) -> str?`, called `qr.to_svg(code, options)`: `code` as an SVG document: one path for the dark modules over a rectangle of the light colour, crisp at every scale. Fails `invalid`.
- `function to_pixels(code: Code, scale: i64, border: i64) -> [u8]`, called `qr.to_pixels(code, scale: scale, border: border)`: `code` as 8-bit gray samples, row after row, 0 for a dark module and 255 for a light one: the pixels `image.from_pixels` takes with `.gray`, which `image/png` then writes.
- `variant WifiSecurity = .wpa | .wep | .open`: The security a Wi-Fi network asks, as the readers of a Wi-Fi code name it in its `T:` field.
- `function wifi_text(ssid: str, password: str, security: WifiSecurity, hidden: bool) -> str`, called `qr.wifi_text(ssid: ssid, password: password, security, hidden)`: The text that tells a phone to join a Wi-Fi network, in the form readers share: `WIFI:T:WPA;S:<name>;P:<password>;;`, each value's `\`, `;`, `,`, `:` and `"` escaped by a backslash.


### containers/trie

Layer 0, named `use <rebel>/containers/trie`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/containers/trie/).

A prefix tree of texts: keys found, added and taken out at a cost of their length whatever the number held, with what a trie alone answers quickly: whether some key begins with a text, every key that does in byte order and how many, and the longest or the shortest key that begins a text, which is what a router asks of a path and a tokenizer of the text still to read.

- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `codes.NOT_FOUND`: The code of a search that found nothing, which every function of this package whose `Fails` names `not_found` answers.
- `record Trie(nodes: layout.Nodes)`: The shape of a trie of texts, a map's or a set's: its nodes, and the keys by slot.
- `function new_map() -> Trie`, called `trie.new_map()`: An empty trie of texts to values, whose program keeps an empty value list beside it.
- `function new_set() -> Trie`, called `trie.new_set()`: An empty trie of texts alone.
- `function size(trie: Trie) -> i64`, called `trie.size(trie)`: How many keys a trie holds.
- `function put<V>(@trie: Trie, @value_list: [V], key: str, value: V)`, called `trie.put(@trie, @value_list, key, value)`: Puts `value` under `key` in a map, replacing the value of a key it holds.
- `function get<V>(trie: Trie, value_list: [V] lent, key: str) -> V?`, called `trie.get(trie, value_list, key)`: The value under `key` in a map. Fails `not_found`.
- `function remove<V>(@trie: Trie, @value_list: [V], key: str) -> V?`, called `trie.remove(@trie, @value_list, key)`: Takes `key` and its value out of a map, answering the value. Fails `not_found`.
- `function remove_at<V>(@trie: Trie, @value_list: [V], at: i64)`, called `trie.remove_at(@trie, @value_list, at)`: Takes the key at slot `at` and its value out of a map.
- `function remove_with_prefix<V>(@trie: Trie, @value_list: [V], prefix: str) -> i64`, called `trie.remove_with_prefix(@trie, @value_list, prefix)`: Takes every key that begins with `prefix` out of a map, with its value, answering how many.
- `function add(@trie: Trie, key: str) -> bool`, called `trie.add(@trie, key)`: Adds `key` to a set, answering whether it was new.
- `function discard(@trie: Trie, key: str) -> bool`, called `trie.discard(@trie, key)`: Takes `key` out of a set, answering whether it was there.
- `function discard_at(@trie: Trie, at: i64)`, called `trie.discard_at(@trie, at)`: Takes the key at slot `at` out of a set.
- `function discard_with_prefix(@trie: Trie, prefix: str) -> i64`, called `trie.discard_with_prefix(@trie, prefix)`: Takes every key that begins with `prefix` out of a set, answering how many.
- `function contains(trie: Trie, key: str) -> bool`, called `trie.contains(trie, key)`: Whether a trie holds `key`.
- `function slot_of(trie: Trie, key: str) -> i64?`, called `trie.slot_of(trie, key)`: The slot of `key`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function key_at(trie: Trie, at: i64) -> str`, called `trie.key_at(trie, at)`: The key at slot `at`.
- `function has_prefix(trie: Trie, prefix: str) -> bool`, called `trie.has_prefix(trie, prefix)`: Whether some key held begins with `prefix`, the key equal to it included.
- `function count_with_prefix(trie: Trie, prefix: str) -> i64`, called `trie.count_with_prefix(trie, prefix)`: How many keys begin with `prefix`, the key equal to it included.
- `function slots_with_prefix(trie: Trie, prefix: str) -> [i64]`, called `trie.slots_with_prefix(trie, prefix)`: The slots of every key that begins with `prefix`, in the order of the keys' bytes.
- `function keys_with_prefix(trie: Trie, prefix: str) -> [str]`, called `trie.keys_with_prefix(trie, prefix)`: Every key that begins with `prefix`, in the order of their bytes.
- `function longest_prefix_slot(trie: Trie, text: str, from: i64) -> i64?`, called `trie.longest_prefix_slot(trie, text, from)`: The slot of the longest key that `text` holds from byte `from`: the key a router takes for a path, and a tokenizer for the text it has still to read. Fails `not_found`.
- `function shortest_prefix_slot(trie: Trie, text: str, from: i64) -> i64?`, called `trie.shortest_prefix_slot(trie, text, from)`: The slot of the shortest key that `text` holds from byte `from`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function prefix_slots(trie: Trie, text: str, from: i64) -> [i64]`, called `trie.prefix_slots(trie, text, from)`: The slots of every key that `text` holds from byte `from`, the shortest first.
- `function first_slot(trie: Trie) -> i64?`, called `trie.first_slot(trie)`: The slot of the first key in the order of their bytes. Fails `not_found`.
- `function last_slot(trie: Trie) -> i64?`, called `trie.last_slot(trie)`: The slot of the last key in the order of their bytes. Fails `not_found`.
- `function next_slot(trie: Trie, at: i64) -> i64?`, called `trie.next_slot(trie, at)`: The slot of the key just after the one at `at`, in the order of their bytes. Fails `not_found`.
- `function previous_slot(trie: Trie, at: i64) -> i64?`, called `trie.previous_slot(trie, at)`: The slot of the key just before the one at `at`, in the order of their bytes. Fails `not_found`.
- `function keys_in_order(trie: Trie) -> [str]`, called `trie.keys_in_order(trie)`: Every key of a trie in byte order: `keys_with_prefix` of the empty text.
- `function clear<V>(@trie: Trie, @value_list: [V])`, called `trie.clear(@trie, @value_list)`: Empties a trie of texts to values, every key and value let go.
- `function clear_set(@trie: Trie)`, called `trie.clear_set(@trie)`: Empties a trie of texts alone, every key let go.


### containers/disjoint

Layer 0, named `use <rebel>/containers/disjoint`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/containers/disjoint/).

Union-find: elements gathered into sets that only ever merge, each set answered by one element that stands for it, so that whether two elements stand in one set is known at once.

- `record Disjoint(forest: forest.Forest)`: The sets of union-find over the elements 0 to the size less one: every element stands in exactly one set, and the sets only merge.
- `function new(count: i64) -> Disjoint`, called `disjoint.new(count)`: `count` elements, from 0 to `count` less one, each alone in a set of its own.
- `function add(@disjoint: Disjoint) -> i64`, called `disjoint.add(@disjoint)`: Adds one element alone in a new set, answering its number, which is the size before the call.
- `function size(disjoint: Disjoint) -> i64`, called `disjoint.size(disjoint)`: How many elements there are, in every set together.
- `function set_count(disjoint: Disjoint) -> i64`, called `disjoint.set_count(disjoint)`: How many sets there are: the size where nothing has merged, one less for every merge of two sets apart.
- `function root_of(@disjoint: Disjoint, element: i64) -> i64`, called `disjoint.root_of(@disjoint, element)`: The element that stands for the set holding `element`, the same for every element of that set until it merges.
- `function merge(@disjoint: Disjoint, a: i64, b: i64) -> bool`, called `disjoint.merge(@disjoint, a: a, b: b)`: Merges the set holding `a` with the set holding `b`, answering whether they were apart.
- `function is_same_set(@disjoint: Disjoint, a: i64, b: i64) -> bool`, called `disjoint.is_same_set(@disjoint, a: a, b: b)`: Whether `a` and `b` stand in one set.
- `function size_of(@disjoint: Disjoint, element: i64) -> i64`, called `disjoint.size_of(@disjoint, element)`: How many elements the set holding `element` holds, itself included.
- `function members_of(disjoint: Disjoint, element: i64) -> [i64]`, called `disjoint.members_of(disjoint, element)`: The elements of the set holding `element`, in increasing order.
- `function to_lists(disjoint: Disjoint) -> [[i64]]`, called `disjoint.to_lists(disjoint)`: Every set, each as its elements in increasing order, the sets in the order of their smallest elements.
- `function to_labels(disjoint: Disjoint) -> [i64]`, called `disjoint.to_labels(disjoint)`: For every element, the smallest element of its set: a label its whole set shares, the same for the same sets however they were merged.


### unicode/normalize

Layer 1, named `use <rebel>/unicode/normalize`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/unicode/normalize/).

A text put in one of Unicode's four normal forms, so that two texts that write the same characters in different code points compare equal: "é" as one character and "e" followed by a combining acute accent are the same text in NFC and in NFD.

- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `"not_found"`: The code `decomposition` fails with where the character has none.
- `constant UNICODE_VERSION: str`, value `"17.0.0"`: The version of Unicode the tables hold.
- `variant Form = .nfc | .nfd | .nfkc | .nfkd`: The four normal forms of UAX #15, which `quick_check` is asked about.
- `variant QuickCheck = .yes | .no | .maybe`: What `quick_check` answers, UAX #15's three answers.
- `function to_nfc(s: str) -> str`, called `normalize.to_nfc(s)`: `s` in Normalization Form C, UAX #15's canonical composition: each character decomposed canonically, its marks put in their canonical order, then composed again where a composition is allowed.
- `function to_nfd(s: str) -> str`, called `normalize.to_nfd(s)`: `s` in Normalization Form D, UAX #15's canonical decomposition: each character taken apart into its base and its combining marks, the marks put in their canonical order, Hangul syllables into their jamo.
- `function to_nfkc(s: str) -> str`, called `normalize.to_nfkc(s)`: `s` in Normalization Form KC, UAX #15's compatibility composition: as `to_nfc`, after every compatibility mapping, so ligatures, circled and full-width characters become their plain letters and digits.
- `function to_nfkd(s: str) -> str`, called `normalize.to_nfkd(s)`: `s` in Normalization Form KD, UAX #15's compatibility decomposition: as `to_nfd`, after every compatibility mapping.
- `function is_nfc(s: str) -> bool`, called `normalize.is_nfc(s)`: Whether `s` is in Normalization Form C, so `to_nfc` would answer it as it is.
- `function is_nfd(s: str) -> bool`, called `normalize.is_nfd(s)`: Whether `s` is in Normalization Form D, so `to_nfd` would answer it as it is.
- `function is_nfkc(s: str) -> bool`, called `normalize.is_nfkc(s)`: Whether `s` is in Normalization Form KC, so `to_nfkc` would answer it as it is.
- `function is_nfkd(s: str) -> bool`, called `normalize.is_nfkd(s)`: Whether `s` is in Normalization Form KD, so `to_nfkd` would answer it as it is.
- `function quick_check(s: str, form: Form) -> QuickCheck`, called `normalize.quick_check(s, form)`: UAX #15's quick check of `s` for `form`: `yes` where every character may stand in the form and the marks are in their canonical order, `no` where one may not, and `maybe` where only normalizing can tell.
- `constant CANONICAL: str`, value `"canonical"`: The name the decompositions of the Unicode Character Database give a canonical one, which no tag names.
- `record Decomposition(kind: str, text: str)`: What `decomposition` answers: the one step by which the Unicode Character Database takes a character apart.
- `function decomposition(c: str) -> Decomposition?`, called `normalize.decomposition(c)`: The decomposition the Unicode Character Database gives `c`, one step of it, with its kind. Fails `not_found`.
- `function combining_class(c: str) -> i64`, called `normalize.combining_class(c)`: The canonical combining class of `c`, which orders the marks after a base: 0 for a base and every character that is no reordered mark, 1 to 254 for a mark, 230 for most marks drawn above and 220 for most below.
- `function to_caseless(s: str) -> str`, called `normalize.to_caseless(s)`: The form of `s` that Unicode's canonical caseless match compares: NFD of the full case folding of NFD of `s` (D145).
- `function to_caseless_compat(s: str) -> str`, called `normalize.to_caseless_compat(s)`: The form of `s` that Unicode's compatibility caseless match compares: NFKD of the case folding of NFKD of the case folding of NFD of `s` (D146), so "ﬁ" and "FI" both match "fi".
- `function to_nfkc_casefold(s: str) -> str`, called `normalize.to_nfkc_casefold(s)`: `s` mapped by Unicode's NFKC_Casefold, the form UAX #31 compares identifiers in: compatibility mappings, full case folding and the default ignorable characters taken out, in NFC.
- `function to_lower_for(s: str, language: str) -> str`, called `normalize.to_lower_for(s: s, language: language)`: `s` in lower case by Unicode's full mappings and the rules of `language`: in Turkish and Azeri "I" becomes the dotless "ı" and "İ" becomes "i"; in Lithuanian an "i" keeps its dot under an accent above; in every language a final sigma becomes "ς".
- `function to_upper_for(s: str, language: str) -> str`, called `normalize.to_upper_for(s: s, language: language)`: `s` in upper case by Unicode's full mappings and the rules of `language`: in Turkish and Azeri "i" becomes "İ"; in Lithuanian a dot above after a soft-dotted letter goes; in every language "ß" becomes "SS".
- `function to_casefold_for(s: str, language: str) -> str`, called `normalize.to_casefold_for(s: s, language: language)`: `s` folded for comparing by Unicode's full case folding and the rules of `language`: in Turkish and Azeri "I" folds to "ı" and "İ" to "i", where every other language folds them to "i" and "i" with a dot above.


### unicode/segment

Layer 1, named `use <rebel>/unicode/segment`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/unicode/segment/).

A text cut where Unicode says its parts end: into graphemes, what a reader sees as one character (UAX #29); into words and sentences (UAX #29); at the places a line may break (UAX #14).

- `constant UNICODE_VERSION: str`, value `"17.0.0"`: The version of Unicode the tables hold.
- `function graphemes(s: str) -> [str]`, called `segment.graphemes(s)`: The graphemes of `s`, UAX #29's extended grapheme clusters: what a reader takes for one character, a letter with its marks, a Hangul syllable written in jamo, a flag, an emoji joined to others.
- `function grapheme_boundaries(s: str) -> [i64]`, called `segment.grapheme_boundaries(s)`: Where the graphemes of `s` begin and end, as byte indices, ascending: 0, then the end of each grapheme.
- `function next_grapheme_boundary(s: str, at: i64) -> i64`, called `segment.next_grapheme_boundary(s, at)`: Where the grapheme that holds byte `at` of `s` ends: the first grapheme boundary after `at`.
- `function previous_grapheme_boundary(s: str, at: i64) -> i64`, called `segment.previous_grapheme_boundary(s, at)`: Where the grapheme that ends at or holds byte `at` of `s` begins: the last grapheme boundary before `at`.
- `function grapheme_break_class(c: str) -> str`, called `segment.grapheme_break_class(c)`: The Grapheme_Cluster_Break value of `c`, by which UAX #29 cuts graphemes, as `GraphemeBreakProperty.txt` writes it: "CR", "LF", "Control", "Extend", "ZWJ", "Regional_Indicator", "Prepend", "SpacingMark", "L", "V", "T", "LV", "LVT", or "Other".
- `function indic_conjunct_break_class(c: str) -> str`, called `segment.indic_conjunct_break_class(c)`: The Indic_Conjunct_Break value of `c`, by which UAX #29 keeps a conjunct of an Indic script in one grapheme: "Consonant", "Linker", "Extend", or "None".
- `function words(s: str) -> [str]`, called `segment.words(s)`: The words of `s` by UAX #29: the pieces between its word boundaries that hold a letter, a digit or an ideograph, in order.
- `function word_segments(s: str) -> [str]`, called `segment.word_segments(s)`: Every piece of `s` between two of its word boundaries by UAX #29: the words, and each run of spaces and each mark of punctuation between them.
- `function word_boundaries(s: str) -> [i64]`, called `segment.word_boundaries(s)`: Where the word boundaries of `s` stand by UAX #29, as byte indices, ascending, 0 and the length among them.
- `function word_break_class(c: str) -> str`, called `segment.word_break_class(c)`: The Word_Break value of `c`, by which UAX #29 cuts words, as `WordBreakProperty.txt` writes it: "ALetter", "Hebrew_Letter", "Numeric", "Katakana", "ExtendNumLet", "MidLetter", "MidNum", "MidNumLet", "Single_Quote", "Double_Quote", "Extend", "Format", "ZWJ", "WSegSpace", "Regional_Indicator", "CR", "LF", "Newline", or "Other".
- `function sentences(s: str) -> [str]`, called `segment.sentences(s)`: The sentences of `s` by UAX #29, each with the spaces and the line break that follow it.
- `function sentence_boundaries(s: str) -> [i64]`, called `segment.sentence_boundaries(s)`: Where the sentence boundaries of `s` stand by UAX #29, as byte indices, ascending, 0 and the length among them.
- `function sentence_break_class(c: str) -> str`, called `segment.sentence_break_class(c)`: The Sentence_Break value of `c`, by which UAX #29 cuts sentences, as `SentenceBreakProperty.txt` writes it: "CR", "LF", "Extend", "Sep", "Format", "Sp", "Lower", "Upper", "OLetter", "Numeric", "ATerm", "SContinue", "STerm", "Close", or "Other".
- `record LineBreak(at: i64, mandatory: bool)`: A place where a line may begin, which `line_breaks` answers.
- `function line_breaks(s: str) -> [LineBreak]`, called `segment.line_breaks(s)`: The places where a line of `s` may break by UAX #14 and its default rules, in order, the end of `s` the last.
- `function line_break_class(c: str) -> str`, called `segment.line_break_class(c)`: The Line_Break value of `c`, by which UAX #14 breaks lines, as `LineBreak.txt` writes it, in two or three capitals: "AL", "BA", "CM", "ID", "SP" and the rest of the forty-eight classes.
- `constant WIDE: str`, value `"W"`: The East_Asian_Width value `east_asian_width` answers for a character that is wide in every context: a Han ideograph, a kana, an emoji.
- `constant FULLWIDTH: str`, value `"F"`: The East_Asian_Width value of a full-width form of a narrow character: "Ａ".
- `constant HALFWIDTH: str`, value `"H"`: The East_Asian_Width value of a half-width form of a wide character: "ｱ".
