- `constant NARROW: str`, value `"Na"`: The East_Asian_Width value of a character that is narrow in every context: the letters and digits of ASCII.
- `constant AMBIGUOUS: str`, value `"A"`: The East_Asian_Width value of a character that is wide in East Asian text and narrow elsewhere: "±", "é", the Greek and Cyrillic letters.
- `constant NEUTRAL: str`, value `"N"`: The East_Asian_Width value of a character East Asian text does not hold: neither narrow nor wide, drawn narrow.
- `function east_asian_width(c: str) -> str`, called `segment.east_asian_width(c)`: The East_Asian_Width value of `c` by UAX #11: `WIDE`, `FULLWIDTH`, `HALFWIDTH`, `NARROW`, `AMBIGUOUS` or `NEUTRAL`.
- `function width_of(s: str) -> i64`, called `segment.width_of(s)`: How many columns of a terminal `s` takes, grapheme by grapheme: two for a grapheme whose first character is wide or full-width, as every character drawn as a picture by default is, for a pair of regional indicators (a flag) and for an emoji followed by U+FE0F; one for an emoji followed by U+FE0E; none for a grapheme that is a control, a lone mark, a Hangul vowel or final consonant alone, or a character drawn as nothing; one for every other.
- `function width_of_east_asian(s: str) -> i64`, called `segment.width_of_east_asian(s)`: How many columns of a terminal set for East Asian text `s` takes: as `width_of`, but a grapheme whose first character is ambiguous takes two.
- `record WrapOptions(width: i64, first_indent: str, rest_indent: str, break_long_words: bool)`: How `wrap` lays out a text: built by `wrap_options`, then changed field by field.
- `function wrap_options(width: i64) -> WrapOptions`, called `segment.wrap_options(width)`: The options `wrap` takes for lines of `width` columns: no indent, and a word wider than a line cut to fit, as Python's `textwrap` wraps.
- `function wrap(s: str, options: WrapOptions) -> [str]`, called `segment.wrap(s, options)`: The lines of `s` wrapped to `options.width` columns: each paragraph, ended by a line break of `s`, broken at the places UAX #14 allows, as many words on a line as fit, measured as `width_of` measures.
- `function truncate(s: str, width: i64, ellipsis: str) -> str`, called `segment.truncate(s: s, width, ellipsis: ellipsis)`: `s` cut to at most `width` columns, with `ellipsis` written at its end where anything was cut.
- `function pad_start_columns(s: str, width: i64, pad: str) -> str`, called `segment.pad_start_columns(s: s, width, pad: pad)`: `s` with `pad` written before it until the whole takes `width` columns, as `width_of` counts them, where `strings.pad_start` counts characters: how a column of numbers or of words in any script is aligned to the right in a terminal.
- `function pad_end_columns(s: str, width: i64, pad: str) -> str`, called `segment.pad_end_columns(s: s, width, pad: pad)`: `s` with `pad` written after it until the whole takes `width` columns, as `width_of` counts them: how a cell of a table drawn in a terminal is filled, whatever script it holds.
- `function center_columns(s: str, width: i64, pad: str) -> str`, called `segment.center_columns(s: s, width, pad: pad)`: `s` with `pad` written on both sides until the whole takes `width` columns, half of the padding before and half after, the odd column after.


### unicode/names

Layer 1, named `use <rebel>/unicode/names`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/unicode/names/).

What the Unicode Character Database tells of a character beyond its class and its case: its name and the character a name gives, its aliases, its script and the scripts it is used with, its block, the properties Unicode lists by name, the number it writes and its direction in text written right to left.

- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `"not_found"`: The code of a name that names no character, a script or a property that names none, and a character with no name, no number or no mirror.
- `constant UNICODE_VERSION: str`, value `"17.0.0"`: The version of Unicode the tables hold.
- `function name(c: str) -> str?`, called `names.name(c)`: The name Unicode gives `c`: "LATIN SMALL LETTER E WITH ACUTE" for "é". Fails `not_found`.
- `function character_named(text: str) -> str?`, called `names.character_named(text)`: The character `text` names: a name, an alias, or the name of a named sequence, which answers several characters, as Python's `unicodedata.lookup` reads them. Fails `not_found`.
- `constant ALIAS_CORRECTION: str`, value `"correction"`: The name `ALIAS_CORRECTION` gives an alias that corrects a mistake in a character's name, which Unicode never changes.
- `constant ALIAS_CONTROL: str`, value `"control"`: The kind of an alias that names a control character: "NULL", "LINE FEED".
- `constant ALIAS_ALTERNATE: str`, value `"alternate"`: The kind of an alias that is a name a character is widely known by: "BYTE ORDER MARK".
- `constant ALIAS_FIGMENT: str`, value `"figment"`: The kind of an alias for a name a standard once gave a character that was never there.
- `constant ALIAS_ABBREVIATION: str`, value `"abbreviation"`: The kind of an alias that is an abbreviation: "NUL", "LF", "ZWSP".
- `record Alias(name: str, kind: str)`: One alias of a character, which `aliases` answers.
- `function aliases(c: str) -> [Alias]`, called `names.aliases(c)`: The aliases Unicode gives `c` in `NameAliases.txt`, in the order the file lists them.
- `function script(c: str) -> str`, called `names.script(c)`: The script `c` belongs to, by its long name in Unicode's property value aliases: "Latin", "Greek", "Han", "Old_Italic"; "Common" for a character many scripts use, "Inherited" for a mark that takes its base's script, and "Unknown" for a code point no character has yet.
- `function script_extensions(c: str) -> [str]`, called `names.script_extensions(c)`: The scripts `c` is used with, by their long names in the order `ScriptExtensions.txt` gives them: "ー" is used with Hiragana and Katakana.
- `function scripts() -> [str]`, called `names.scripts()`: The long name of every script Unicode 17.0.0 holds, "Common", "Inherited" and "Unknown" among them, in the order of their names' bytes.
- `function script_named(alias: str) -> str?`, called `names.script_named(alias)`: The long name of the script `alias` names: its long name, its four-letter code of ISO 15924, or another alias, matched loosely by UAX #44's rule LM3 (case, spaces, underscores and hyphens ignored), so "Grek", "greek" and "GREEK" all answer "Greek". Fails `not_found`.
- `record Block(name: str, first: i64, last: i64)`: What `block` names and `blocks` lists: a range of code points Unicode sets aside together.
- `constant NO_BLOCK: str`, value `"No_Block"`: What `block` answers for a code point no block holds.
- `function block(c: str) -> str`, called `names.block(c)`: The name of the block `c` stands in, "Latin-1 Supplement" for "é", or `NO_BLOCK` where no block holds it, as Python's `unicodedata.block` answers.
- `function blocks() -> [Block]`, called `names.blocks()`: Every block of Unicode 17.0.0, in the order of their code points.
- `function has_property(c: str, property: str) -> bool?`, called `names.has_property(c: c, property: property)`: Whether `c` has the binary property `property`, one of those Unicode lists by name in `PropList.txt`, `DerivedCoreProperties.txt` and `emoji-data.txt`: "White_Space", "Alphabetic", "Dash", "Emoji", "Extended_Pictographic" and the rest `properties` lists. Fails `not_found`.
- `function properties() -> [str]`, called `names.properties()`: The long name of every binary property `has_property` reads, in the order of their names' bytes.
- `function is_identifier_start(c: str) -> bool`, called `names.is_identifier_start(c)`: Whether `c` may begin an identifier by UAX #31: its property XID_Start, the letters of every script and the numbers written as letters, "_" not among them.
- `function is_identifier_continue(c: str) -> bool`, called `names.is_identifier_continue(c)`: Whether `c` may stand in an identifier after its first character by UAX #31: its property XID_Continue, the letters, the marks, the digits and the connecting punctuation such as "_".
- `function is_identifier(s: str) -> bool`, called `names.is_identifier(s)`: Whether `s` is an identifier as Python's `str.isidentifier` reads one: a first character that `is_identifier_start` accepts or "_", then characters that `is_identifier_continue` accepts.
- `function is_default_ignorable(c: str) -> bool`, called `names.is_default_ignorable(c)`: Whether `c` is drawn as nothing where no font knows it, Unicode's Default_Ignorable_Code_Point: the zero-width joiners, the variation selectors, the soft hyphen and the code points set aside for more of them.
- `constant NUMERIC_DECIMAL: str`, value `"decimal"`: What `numeric_value` answers for a character `NUMERIC_DECIMAL` describes: a digit of a decimal system, which `unicode.digit_value` also reads.
- `constant NUMERIC_DIGIT: str`, value `"digit"`: What `numeric_value` answers for a digit that is no digit of a decimal system: a superscript or a circled digit, "²", "①".
- `constant NUMERIC_OTHER: str`, value `"numeric"`: What `numeric_value` answers for any other character that writes a number: a fraction, a Roman numeral, a Han numeral, "½", "Ⅻ", "万".
- `record NumericValue(numerator: i64, denominator: i64, kind: str)`: The number a character writes, exact, which `numeric_value` answers.
- `function numeric_value(c: str) -> NumericValue?`, called `names.numeric_value(c)`: The number `c` writes, as a fraction, and its kind. Fails `not_found`.
- `function bidi_class(c: str) -> str`, called `names.bidi_class(c)`: The Bidi_Class of `c`, which orders it in text written right to left, as `DerivedBidiClass.txt` writes it: "L" for a letter written left to right, "R" for Hebrew, "AL" for Arabic, "EN" for a European digit, and the rest of its twenty-three values.
- `function is_mirrored(c: str) -> bool`, called `names.is_mirrored(c)`: Whether `c` is drawn mirrored in text written right to left, Unicode's Bidi_Mirrored: "(" is drawn as ")".
- `function mirror(c: str) -> str?`, called `names.mirror(c)`: The character whose shape draws `c` mirrored, by `BidiMirroring.txt`: ")" for "(", "»" for "«". Fails `not_found`.


### strings

Layer 1, named `use <rebel>/strings`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/strings/).

Text searched, cut, trimmed, replaced, padded, indented and cased.

- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `"not_found"`: The code a search fails with where the text holds nothing of what was asked.
- `constant INVALID: str`, value `"invalid"`: The code `slice_checked` fails with where its indices cut no part of the text, `split_shell` where a quote is never closed or a backslash ends the line, and `quote_windows_args` where a program name holds a double quote.
- `function contains(s: str, substr: str) -> bool`, called `strings.contains(s: s, substr: substr)`: Whether `s` holds `substr`.
- `function contains_any(s: str, set: str) -> bool`, called `strings.contains_any(s: s, set: set)`: Whether `s` holds any character of `set`.
- `function has_prefix(s: str, prefix: str) -> bool`, called `strings.has_prefix(s: s, prefix: prefix)`: Whether `s` begins with `prefix`.
- `function has_prefix_at(s: str, prefix: str, at: i64) -> bool`, called `strings.has_prefix_at(s: s, prefix: prefix, at)`: Whether `prefix` stands in `s` at byte `at`.
- `function has_suffix(s: str, suffix: str) -> bool`, called `strings.has_suffix(s: s, suffix: suffix)`: Whether `s` ends with `suffix`.
- `function index_of(s: str, substr: str) -> i64?`, called `strings.index_of(s: s, substr: substr)`: Where `substr` first begins in `s`, as a byte index. Fails `not_found`.
- `function index_of_from(s: str, substr: str, from: i64) -> i64?`, called `strings.index_of_from(s: s, substr: substr, from)`: Where `substr` first begins in `s` at or after byte `from`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function index_of_last(s: str, substr: str) -> i64?`, called `strings.index_of_last(s: s, substr: substr)`: Where `substr` last begins in `s`, as a byte index. Fails `not_found`.
- `function index_of_any(s: str, set: str) -> i64?`, called `strings.index_of_any(s: s, set: set)`: Where the first character of `s` that `set` holds begins, as a byte index. Fails `not_found`.
- `function index_of_any_from(s: str, set: str, from: i64) -> i64?`, called `strings.index_of_any_from(s: s, set: set, from)`: Where the first character that `set` holds begins in `s` at or after byte `from`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function index_of_any_last(s: str, set: str) -> i64?`, called `strings.index_of_any_last(s: s, set: set)`: Where the last character of `s` that `set` holds begins, as a byte index. Fails `not_found`.
- `function index_where(s: str, accepts: (function(str) -> bool)) -> i64?`, called `strings.index_where(s, accepts)`: Where the first character of `s` that `accepts` accepts begins, as a byte index. Fails `not_found`.
- `function index_where_from(s: str, accepts: (function(str) -> bool), from: i64) -> i64?`, called `strings.index_where_from(s, accepts, from)`: Where the first character that `accepts` accepts begins in `s` at or after byte `from`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function index_where_last(s: str, accepts: (function(str) -> bool)) -> i64?`, called `strings.index_where_last(s, accepts)`: Where the last character of `s` that `accepts` accepts begins, as a byte index. Fails `not_found`.
- `function count_of(s: str, substr: str) -> i64`, called `strings.count_of(s: s, substr: substr)`: How many times `s` holds `substr`, counted from the start with no two occurrences sharing a byte: "aaaa" holds "aa" twice.
- `function index_of_all(s: str, substr: str) -> [i64]`, called `strings.index_of_all(s: s, substr: substr)`: Where each occurrence of `substr` begins in `s`, in order, as byte indices, taken from the start with no two sharing a byte.
- `function compare(a: str, b: str) -> i64`, called `strings.compare(a: a, b: b)`: Which of `a` and `b` orders first: -1 where `a` does, 1 where `b` does, 0 where they are the same text.
- `function equals_ignoring_case(a: str, b: str) -> bool`, called `strings.equals_ignoring_case(a: a, b: b)`: Whether `a` and `b` are the same text once the case of their letters is set aside, by Unicode's case folding, which is the same for every language.
- `function equals_ignoring_case_ascii(a: str, b: str) -> bool`, called `strings.equals_ignoring_case_ascii(a: a, b: b)`: Whether `a` and `b` are the same text once the case of their ASCII letters, "a" to "z", is set aside.
- `record Halves(before: str, after: str)`: What `split_once` and `split_once_last` answer: a text cut in two around a separator, which is in neither part.
- `function split_once(s: str, sep: str) -> Halves?`, called `strings.split_once(s: s, sep: sep)`: The text of `s` before its first `sep` and the text after it. Fails `not_found`.
- `function split_once_last(s: str, sep: str) -> Halves?`, called `strings.split_once_last(s: s, sep: sep)`: The text of `s` before its last `sep` and the text after it. Fails `not_found`.
- `function split(s: str, sep: str) -> [str]`, called `strings.split(s: s, sep: sep)`: The pieces of `s` between its `sep`s, one more than `count_of` counts: a `sep` at either end leaves an empty piece there, and a text holding no `sep` is its own one piece, the empty text included.
- `function split_n(s: str, sep: str, n: u64) -> [str]`, called `strings.split_n(s: s, sep: sep, n)`: At most `n` pieces of `s` between its `sep`s, cut from the start; the last piece holds the rest of `s`, later `sep`s included.
- `function split_n_last(s: str, sep: str, n: u64) -> [str]`, called `strings.split_n_last(s: s, sep: sep, n)`: At most `n` pieces of `s` between its `sep`s, cut from the end; the first piece holds the rest of `s`, earlier `sep`s included.
- `function split_after(s: str, sep: str) -> [str]`, called `strings.split_after(s: s, sep: sep)`: The pieces of `s`, each ending with the `sep` that follows it, and a last piece for what follows the last `sep` where anything does.
- `function split_after_n(s: str, sep: str, n: u64) -> [str]`, called `strings.split_after_n(s: s, sep: sep, n)`: At most `n` pieces of `s`, each ending with the `sep` that follows it, cut from the start; the last piece holds the rest of `s`.
- `function split_terminated(s: str, sep: str) -> [str]`, called `strings.split_terminated(s: s, sep: sep)`: The pieces of `s` that `sep` ends: what `split` answers without the empty piece after a final `sep`, so "a;b;" and "a;b" are both "a" and "b".
- `function split_any(s: str, set: str) -> [str]`, called `strings.split_any(s: s, set: set)`: The pieces of `s` between its characters that `set` holds, one more than there are such characters.
- `function split_where(s: str, separates: (function(str) -> bool)) -> [str]`, called `strings.split_where(s, separates)`: The pieces of `s` between its characters that `separates` accepts, one more than there are such characters, so two of them side by side leave an empty piece between; `words_where` leaves none.
- `function words(s: str) -> [str]`, called `strings.words(s)`: The words of `s`: the pieces between its runs of white space, none of them empty, so a text of white space alone has no words.
- `function words_where(s: str, separates: (function(str) -> bool)) -> [str]`, called `strings.words_where(s, separates)`: The pieces of `s` between its runs of characters that `separates` accepts, none of them empty.
- `function words_n(s: str, n: u64) -> [str]`, called `strings.words_n(s, n)`: At most `n` words of `s`, read from the start, as Python's `split` with no separator reads them: the white space at the start is passed over, and the last word holds the rest of `s` from where it begins, the white space at its end kept.
- `function words_n_last(s: str, n: u64) -> [str]`, called `strings.words_n_last(s, n)`: At most `n` words of `s`, read from the end, in the order of the text: the white space at the end is passed over, and the first word holds the rest of `s` up to where it ends, the white space at its start kept.
- `function lines(s: str) -> [str]`, called `strings.lines(s)`: The lines of `s`, each without its end, which is "\n" or "\r\n".
- `function trim(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.trim(s)`: `s` without the white space at either end.
- `function trim_start(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.trim_start(s)`: `s` without the white space at its start, white space being `trim`'s.
- `function trim_end(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.trim_end(s)`: `s` without the white space at its end, white space being `trim`'s.
- `function trim_any(s: str, set: str) -> str`, called `strings.trim_any(s: s, set: set)`: `s` without the characters of `set` at either end: a character is taken off an end for as long as `set` holds it.
- `function trim_start_any(s: str, set: str) -> str`, called `strings.trim_start_any(s: s, set: set)`: `s` without the characters of `set` at its start.
- `function trim_end_any(s: str, set: str) -> str`, called `strings.trim_end_any(s: s, set: set)`: `s` without the characters of `set` at its end.
- `function trim_where(s: str, accepts: (function(str) -> bool)) -> str`, called `strings.trim_where(s, accepts)`: `s` without the characters that `accepts` accepts at either end.
- `function trim_start_where(s: str, accepts: (function(str) -> bool)) -> str`, called `strings.trim_start_where(s, accepts)`: `s` without the characters that `accepts` accepts at its start.
- `function trim_end_where(s: str, accepts: (function(str) -> bool)) -> str`, called `strings.trim_end_where(s, accepts)`: `s` without the characters that `accepts` accepts at its end.
- `function trim_prefix(s: str, prefix: str) -> str`, called `strings.trim_prefix(s: s, prefix: prefix)`: `s` without `prefix` at its start, or `s` itself where it does not begin with it.
- `function trim_suffix(s: str, suffix: str) -> str`, called `strings.trim_suffix(s: s, suffix: suffix)`: `s` without `suffix` at its end, or `s` itself where it does not end with it.
- `function trim_prefix_all(s: str, prefix: str) -> str`, called `strings.trim_prefix_all(s: s, prefix: prefix)`: `s` without `prefix` at its start, taken off for as many times as what is left begins with it: "ababc" without "ab" is "c".
- `function trim_suffix_all(s: str, suffix: str) -> str`, called `strings.trim_suffix_all(s: s, suffix: suffix)`: `s` without `suffix` at its end, taken off for as many times as what is left ends with it: "cabab" without "ab" is "c".
- `function after_prefix(s: str, prefix: str) -> str?`, called `strings.after_prefix(s: s, prefix: prefix)`: The text of `s` after `prefix`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function before_suffix(s: str, suffix: str) -> str?`, called `strings.before_suffix(s: s, suffix: suffix)`: The text of `s` before `suffix`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function between(s: str, prefix: str, suffix: str) -> str?`, called `strings.between(s: s, prefix: prefix, suffix: suffix)`: The text of `s` between `prefix` at its start and `suffix` at its end. Fails `not_found`.
- `function replace_all(s: str, old: str, new: str) -> str`, called `strings.replace_all(s: s, old: old, new: new)`: `s` with every `old` replaced by `new`, the occurrences taken from the start with no two sharing a byte.
- `function replace_n(s: str, old: str, new: str, n: u64) -> str`, called `strings.replace_n(s: s, old: old, new: new, n)`: `s` with its first `n` occurrences of `old` replaced by `new`, taken as `replace_all` takes them; `s` itself for an `n` of 0.
- `function replace_last(s: str, old: str, new: str) -> str`, called `strings.replace_last(s: s, old: old, new: new)`: `s` with its last `old` replaced by `new`, or `s` itself where it holds none.
- `function replace_pairs(s: str, pairs: {str: str}) -> str`, called `strings.replace_pairs(s, pairs)`: `s` with each key of `pairs` replaced by its value, in one pass from the start: at each position the first key, in the order the map was filled, that stands there is replaced, and the search goes on after it, so what a replacement wrote is never replaced again and two pairs can swap two texts.
- `function pad_start(s: str, width: i64, pad: str) -> str`, called `strings.pad_start(s: s, width, pad: pad)`: `s` with `pad` written before it until the whole is `width` characters long.
- `function pad_end(s: str, width: i64, pad: str) -> str`, called `strings.pad_end(s: s, width, pad: pad)`: `s` with `pad` written after it until the whole is `width` characters long, or `s` itself where it is that long already or `pad` is empty.
- `function center(s: str, width: i64, pad: str) -> str`, called `strings.center(s: s, width, pad: pad)`: `s` with `pad` written on both sides until the whole is `width` characters long, half of the padding before and half after, the odd character after; `s` itself where it is that long already or `pad` is empty.
- `function pad_zeros(s: str, width: i64) -> str`, called `strings.pad_zeros(s, width)`: `s`, the text of a number, with zeros written after its sign, "+" or "-", or at its start where it has none, until the whole is `width` characters long; `s` itself where it is that long already.
- `function expand_tabs(s: str, tab_width: i64) -> str`, called `strings.expand_tabs(s, tab_width)`: `s` with each tab replaced by the spaces that reach the next tab stop, a stop standing every `tab_width` characters from the start of the line.
- `function indent(s: str, prefix: str) -> str`, called `strings.indent(s: s, prefix: prefix)`: `s` with `prefix` written before each of its lines that is not blank, as a quoted mail or a block of a help text is written.
- `function indent_where(s: str, prefix: str, accepts: (function(str) -> bool)) -> str`, called `strings.indent_where(s: s, prefix: prefix, accepts)`: `s` with `prefix` written before each of its lines that `accepts` accepts.
- `function dedent(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.dedent(s)`: `s` with the margin of spaces and tabs its lines share taken away: the longest run of spaces and tabs that every line that is not blank begins with, so a block written indented in a program's source reads from the left edge.
- `function to_lower(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.to_lower(s)`: `s` in lower case by Unicode's full mapping, the same for every language: each character lowered alone but the capital sigma, which becomes "ς" where it ends a word and "σ" elsewhere, by Unicode's Final_Sigma (a cased letter before it and none after it, an apostrophe or another case-ignorable character passed over), as Python and Rust write it: "ΣΊΣΥΦΟΣ" is "σίσυφος".
- `function to_upper(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.to_upper(s)`: `s` in upper case, each character by Unicode's mapping, which is the same for every language.
- `function to_title(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.to_title(s)`: `s` with the first letter of each word in title case and its other letters in lower case.
- `function capitalize(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.capitalize(s)`: `s` with its first character in title case and every other in lower case.
- `function swap_case(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.swap_case(s)`: `s` with each upper case letter in lower case and each lower case letter in upper case.
- `function to_casefold(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.to_casefold(s)`: `s` folded, the form two texts take where they differ only in the case of their letters, by Unicode's full case folding: "Straße" and "STRASSE" fold alike.
- `function to_lower_ascii(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.to_lower_ascii(s)`: `s` with its ASCII letters "A" to "Z" in lower case and every other character as it was.
- `function to_upper_ascii(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.to_upper_ascii(s)`: `s` with its ASCII letters "a" to "z" in upper case and every other character as it was.
- `function is_lower(s: str) -> bool`, called `strings.is_lower(s)`: Whether `s` holds a letter that has a case and none of them is upper or title case.
- `function is_upper(s: str) -> bool`, called `strings.is_upper(s)`: Whether `s` holds a letter that has a case and none of them is lower or title case.
- `function is_title(s: str) -> bool`, called `strings.is_title(s)`: Whether `s` is in the form `to_title` writes: it holds a letter that has a case, every word begins with an upper or title case letter, and every other cased letter is lower case.
- `function case_words(s: str) -> [str]`, called `strings.case_words(s)`: The words of `s` as the case style functions cut them, each as it stands in `s`: its runs of letters and numbers, every other character ending one, each run cut after a lower case letter that an upper case one follows, and before the last capital of a run of them that a lower case letter follows, so "XMLHttpRequest" is "XML", "Http" and "Request".
- `function to_snake_case(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.to_snake_case(s)`: `s` as snake_case: the words of `case_words` in lower case, joined by `_`.
- `function to_kebab_case(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.to_kebab_case(s)`: `s` as kebab-case: the words of `case_words` in lower case, joined by `-`.
- `function to_screaming_snake_case(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.to_screaming_snake_case(s)`: `s` as SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE: the words of `case_words` in upper case, joined by `_`, the form of a constant's name.
- `function to_screaming_kebab_case(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.to_screaming_kebab_case(s)`: `s` as SCREAMING-KEBAB-CASE: the words of `case_words` in upper case, joined by `-`.
- `function to_camel_case(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.to_camel_case(s)`: `s` as camelCase: the first word of `case_words` in lower case and every other with its first character in title case and the rest in lower case, joined with nothing between.
- `function to_pascal_case(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.to_pascal_case(s)`: `s` as PascalCase: every word of `case_words` with its first character in title case and the rest in lower case, joined with nothing between.
- `function to_title_case(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.to_title_case(s)`: `s` as Title Case: the words of `case_words`, each capitalised as `to_pascal_case` capitalises it, joined by one space.
- `function to_train_case(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.to_train_case(s)`: `s` as Train-Case: the words of `case_words`, each capitalised as `to_pascal_case` capitalises it, joined by `-`, the form of an HTTP header's name.
- `function to_slug(s: str) -> str`, called `strings.to_slug(s)`: The slug of `s`, the part of a URL that names a page, as Django's `slugify` makes it: `s` in lower case, kept to its letters, numbers, underscores, hyphens and white space, each run of white space and hyphens written as one `-`, and `-` and `_` taken off both ends.
- `function split_shell(s: str) -> [str]?`, called `strings.split_shell(s)`: The words a POSIX shell reads in `s`, by its quoting alone: blanks (space, tab, line feed) between words; single quotes, inside which every character stands as it is; double quotes, inside which a backslash takes `$`, a backquote, `"`, a backslash or a line feed as itself and stands as itself before any other character; a backslash outside quotes that takes the character after it as itself; a backslash before a line feed taken away with it; and a comment from a `#` that begins a word to the end of its line. Fails `invalid`.
- `function split_windows_args(s: str) -> [str]`, called `strings.split_windows_args(s)`: The arguments of a Windows command line, the program name first, as the C runtime reads them into a program's `argv` by Microsoft's documented rules since Visual Studio 2008: arguments between spaces and tabs; double quotes that group, two side by side inside a quoted part making one quote and the part going on; backslashes as they stand but before a double quote, where they are halved and an odd one left makes the quote itself; and a program name that runs to the first blank outside double quotes, its quotes taken away and its backslashes as they stand.
- `function quote_windows_arg(argument: str) -> str`, called `strings.quote_windows_arg(argument)`: `argument` written as one argument of a Windows command line, read back whole by `split_windows_args` after the program name: as it stands where it is not empty and holds no space or tab, else between double quotes; each double quote after a backslash, and the backslashes before it doubled, and the backslashes that end a quoted argument doubled, as Python's `subprocess.list2cmdline` writes it.
- `function quote_windows_args(arguments: [str]) -> str?`, called `strings.quote_windows_args(arguments)`: The Windows command line whose arguments are `arguments`, read back by `split_windows_args` as the same list: the program name `arguments[0]` between double quotes where it is empty or holds a space or a tab, each other argument by `quote_windows_arg`, one space between. Fails `invalid`.
- `function is_ascii(s: str) -> bool`, called `strings.is_ascii(s)`: Whether every character of `s` is ASCII, which is whether every byte is below 128.
- `function is_boundary(s: str, at: i64) -> bool`, called `strings.is_boundary(s, at)`: Whether byte index `at` of `s` stands between two characters: at 0, at `s.len()`, or where a character begins.
- `function floor_boundary(s: str, at: i64) -> i64`, called `strings.floor_boundary(s, at)`: The nearest index at or below `at` where `is_boundary` holds, so that `s.slice(from: 0, to: floor_boundary(s, at))` is `s` cut to at most `at` bytes without splitting a character.
- `function ceil_boundary(s: str, at: i64) -> i64`, called `strings.ceil_boundary(s, at)`: The nearest index at or above `at` where `is_boundary` holds.
- `function slice_checked(s: str, from: i64, to: i64) -> str?`, called `strings.slice_checked(s, from: from, to: to)`: The part of `s` from byte `from` up to byte `to`, which is not included. Fails `invalid`.
- `variant MatchKind = .standard | .leftmost_first | .leftmost_longest`: How a search for many patterns at once chooses among the matches that overlap or begin at one place, the three kinds of Rust's crate aho-corasick.
- `record Patterns(texts: [str], kind: MatchKind, ignores_case_ascii: bool, compiled: automaton.Machine)`: Many patterns made into one automaton, the one of Aho and Corasick, so that a text is searched for all of them in one pass.
- `record PatternMatch(pattern: i64, start: i64, end: i64, text: str)`: One match of one of many patterns in a text.
- `function compile_patterns(patterns: [str], kind: MatchKind) -> Patterns`, called `strings.compile_patterns(patterns, kind)`: `patterns` compiled into one automaton, searched by `kind`, every byte matching only itself.
- `function compile_patterns_ignoring_case_ascii(patterns: [str], kind: MatchKind) -> Patterns`, called `strings.compile_patterns_ignoring_case_ascii(patterns, kind)`: `patterns` compiled into one automaton, searched by `kind`, each ASCII letter matching itself in either case, so "Rebel" matches "REBEL" and "rebel".
- `function has_match(s: str, patterns: Patterns lent) -> bool`, called `strings.has_match(s, patterns)`: Whether `s` holds any of the patterns.
- `function search_patterns(s: str, patterns: Patterns lent) -> PatternMatch?`, called `strings.search_patterns(s, patterns)`: The first match of the patterns in `s`, chosen by their kind. Fails `not_found`.
- `function search_patterns_from(s: str, patterns: Patterns lent, from: i64) -> PatternMatch?`, called `strings.search_patterns_from(s, patterns, from)`: The first match of the patterns that begins in `s` at or after byte `from`, chosen by their kind. Fails `not_found`.
- `function match_patterns_at(s: str, patterns: Patterns lent, at: i64) -> PatternMatch?`, called `strings.match_patterns_at(s, patterns, at)`: The match of the patterns that begins at byte `at` of `s`, as a lexer reads a token where the last one ended: the shortest for `standard`, the first in the list for `leftmost_first`, the longest for `leftmost_longest`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function search_patterns_all(s: str, patterns: Patterns lent) -> [PatternMatch]`, called `strings.search_patterns_all(s, patterns)`: Every match of the patterns in `s`, one after another from the start, each chosen by their kind where the one before ended, none overlapping another.
- `function search_patterns_overlapping(s: str, patterns: Patterns lent) -> [PatternMatch]`, called `strings.search_patterns_overlapping(s, patterns)`: Every match of every pattern in `s`, overlapping or not, whatever the patterns' kind: "abcd" holds "b", "abc" and "abcd" at once.
- `function replace_patterns_all(s: str, patterns: Patterns lent, replacements: [str]) -> str`, called `strings.replace_patterns_all(s, patterns, replacements)`: `s` with every match of the patterns replaced, each by the replacement of its pattern, in one pass: what a replacement wrote is never searched again, so two patterns can swap two texts.
- `function replace_patterns_all_by(s: str, patterns: Patterns lent, by: (function(PatternMatch) -> str)) -> str`, called `strings.replace_patterns_all_by(s, patterns, by)`: `s` with every match of the patterns replaced by what `by` answers for it, in one pass.


### bytes

Layer 1, named `use <rebel>/bytes`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/bytes/).

A `[u8]` searched, cut, joined and compared, and bytes written as text and read back from it: as UTF-8, as hexadecimal, as base 32 and as base 64.

- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `codes.NOT_FOUND`: The code a search fails with where the bytes hold nothing of what was asked.
- `constant INVALID: str`, value `codes.INVALID`: The code a reading fails with where the text is not what the function reads: hexadecimal, base 32 or base 64 with a byte that does not belong, or cut short.
- `constant NOT_TEXT: str`, value `codes.NOT_TEXT`: The code `to_text` fails with where the bytes are not UTF-8, the language's own.
- `constant DOES_NOT_FIT: str`, value `codes.DOES_NOT_FIT`: The code `decode_uvarint` and `decode_varint` fail with where the bytes hold a number wider than 64 bits, the language's own.
- `function from_text(s: str) -> [u8]`, called `bytes.from_text(s)`: The bytes of `s`, which are its UTF-8.
- `function to_text(s: [u8]) -> str?`, called `bytes.to_text(s)`: The text `s` holds. Fails `not_text`.
- `function to_text_lossy(s: [u8]) -> str`, called `bytes.to_text_lossy(s)`: The text `s` holds, with U+FFFD, the replacement character, in place of what is not UTF-8.
- `function format_escaped(s: [u8]) -> str`, called `bytes.format_escaped(s)`: `s` as ASCII text that a reader can see whole: a printable ASCII byte as itself; tab, line feed and carriage return as `\t`, `\n` and `\r`; `\`, `"` and `'` behind a `\`; every other byte as `\x` and its two hexadecimal digits in lower case.
- `function contains(s: [u8], substr: [u8]) -> bool`, called `bytes.contains(s: s, substr: substr)`: Whether `s` holds `substr`.
- `function contains_any(s: [u8], set: [u8]) -> bool`, called `bytes.contains_any(s: s, set: set)`: Whether `s` holds any byte of `set`.
- `function has_prefix(s: [u8], prefix: [u8]) -> bool`, called `bytes.has_prefix(s: s, prefix: prefix)`: Whether `s` begins with `prefix`.
- `function has_prefix_at(s: [u8], prefix: [u8], at: i64) -> bool`, called `bytes.has_prefix_at(s: s, prefix: prefix, at)`: Whether `prefix` stands in `s` at index `at`.
- `function has_suffix(s: [u8], suffix: [u8]) -> bool`, called `bytes.has_suffix(s: s, suffix: suffix)`: Whether `s` ends with `suffix`.
- `function index_of(s: [u8], substr: [u8]) -> i64?`, called `bytes.index_of(s: s, substr: substr)`: Where `substr` first begins in `s`, as an index. Fails `not_found`.
- `function index_of_from(s: [u8], substr: [u8], from: i64) -> i64?`, called `bytes.index_of_from(s: s, substr: substr, from)`: Where `substr` first begins in `s` at or after index `from`. Fails `not_found`.

- `function encode_f64_le(x: f64) -> [u8]`, called `bytes.encode_f64_le(x)`: The 8 bytes of `x` as IEEE 754 lays them out, the lowest byte first (little endian), Python's `struct` format `<d`.
- `function decode_f32_be(s: [u8], at: i64) -> f32?`, called `bytes.decode_f32_be(s, at)`: The `f32` that the 4 bytes of `s` from index `at` hold as IEEE 754 lays them out, the highest byte first (big endian, the order of the network). Fails `invalid`.
- `function decode_f32_le(s: [u8], at: i64) -> f32?`, called `bytes.decode_f32_le(s, at)`: The `f32` that the 4 bytes of `s` from index `at` hold as IEEE 754 lays them out, the lowest byte first (little endian). Fails `invalid`.
- `function decode_f64_be(s: [u8], at: i64) -> f64?`, called `bytes.decode_f64_be(s, at)`: The `f64` that the 8 bytes of `s` from index `at` hold as IEEE 754 lays them out, the highest byte first (big endian, the order of the network). Fails `invalid`.
- `function decode_f64_le(s: [u8], at: i64) -> f64?`, called `bytes.decode_f64_le(s, at)`: The `f64` that the 8 bytes of `s` from index `at` hold as IEEE 754 lays them out, the lowest byte first (little endian). Fails `invalid`.
- `record DecodedUvarint(value: u64, width: i64)`: What `decode_uvarint` answers: an unsigned integer read from bytes, and how many bytes it took.
- `record DecodedVarint(value: i64, width: i64)`: What `decode_varint` answers: a signed integer read from bytes, and how many bytes it took.
- `function encode_uvarint(n: u64) -> [u8]`, called `bytes.encode_uvarint(n)`: `n` as an unsigned varint, the form of Go's `binary.PutUvarint` and of protocol buffers (LEB128): seven bits to a byte, the lowest seven first, and the highest bit of every byte but the last set.
- `function decode_uvarint(s: [u8], at: i64) -> DecodedUvarint?`, called `bytes.decode_uvarint(s, at)`: The unsigned varint that begins at index `at` of `s`, and how many bytes it took. Fails `invalid`, `does_not_fit`.
- `function encode_varint(n: i64) -> [u8]`, called `bytes.encode_varint(n)`: `n` as a zig-zag varint, the signed form of Go's `binary.PutVarint` and of protocol buffers' `sint64`: 0, -1, 1, -2, 2 become 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, written as `encode_uvarint` writes them, so a number near zero takes few bytes either side of it.
- `function decode_varint(s: [u8], at: i64) -> DecodedVarint?`, called `bytes.decode_varint(s, at)`: The zig-zag varint that begins at index `at` of `s`, and how many bytes it took. Fails `invalid`, `does_not_fit`.
- `variant MatchKind = .standard | .leftmost_first | .leftmost_longest`: How a search for many patterns at once chooses among the matches that overlap or begin at one place, the three kinds of Rust's crate aho-corasick, as `strings.MatchKind` chooses for text.
- `record Patterns(texts: [[u8]], kind: MatchKind, ignores_case_ascii: bool, compiled: automaton.Machine)`: Many patterns of bytes made into one automaton, the one of Aho and Corasick, so that bytes are searched for all of them in one pass.
- `record PatternMatch(pattern: i64, start: i64, end: i64, text: [u8])`: One match of one of many patterns in bytes.
- `function compile_patterns(patterns: [[u8]], kind: MatchKind) -> Patterns`, called `bytes.compile_patterns(patterns, kind)`: `patterns` compiled into one automaton, searched by `kind`, every byte matching only itself.
- `function compile_patterns_ignoring_case_ascii(patterns: [[u8]], kind: MatchKind) -> Patterns`, called `bytes.compile_patterns_ignoring_case_ascii(patterns, kind)`: `patterns` compiled into one automaton, searched by `kind`, each ASCII letter matching itself in either case.
- `function has_match(s: [u8], patterns: Patterns lent) -> bool`, called `bytes.has_match(s, patterns)`: Whether `s` holds any of the patterns.
- `function search_patterns(s: [u8], patterns: Patterns lent) -> PatternMatch?`, called `bytes.search_patterns(s, patterns)`: The first match of the patterns in `s`, chosen by their kind. Fails `not_found`.
- `function search_patterns_from(s: [u8], patterns: Patterns lent, from: i64) -> PatternMatch?`, called `bytes.search_patterns_from(s, patterns, from)`: The first match of the patterns that begins in `s` at or after index `from`, chosen by their kind. Fails `not_found`.
- `function match_patterns_at(s: [u8], patterns: Patterns lent, at: i64) -> PatternMatch?`, called `bytes.match_patterns_at(s, patterns, at)`: The match of the patterns that begins at index `at` of `s`: the shortest for `standard`, the first in the list for `leftmost_first`, the longest for `leftmost_longest`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function search_patterns_all(s: [u8], patterns: Patterns lent) -> [PatternMatch]`, called `bytes.search_patterns_all(s, patterns)`: Every match of the patterns in `s`, one after another from the start, each chosen by their kind where the one before ended, none overlapping another.
- `function search_patterns_overlapping(s: [u8], patterns: Patterns lent) -> [PatternMatch]`, called `bytes.search_patterns_overlapping(s, patterns)`: Every match of every pattern in `s`, overlapping or not, whatever the patterns' kind.
- `function replace_patterns_all(s: [u8], patterns: Patterns lent, replacements: [[u8]]) -> [u8]`, called `bytes.replace_patterns_all(s, patterns, replacements)`: `s` with every match of the patterns replaced, each by the replacement of its pattern, in one pass: what a replacement wrote is never searched again.
- `function replace_patterns_all_by(s: [u8], patterns: Patterns lent, by: (function(PatternMatch) -> [u8])) -> [u8]`, called `bytes.replace_patterns_all_by(s, patterns, by)`: `s` with every match of the patterns replaced by what `by` answers for it, in one pass.


### regex

Layer 1, named `use <rebel>/regex`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/regex/).

A regular expression compiled once and matched in time linear in the text, for every pattern: the pattern becomes an automaton, and a search runs the automaton over the text with every state at once and never goes back.

- `constant INVALID: str`, value `"invalid"`: The code of a pattern or a template this package does not read.
- `constant LIMIT: str`, value `"limit"`: The code of a pattern past one of the three bounds below.
- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `"not_found"`: The code of a search that found no match, and of a group that took no part.
- `constant MAX_REPEAT: i64`, value `1000`: The largest count a pattern may write: `x{1000}` compiles, `x{1001}` fails `limit`.
- `constant MAX_GROUPS: i64`, value `200`: The most groups a pattern may capture.
- `constant MAX_STATES: i64`, value `100000`: The most states a pattern's automaton may have.
- `constant MAX_NESTING: i64`, value `1000`: The most groups a pattern may open inside one another, those that capture nothing included; past it a pattern fails `limit`.
- `record Regex(pattern: str, compiled: program.Program)`: A compiled pattern, ready to be matched any number of times.
- `function compile(pattern: str) -> Regex?`, called `regex.compile(pattern)`: The pattern `pattern` compiled. Fails `invalid`, `limit`.
- `function escape(s: str) -> str`, called `regex.escape(s)`: `s` with a `\` before each character a pattern reads specially, so that compiled it matches `s` itself and nothing else.
- `function group_count(re: Regex) -> i64`, called `regex.group_count(re)`: How many groups `re` captures, the whole match not counted.
- `function group_names(re: Regex) -> [str]`, called `regex.group_names(re)`: The name of each group of `re`, the group 1 first, "" for a group without a name.
- `function group_number(re: Regex, name: str) -> i64?`, called `regex.group_number(re, name)`: The number of the group of `re` named `name`. Fails `not_found`.
- `record Span(start: i64, end: i64)`: A stretch of a text: where it begins and where it ends.
- `record Match(start: i64, end: i64, text: str, captured: capture.Groups)`: One match of a pattern in a text.
- `function contains(s: str, re: Regex) -> bool`, called `regex.contains(s, re)`: Whether `s` holds a match of `re`, anywhere in it.
- `function search(s: str, re: Regex) -> Match?`, called `regex.search(s, re)`: The first match of `re` in `s`: the leftmost, and of those the one Perl's rule prefers. Fails `not_found`.
- `function search_from(s: str, re: Regex, from: i64) -> Match?`, called `regex.search_from(s, re, from)`: The first match of `re` in `s` that begins at the byte `from` or after it. Fails `not_found`.
- `function match_at(s: str, re: Regex, at: i64) -> Match?`, called `regex.match_at(s, re, at)`: The match of `re` that begins exactly at the byte `at` of `s`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function full_match(s: str, re: Regex) -> Match?`, called `regex.full_match(s, re)`: The match of `re` that is the whole of `s`, from its first byte to its last. Fails `not_found`.
- `function search_all(s: str, re: Regex) -> [Match]`, called `regex.search_all(s, re)`: Every match of `re` in `s`, in order, none overlapping another.
- `function search_n(s: str, re: Regex, n: u64) -> [Match]`, called `regex.search_n(s, re, n)`: The first `n` matches of `search_all`, or all of them where they are fewer.
- `function group(m: Match, n: i64) -> str?`, called `regex.group(m, n)`: The text the group `n` matched, the group 0 being the whole match. Fails `not_found`, `invalid`.
- `function group_named(m: Match, name: str) -> str?`, called `regex.group_named(m, name)`: The text the group named `name` matched. Fails `not_found`, `invalid`.
- `function span(m: Match, n: i64) -> Span?`, called `regex.span(m, n)`: Where the group `n` matched in the text searched, the group 0 being the whole match. Fails `not_found`, `invalid`.
- `function span_named(m: Match, name: str) -> Span?`, called `regex.span_named(m, name)`: Where the group named `name` matched in the text searched. Fails `not_found`, `invalid`.
- `function groups(m: Match, absent: str) -> [str]`, called `regex.groups(m, absent)`: The text of every group, the group 1 first, with `absent` for each group that took no part in the match.
- `function groups_by_name(m: Match, absent: str) -> {str: str}`, called `regex.groups_by_name(m, absent)`: The text of every group that has a name, by its name, with `absent` for each that took no part in the match.
- `function last_group(m: Match) -> i64?`, called `regex.last_group(m)`: The number of the group that closed last in the match, which says which alternative matched where each is a group. Fails `not_found`.
- `function expand(m: Match, template: str) -> str?`, called `regex.expand(m, template)`: `template` with each `$` filled from the match: `$1` and `${1}` are the text of the group 1, `$name` and `${name}` of the group so named, `$0` the whole match, and `$$` one `$`; a group that took no part writes nothing. Fails `invalid`.
- `function replace(s: str, re: Regex, new: str) -> str`, called `regex.replace(s: s, re, new: new)`: `s` with its first match of `re` replaced by `new`, which is taken as it is: a `$` in it is a `$`.
- `function replace_all(s: str, re: Regex, new: str) -> str`, called `regex.replace_all(s: s, re, new: new)`: `s` with every match of `re` replaced by `new`, which is taken as it is.
- `function replace_n(s: str, re: Regex, new: str, n: u64) -> str`, called `regex.replace_n(s: s, re, new: new, n)`: `s` with its first `n` matches of `re` replaced by `new`, which is taken as it is.
- `function substitute(s: str, re: Regex, template: str) -> str?`, called `regex.substitute(s: s, re, template: template)`: `s` with its first match of `re` replaced by `template` filled from that match, as `expand` fills it. Fails `invalid`.
- `function substitute_all(s: str, re: Regex, template: str) -> str?`, called `regex.substitute_all(s: s, re, template: template)`: `s` with every match of `re` replaced by `template` filled from that match, as `expand` fills it. Fails `invalid`.
- `function substitute_n(s: str, re: Regex, template: str, n: u64) -> str?`, called `regex.substitute_n(s: s, re, template: template, n)`: `s` with its first `n` matches of `re` replaced by `template` filled from each, as `expand` fills it. Fails `invalid`.
- `function replace_by(s: str, re: Regex, by: (function(Match) -> str)) -> str`, called `regex.replace_by(s, re, by)`: `s` with its first match of `re` replaced by what `by` answers for it.
- `function replace_all_by(s: str, re: Regex, by: (function(Match) -> str)) -> str`, called `regex.replace_all_by(s, re, by)`: `s` with every match of `re` replaced by what `by` answers for it, called once for each match, in order.
- `function replace_n_by(s: str, re: Regex, by: (function(Match) -> str), n: u64) -> str`, called `regex.replace_n_by(s, re, by, n)`: `s` with its first `n` matches of `re` replaced by what `by` answers for each.
- `function split(s: str, re: Regex) -> [str]`, called `regex.split(s, re)`: The pieces of `s` between its matches of `re`, in order: one more piece than there are matches, so a text with no match answers itself alone, and a match at either end leaves an empty piece there.
- `function split_n(s: str, re: Regex, n: u64) -> [str]`, called `regex.split_n(s, re, n)`: The pieces of `split`, at most `n` of them: the first `n - 1` matches cut, and the last piece is the rest of `s`, uncut.


### random

Layer 1, named `use <rebel>/random`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/random/).

Numbers drawn at random from a seeded generator the caller holds: whole numbers below a bound or in a range without bias, floats in [0, 1), bytes, a list shuffled, an element chosen, a sample drawn without replacement, a choice by weights, and numbers drawn from a distribution: uniform, normal, lognormal, exponential, gamma, beta, von Mises, Pareto, Weibull, triangular, binomial and Zipf's; and from the system's generator for keys, a number below a bound, an element chosen, and a token written as text.

- `constant INVALID: str`, value `codes.INVALID`: The code `choose`, `sample` and `choose_weighted` and their `_chacha8` forms fail with where the list or the weights cannot be drawn from, `from_seed_chacha8` where the seed is not 32 bytes, and `secure_choose` where the list is empty.
- `constant DOES_NOT_FIT: str`, value `codes.DOES_NOT_FIT`: The code `draw` and `draw_chacha8` fail with where the number drawn lies beyond the largest float.
- `record Generator(high: u64, low: u64)`: A generator of numbers that look random: PCG's state of 128 bits, which the caller holds and every draw advances with `@`.
- `function from_system() -> Generator?`, called `random.from_system()`: A generator whose state is 16 bytes of the system's generator for keys, different on every call: for numbers that need not repeat from one run to the next. Fails with the code of `os.random_bytes` where the system's generator refuses.
- `function next_u64(@generator: Generator) -> u64`, called `random.next_u64(@generator)`: The next number of `generator`, any `u64` as likely as any other.
- `function next_f64(@generator: Generator) -> f64`, called `random.next_f64(@generator)`: A float from 0 to 1, 0 included and 1 left out, every multiple of 2^-53 in it as likely: the low 53 bits of the next number, divided by 2^53, as Go's `Float64` takes them.
- `function next_bytes(@generator: Generator, count: i64) -> [u8]`, called `random.next_bytes(@generator, count)`: `count` bytes from `generator`, eight from each number, its lowest byte first.
- `function below(@generator: Generator, n: u64) -> u64`, called `random.below(@generator, n)`: A number from 0 to `n` - 1, every one as likely: the low bits of a number for a power of two, else Lemire's method.
- `function int_in(@generator: Generator, from: i64, to: i64) -> i64`, called `random.int_in(@generator, from: from, to: to)`: A whole number from `from` to `to`, `to` left out as the built-in `range` leaves it, every one as likely.
- `function shuffle<T>(@generator: Generator, @xs: [T])`, called `random.shuffle(@generator, @xs)`: Puts the elements of `xs` in an order drawn at random, every order as likely, by Fisher and Yates's method; Go's `Shuffle` puts them in another order from the same state.
- `function choose<T>(@generator: Generator, xs: [T]) -> T?`, called `random.choose(@generator, xs)`: An element of `xs` drawn at random, every place as likely. Fails `invalid`.
- `function sample<T>(@generator: Generator, xs: [T], count: i64) -> [T]?`, called `random.sample(@generator, xs, count)`: `count` elements of `xs` drawn without replacement, in the order drawn: no place of `xs` is drawn twice, though two places may hold equal values. Fails `invalid`.
- `function choose_weighted<T>(@generator: Generator, xs: [T], weights: [f64]) -> T?`, called `random.choose_weighted(@generator, xs, weights)`: An element of `xs` drawn as likely as its weight: one of weight 2 twice as often as one of weight 1, one of weight 0 never. Fails `invalid`.
- `record ChaCha8(state: chacha.State)`: A generator whose numbers nobody can tell from the ones before without its seed: ChaCha with eight rounds, as Go's `math/rand/v2.ChaCha8` runs it, whose key is a seed of 32 bytes and becomes, every 124 numbers, 32 bytes of its own output never given out, so that a state seen later tells nothing of the numbers before it.
- `function from_seed_chacha8(seed: [u8]) -> ChaCha8?`, called `random.from_seed_chacha8(seed)`: A ChaCha8 generator seeded by `seed`, before its first number: Go's `rand.NewChaCha8(seed)`, whose numbers it answers. Fails `invalid`.
- `function from_system_chacha8() -> ChaCha8?`, called `random.from_system_chacha8()`: A ChaCha8 generator seeded by 32 bytes of the system's generator for keys, different on every call: as strong as its seed, and reading the system only once. Fails with the code of `os.random_bytes` where the system's generator refuses.
- `function next_u64_chacha8(@generator: ChaCha8) -> u64`, called `random.next_u64_chacha8(@generator)`: The next number of `generator`, any `u64` as likely as any other: Go's `ChaCha8.Uint64`.
- `function next_f64_chacha8(@generator: ChaCha8) -> f64`, called `random.next_f64_chacha8(@generator)`: A float from 0 to 1, 0 included and 1 left out, every multiple of 2^-53 in it as likely, as `next_f64` takes it.
- `function next_bytes_chacha8(@generator: ChaCha8, count: i64) -> [u8]`, called `random.next_bytes_chacha8(@generator, count)`: `count` bytes from `generator`, as Go's `ChaCha8.Read` gives them: first the bytes an earlier call left, then eight from each number, its lowest byte first; the bytes of the last number not used wait for the next call.
- `function below_chacha8(@generator: ChaCha8, n: u64) -> u64`, called `random.below_chacha8(@generator, n)`: A number from 0 to `n` - 1, every one as likely, drawn as `below` draws: Go's `Uint64N` from the same ChaCha8.
- `function int_in_chacha8(@generator: ChaCha8, from: i64, to: i64) -> i64`, called `random.int_in_chacha8(@generator, from: from, to: to)`: A whole number from `from` to `to`, `to` left out, every one as likely, as `int_in` draws it.
- `function shuffle_chacha8<T>(@generator: ChaCha8, @xs: [T])`, called `random.shuffle_chacha8(@generator, @xs)`: Puts the elements of `xs` in an order drawn at random, every order as likely, as `shuffle` does.
- `function choose_chacha8<T>(@generator: ChaCha8, xs: [T]) -> T?`, called `random.choose_chacha8(@generator, xs)`: An element of `xs` drawn at random, every place as likely. Fails `invalid`.
- `function sample_chacha8<T>(@generator: ChaCha8, xs: [T], count: i64) -> [T]?`, called `random.sample_chacha8(@generator, xs, count)`: `count` elements of `xs` drawn without replacement, in the order drawn, as `sample` draws them. Fails `invalid`.
- `function choose_weighted_chacha8<T>(@generator: ChaCha8, xs: [T], weights: [f64]) -> T?`, called `random.choose_weighted_chacha8(@generator, xs, weights)`: An element of `xs` drawn as likely as its weight, as `choose_weighted` draws it. Fails `invalid`.
- `function secure_below(n: u64) -> u64?`, called `random.secure_below(n)`: A number from 0 to `n` - 1, every one as likely, drawn from the system's generator for keys and not from a `Generator`: Python's `secrets.randbelow`. Fails with the code of `os.random_bytes` where the system's generator refuses.
- `function secure_choose<T>(xs: [T]) -> T?`, called `random.secure_choose(xs)`: An element of `xs` drawn from the system's generator for keys, every place as likely: Python's `secrets.choice`, for a word of a passphrase or a character of a password. Fails `invalid`.
- `function secure_token_hex(count: i64) -> str?`, called `random.secure_token_hex(count)`: A token of `count` bytes from the system's generator for keys, written as two lower-case hexadecimal digits a byte: Python's `secrets.token_hex`. Fails `invalid`.
- `function secure_token_base64_url(count: i64) -> str?`, called `random.secure_token_base64_url(count)`: A token of `count` bytes from the system's generator for keys, written in base 64's URL-safe alphabet with no padding, fit for a URL or a file name: Python's `secrets.token_urlsafe`. Fails `invalid`.
- `record Distribution(law: laws.Law)`: A distribution of real numbers to draw from, built by `uniform`, `normal`, `lognormal`, `exponential`, `gamma`, `beta`, `von_mises`, `pareto`, `weibull` or `triangular`, which check its parameters once and compute what its draws need; drawn by `draw` and `draw_chacha8`.
- `record Discrete(law: laws.Count)`: A distribution of whole numbers to draw from, built by `binomial` or `zipf`; drawn by `draw_discrete` and `draw_discrete_chacha8`.
- `function uniform(from: f64, to: f64) -> Distribution?`, called `random.uniform(from: from, to: to)`: Every number from `from` to `to` as likely, `to` left out as `int_in` leaves it: Python's `uniform`, drawn as `from + (to - from) * u` from a fraction `u` of `next_f64`, again in the rare case rounding reaches `to`. Fails `invalid`.
- `function normal(mean: f64, deviation: f64) -> Distribution?`, called `random.normal(mean: mean, deviation: deviation)`: The normal distribution, the bell curve of a mean and a standard deviation: Python's `gauss` and `normalvariate`, and Go's `NormFloat64` and Java's `nextGaussian` scaled. Fails `invalid`.
- `function lognormal(log_mean: f64, log_deviation: f64) -> Distribution?`, called `random.lognormal(log_mean: log_mean, log_deviation: log_deviation)`: The lognormal distribution, of a number whose natural logarithm is normal: Python's `lognormvariate`, drawn as exp of a normal number. Fails `invalid`.
- `function exponential(rate: f64) -> Distribution?`, called `random.exponential(rate)`: The exponential distribution: the wait for an event that comes `rate` times a unit of time on average, whose mean is 1 / `rate`. Fails `invalid`.
- `function gamma(shape: f64, scale: f64) -> Distribution?`, called `random.gamma(shape: shape, scale: scale)`: The gamma distribution of a shape and a scale, whose mean is their product: Python's `gammavariate`, its `alpha` the shape and its `beta` the scale. Fails `invalid`.
- `function beta(a: f64, b: f64) -> Distribution?`, called `random.beta(a: a, b: b)`: The beta distribution of numbers from 0 to 1 whose mean is `a` / (`a` + `b`): Python's `betavariate`, its `alpha` and `beta` here `a` and `b`. Fails `invalid`.
- `function von_mises(mean: f64, concentration: f64) -> Distribution?`, called `random.von_mises(mean: mean, concentration: concentration)`: The von Mises distribution, the normal of angles: Python's `vonmisesvariate`. Fails `invalid`.
- `function pareto(shape: f64, scale: f64) -> Distribution?`, called `random.pareto(shape: shape, scale: scale)`: Pareto's distribution: numbers from `scale` up, the chance of one above x being (`scale` / x)^`shape`. Fails `invalid`.
- `function weibull(scale: f64, shape: f64) -> Distribution?`, called `random.weibull(scale: scale, shape: shape)`: Weibull's distribution: Python's `weibullvariate`, its `alpha` the scale and its `beta` the shape, drawn as `scale` times an exponential number to the power 1 / `shape`. Fails `invalid`.
- `function triangular(low: f64, high: f64, mode: f64) -> Distribution?`, called `random.triangular(low: low, high: high, mode: mode)`: The triangular distribution, rising from `low` to `mode` and falling to `high`: Python's `triangular`, whose mode is the middle when not given, where here it is always given. Fails `invalid`.
- `function binomial(trials: i64, probability: f64) -> Discrete?`, called `random.binomial(trials, probability)`: The binomial distribution, of the successes among `trials` trials that each succeed with `probability`: Python's `binomialvariate`. Fails `invalid`.
- `function zipf(exponent: f64, offset: f64, largest: i64) -> Discrete?`, called `random.zipf(exponent: exponent, offset: offset, largest)`: Zipf's distribution, of a rank `k` from 0 to `largest` as likely as (`offset` + `k`)^-`exponent`: Go's `NewZipf(r, s, v, imax)`, whose `s` must be above 1 where here any exponent above 0 is drawn, Zipf's own 1 among them. Fails `invalid`.
- `function draw(@generator: Generator, distribution: Distribution) -> f64?`, called `random.draw(@generator, distribution)`: A number drawn from `distribution`. Fails `does_not_fit`.
- `function draw_chacha8(@generator: ChaCha8, distribution: Distribution) -> f64?`, called `random.draw_chacha8(@generator, distribution)`: A number drawn from `distribution` by a ChaCha8 generator, by the method `draw` takes. Fails `does_not_fit`.
- `function draw_discrete(@generator: Generator, distribution: Discrete) -> i64`, called `random.draw_discrete(@generator, distribution)`: A whole number drawn from `distribution`, from 0 to its trials or its largest value.
- `function draw_discrete_chacha8(@generator: ChaCha8, distribution: Discrete) -> i64`, called `random.draw_discrete_chacha8(@generator, distribution)`: A whole number drawn from `distribution` by a ChaCha8 generator, by the method `draw_discrete` takes.


### stats

Layer 1, named `use <rebel>/stats`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/stats/).

The statistics of a list of floats: means, medians, modes, spread, quantiles, and the covariance, correlation and fitted line of two lists.

- `constant INVALID: str`, value `exact.INVALID`: The code of data a statistic cannot read: too few values, a nan where the values are ordered, two lists of different lengths, a constant input.
- `constant DOES_NOT_FIT: str`, value `exact.DOES_NOT_FIT`: The code of an answer past the largest float, from finite data: the variances, `covariance`, `fast_mean`, `weighted_mean` and the regressions fail with it.
- `function mean(data: [f64]) -> f64?`, called `stats.mean(data)`: The arithmetic mean of `data`, computed exactly and rounded once. Fails `invalid`.
- `function fast_mean(data: [f64]) -> f64?`, called `stats.fast_mean(data)`: The arithmetic mean of `data` as their sum rounded once over the count, Python's `fmean`. Fails `invalid`, `does_not_fit`.
- `function weighted_mean(data: [f64], weights: [f64]) -> f64?`, called `stats.weighted_mean(data: data, weights: weights)`: The mean of `data` weighted by `weights`: the sum of their products, over the sum of the weights. Fails `invalid`, `does_not_fit`.
- `function geometric_mean(data: [f64]) -> f64?`, called `stats.geometric_mean(data)`: The geometric mean of `data`: the exponential of the mean of their logarithms. Fails `invalid`.
- `function harmonic_mean(data: [f64]) -> f64?`, called `stats.harmonic_mean(data)`: The harmonic mean of `data`: their count over the sum of their inverses. Fails `invalid`.
- `function median(data: [f64]) -> f64?`, called `stats.median(data)`: The middle value of `data` in order, or the mean of the two middle values. Fails `invalid`.
- `function median_low(data: [f64]) -> f64?`, called `stats.median_low(data)`: The middle value of `data` in order, or the lower of the two middle values: always one of the values. Fails `invalid`.
- `function median_high(data: [f64]) -> f64?`, called `stats.median_high(data)`: The middle value of `data` in order, or the higher of the two middle values: always one of the values. Fails `invalid`.
- `function median_grouped(data: [f64], interval: f64) -> f64?`, called `stats.median_grouped(data, interval)`: The median of `data` read as classes `interval` wide, each centred on a value: the lower edge of the middle value's class plus the share of it the middle of the data reaches. Fails `invalid`.
- `function mode(data: [f64]) -> f64?`, called `stats.mode(data)`: The value of `data` that occurs most often; of several, the first to occur. Fails `invalid`.
- `function multimode(data: [f64]) -> [f64]?`, called `stats.multimode(data)`: Every value of `data` that occurs most often, in the order each first occurred. Fails `invalid`.
- `function variance(data: [f64]) -> f64?`, called `stats.variance(data)`: The sample variance of `data`: the squared distances from their mean, summed, over the count less one; exact, rounded once. Fails `invalid`, `does_not_fit`.
- `function population_variance(data: [f64]) -> f64?`, called `stats.population_variance(data)`: The population variance of `data`: the squared distances from their mean, summed, over the count; exact, rounded once. Fails `invalid`, `does_not_fit`.
- `function standard_deviation(data: [f64]) -> f64?`, called `stats.standard_deviation(data)`: The sample standard deviation of `data`: the square root of the exact sample variance, rounded once. Fails `invalid`.
- `function population_standard_deviation(data: [f64]) -> f64?`, called `stats.population_standard_deviation(data)`: The population standard deviation of `data`: the square root of the exact population variance, rounded once. Fails `invalid`.
- `function quantiles(data: [f64], parts: i64) -> [f64]?`, called `stats.quantiles(data, parts)`: The `parts - 1` points that cut `data` into `parts` groups of equal share, reading `data` as a sample of a population that reaches past it. Fails `invalid`.
- `function quantiles_inclusive(data: [f64], parts: i64) -> [f64]?`, called `stats.quantiles_inclusive(data, parts)`: The `parts - 1` points that cut `data` into `parts` groups of equal share, reading `data` as the whole population: the smallest value is the 0th point and the largest the last. Fails `invalid`.
- `record Line(slope: f64, intercept: f64)`: What `linear_regression` answers: the line `slope` times x plus `intercept`.
- `function covariance(x: [f64], y: [f64]) -> f64?`, called `stats.covariance(x: x, y: y)`: The sample covariance of `x` and `y`: how far they vary together. Fails `invalid`, `does_not_fit`.
- `function correlation(x: [f64], y: [f64]) -> f64?`, called `stats.correlation(x: x, y: y)`: Pearson's correlation of `x` and `y`, from -1 to 1: how close the pairs lie to a line. Fails `invalid`.
- `function rank_correlation(x: [f64], y: [f64]) -> f64?`, called `stats.rank_correlation(x: x, y: y)`: Spearman's rank correlation of `x` and `y`: Pearson's of their ranks, tied values sharing the mean of their ranks, so any rising relation answers 1. Fails `invalid`.
- `function linear_regression(x: [f64], y: [f64]) -> Line?`, called `stats.linear_regression(x: x, y: y)`: The line of least squares through the pairs of `x` and `y`. Fails `invalid`, `does_not_fit`.
- `function proportional_regression(x: [f64], y: [f64]) -> Line?`, called `stats.proportional_regression(x: x, y: y)`: The line of least squares through the pairs of `x` and `y` that passes through the origin: its intercept is 0.0. Fails `invalid`.
- `record Normal(mean: f64, sigma: f64)`: A normal distribution: the bell curve of a mean and a deviation.
- `function normal(center: f64, sigma: f64) -> Normal?`, called `stats.normal(center: center, sigma: sigma)`: The normal distribution of a mean and a deviation. Fails `invalid`.
- `function normal_of(data: [f64]) -> Normal?`, called `stats.normal_of(data)`: The normal distribution fitted to data: its mean and its sample standard deviation, as Python's `NormalDist.from_samples` fits it. Fails `invalid`.
- `function normal_density(dist: Normal, x: f64) -> f64?`, called `stats.normal_density(dist, x)`: The height of the bell curve at `x`: how likely a value is near it. Fails `invalid`.
- `function normal_cumulative(dist: Normal, x: f64) -> f64?`, called `stats.normal_cumulative(dist, x)`: The probability of a value of the distribution up to `x`, found through the complementary error function, so that a tail keeps its digits. Fails `invalid`.
- `function normal_quantile(dist: Normal, p: f64) -> f64?`, called `stats.normal_quantile(dist, p)`: The point a value of the distribution falls below with probability `p`, the inverse of `normal_cumulative`, found to the last float. Fails `invalid`.
- `function normal_quantiles(dist: Normal, parts: i64) -> [f64]?`, called `stats.normal_quantiles(dist, parts)`: The cut points that divide the distribution into `parts` of equal probability: `parts - 1` of them, in order. Fails `invalid`.
- `function normal_z_score(dist: Normal, x: f64) -> f64?`, called `stats.normal_z_score(dist, x)`: How many deviations from the mean `x` is. Fails `invalid`.
- `function normal_overlap(a: Normal, b: Normal) -> f64?`, called `stats.normal_overlap(a: a, b: b)`: The overlap of two distributions: the area under both curves, 1 where they are the same and near 0 where they are far apart. Fails `invalid`.
- `function normal_variance(dist: Normal) -> f64`, called `stats.normal_variance(dist)`: The distribution of the variance, the square of the deviation.
- `function normal_sum(a: Normal, b: Normal) -> Normal`, called `stats.normal_sum(a: a, b: b)`: The distribution of the sum of two independent values: the means add and the deviations add as the sides of a right triangle.
- `function normal_difference(a: Normal, b: Normal) -> Normal`, called `stats.normal_difference(a: a, b: b)`: The distribution of the difference of two independent values: the means subtract and the deviations add as the sides of a right triangle.
- `function normal_shift(dist: Normal, by: f64) -> Normal`, called `stats.normal_shift(dist, by)`: The distribution of the values of `dist` with `by` added to each.
- `function normal_scale(dist: Normal, by: f64) -> Normal`, called `stats.normal_scale(dist, by)`: The distribution of the values of `dist` each multiplied by `by`.


### math/complex

Layer 1, named `use <rebel>/math/complex`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/math/complex/).

Complex numbers, `re + im i`, and their functions as C11's Annex G computes them: arithmetic, the size and the angle, the polar form, the exponential, the logarithms and the powers, and the circular and hyperbolic functions with their inverses, each branch cut on an axis.

- `record Complex(re: f64, im: f64)`: A complex number, `re + im i`, built directly: `complex.Complex(re: 1.0, im: -2.0)`.
- `record Polar(modulus: f64, phase: f64)`: A complex number by its size and its angle: what `to_polar` answers and `from_polar` reads.
- `function add(a: Complex, b: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.add(a: a, b: b)`: The sum `a + b`, part by part.
- `function subtract(a: Complex, b: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.subtract(a: a, b: b)`: The difference `a - b`, part by part.
- `function multiply(a: Complex, b: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.multiply(a: a, b: b)`: The product `a * b`.
- `function divide(a: Complex, b: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.divide(a: a, b: b)`: The quotient `a / b`, by Baudin and Smith's robust algorithm, which scales away from overflow and underflow on the way.
- `function negate(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.negate(z)`: `z` with both parts negated.
- `function conjugate(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.conjugate(z)`: The conjugate of `z`: its imaginary part negated.
- `function abs(z: Complex) -> f64`, called `complex.abs(z)`: The size of `z`, its distance from zero, computed without overflow on the way.
- `function phase(z: Complex) -> f64`, called `complex.phase(z)`: The angle of `z` from the positive real axis, in radians from -pi to pi.
- `function to_polar(z: Complex) -> Polar`, called `complex.to_polar(z)`: `z` by its size and its angle.
- `function from_polar(p: Polar) -> Complex`, called `complex.from_polar(p)`: The complex number `p` stands for: `p.modulus * (cos(p.phase) + sin(p.phase) i)`.
- `function project(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.project(z)`: The point of the Riemann sphere `z` stands for: `z` itself where neither part is infinite, and the one infinity `inf + 0i` where either is, the zero signed as `z.im`.
- `function is_nan(z: Complex) -> bool`, called `complex.is_nan(z)`: Whether a part of `z` is a nan and neither is infinite: of `is_nan`, `is_inf` and `is_finite`, exactly one holds of any number.
- `function is_inf(z: Complex) -> bool`, called `complex.is_inf(z)`: Whether a part of `z` is infinite, whatever the other is.
- `function is_finite(z: Complex) -> bool`, called `complex.is_finite(z)`: Whether both parts of `z` are finite.
- `function is_close(a: Complex, b: Complex, relative: f64, absolute: f64) -> bool`, called `complex.is_close(a: a, b: b, relative: relative, absolute: absolute)`: Whether `a` and `b` are equal, or the size of their difference is within `relative` times the larger of their sizes, or within `absolute`: Python's `cmath.isclose`.
- `function exp(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.exp(z)`: E raised to the power `z`.
- `function ln(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.ln(z)`: The natural logarithm of `z`, the principal one: its imaginary part is the angle of `z`, from -pi to pi.
- `function log10(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.log10(z)`: The logarithm in base 10 of `z`: `ln` with both parts divided by the natural logarithm of 10.
- `function log(z: Complex, base: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.log(z: z, base: base)`: The logarithm of `z` in the base `base`: `ln(z)` divided by `ln(base)`, as Python's `cmath.log` with two arguments.
- `function sqrt(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.sqrt(z)`: The principal square root of `z`: its real part never negative, its imaginary part of the sign of `z.im`.
- `function pow(base: Complex, exponent: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.pow(base: base, exponent: exponent)`: `base` raised to the power `exponent`, the principal power `exp(exponent * ln(base))`.
- `function sin(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.sin(z)`: The sine of `z`.
- `function cos(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.cos(z)`: The cosine of `z`.
- `function tan(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.tan(z)`: The tangent of `z`.
- `function asin(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.asin(z)`: The inverse sine of `z`, its real part from -pi/2 to pi/2.
- `function acos(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.acos(z)`: The inverse cosine of `z`, its real part from 0 to pi.
- `function atan(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.atan(z)`: The inverse tangent of `z`, its real part from -pi/2 to pi/2.
- `function sinh(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.sinh(z)`: The hyperbolic sine of `z`.
- `function cosh(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.cosh(z)`: The hyperbolic cosine of `z`.
- `function tanh(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.tanh(z)`: The hyperbolic tangent of `z`.
- `function asinh(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.asinh(z)`: The inverse hyperbolic sine of `z`, its imaginary part from -pi/2 to pi/2.
- `function acosh(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.acosh(z)`: The inverse hyperbolic cosine of `z`, its real part never negative, its imaginary part from -pi to pi.
- `function atanh(z: Complex) -> Complex`, called `complex.atanh(z)`: The inverse hyperbolic tangent of `z`, its imaginary part from -pi/2 to pi/2.


### math/linear

Layer 1, named `use <rebel>/math/linear`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/math/linear/).

Vectors of two, three and four floats, matrices of two, three and four columns, quaternions, and the transforms of graphics built from them: the geometry of games and of the screen, in `f64`, every value a copy.

- `constant INVALID: str`, value `math.INVALID`: The input has no answer: a zero vector or axis, a singular matrix, an empty view; the message says what was given.
- `variant Hand = .right | .left`: Which way a frame turns: where its z axis points once x points right and y points up.
- `variant Depth = .minus_one_to_one | .zero_to_one`: Where a projection sends the near and the far planes, in the depth of normalized device coordinates.
- `variant EulerOrder = .xyz | .xzy | .yxz | .yzx | .zxy | .zyx | .xyx | .xzx | .yxy | .yzy | .zxz | .zyz`: The axes of three rotations, in the order they are made, each about the axes as the turns before it left them (intrinsic); the same rotation is the three made about the fixed axes in the other order, the last first.
- `record Vec2(x: f64, y: f64)`: A vector of two floats: a point or a direction of the plane.
- `record Vec3(x: f64, y: f64, z: f64)`: A vector of three floats: a point or a direction of space.
- `record Vec4(x: f64, y: f64, z: f64, w: f64)`: A vector of four floats: a point of space with its homogeneous weight `w`, 1 for a point and 0 for a direction, or any four numbers.
- `record Mat2(x_axis: Vec2, y_axis: Vec2)`: A matrix of two rows and two columns, held by its columns.
- `record Mat3(x_axis: Vec3, y_axis: Vec3, z_axis: Vec3)`: A matrix of three rows and three columns, held by its columns: a linear map of space, or an affine map of the plane whose `z_axis` holds its translation.
- `record Mat4(x_axis: Vec4, y_axis: Vec4, z_axis: Vec4, w_axis: Vec4)`: A matrix of four rows and four columns, held by its columns: a transform of space in homogeneous coordinates, its translation in `w_axis`, or a projection.
- `record Quat(x: f64, y: f64, z: f64, w: f64)`: A quaternion `w + xi + yj + zk`, the rotation by the angle `2 acos(w)` about the axis `(x, y, z)` where its length is 1.
- `record AxisAngle(axis: Vec3, angle: f64)`: A rotation as an axis and an angle: what `to_axis_angle` answers.
- `record Euler(order: EulerOrder, first: f64, second: f64, third: f64)`: A rotation as three angles about the axes of an order: what `to_euler` answers and `euler_quat` reads.
- `function add_vec2(a: Vec2, b: Vec2) -> Vec2`, called `linear.add_vec2(a: a, b: b)`: The sum `a + b`, part by part.
