- `function remove_attribute(@doc: Document, node: i64, name: str)`, called `html.remove_attribute(@doc, node, name)`: Removes the attribute `name` of the element `node`; nothing where it has none or is not an element.
- `function create_element(@doc: Document, name: str) -> i64`, called `html.create_element(@doc, name)`: A new HTML element named `name`, with no attribute and no child, held by nothing until it is put in.
- `function create_element_in(@doc: Document, space: Space, name: str) -> i64`, called `html.create_element_in(@doc, space, name)`: A new element of the namespace `space` named `name`, held by nothing until it is put in.
- `function create_text(@doc: Document, text: str) -> i64`, called `html.create_text(@doc, text)`: A new text node holding `text`, held by nothing until it is put in.
- `function create_comment(@doc: Document, text: str) -> i64`, called `html.create_comment(@doc, text)`: A new comment holding `text`, held by nothing until it is put in.
- `function append_child(@doc: Document, to: i64, child: i64) -> ()?`, called `html.append_child(@doc, to: to, child: child)`: Puts `child` last among the children of `to`, taking it from where it stood. Fails `invalid`.
- `function insert_before(@doc: Document, node: i64, sibling: i64) -> ()?`, called `html.insert_before(@doc, node: node, sibling: sibling)`: Puts `node` just before `sibling`, in the parent of `sibling`, taking it from where it stood. Fails `invalid`.
- `function insert_after(@doc: Document, node: i64, sibling: i64) -> ()?`, called `html.insert_after(@doc, node: node, sibling: sibling)`: Puts `node` just after `sibling`, in the parent of `sibling`, taking it from where it stood. Fails `invalid`.
- `function remove(@doc: Document, node: i64)`, called `html.remove(@doc, node)`: Takes `node` out of its parent, with everything inside it; nothing where it has no parent.
- `function replace_node(@doc: Document, old: i64, new: i64) -> ()?`, called `html.replace_node(@doc, old: old, new: new)`: Puts `new` where `old` stands and takes `old` out. Fails `invalid`.
- `function unwrap(@doc: Document, node: i64)`, called `html.unwrap(@doc, node)`: Puts the children of `node` where `node` stands, in order, and takes `node` out; nothing where it has no parent.
- `function set_text(@doc: Document, node: i64, text: str)`, called `html.set_text(@doc, node, text)`: Sets the text of `node`: an element's or a fragment's children replaced by one text node, or a text's, a comment's or an instruction's characters replaced.
- `function remove_children(@doc: Document, node: i64)`, called `html.remove_children(@doc, node)`: Takes every child of `node` out.
- `function set_inner_html(@doc: Document, node: i64, text: str)`, called `html.set_inner_html(@doc, node, text)`: Reads `text` as a fragment inside the element `node`, as setting `innerHTML` does, and puts what it reads in place of the children of `node`.
- `function copy_node(@doc: Document, node: i64) -> i64`, called `html.copy_node(@doc, node)`: A copy of `node` and everything inside it, held by nothing until it is put in.
- `function copy_from(@doc: Document, source: Document, node: i64) -> i64`, called `html.copy_from(doc: @doc, source: source, node)`: A copy, in `doc`, of the node `node` of `source` and everything inside it, held by nothing until it is put in.
- `function format(doc: Document) -> str`, called `html.format(doc)`: `doc` as HTML, by the standard's serialisation algorithm: its doctype, comments and elements in order.
- `function format_node(doc: Document, node: i64) -> str`, called `html.format_node(doc, node)`: `node` as HTML, itself and everything inside it, as `outerHTML` writes it.
- `function format_inner(doc: Document, node: i64) -> str`, called `html.format_inner(doc, node)`: What `node` holds as HTML, without itself, as `innerHTML` writes it.
- `function escape(s: str) -> str`, called `html.escape(s)`: `s` with `&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and `'` written `&amp;`, `&lt;`, `&gt;`, `&quot;` and `&#39;`, so that it stands as text or as a quoted attribute value anywhere.
- `function escape_text(s: str) -> str`, called `html.escape_text(s)`: `s` escaped as the standard's serialisation escapes text: `&`, a no-break space, `<` and `>` written `&amp;`, `&nbsp;`, `&lt;` and `&gt;`.
- `function escape_attribute(s: str) -> str`, called `html.escape_attribute(s)`: `s` escaped as the standard's serialisation escapes an attribute's value: as `escape_text`, and `"` written `&quot;`.
- `function unescape(s: str) -> str`, called `html.unescape(s)`: `s` with its character references read as reading reads them in text: every named reference of the standard, `&amp;` and the old ones written without `;` as `&amp`, and numeric ones, `&#65;` and `&#x41;`.
- `function unescape_attribute(s: str) -> str`, called `html.unescape_attribute(s)`: `s` with its character references read as reading reads them in an attribute's value: as `unescape`, but an old reference written without `;` and followed by a letter, a digit or `=` is kept as it is, so `?a=1&copy=2` keeps its `&copy`.
- `function named_reference(name: str) -> str?`, called `html.named_reference(name)`: The characters the named character reference `name` stands for: `amp;` stands for `&`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function named_references() -> {str: str}`, called `html.named_references()`: Every named character reference of the standard, 2,231, each name as the table writes it (`amp;`, and the old `amp`) to the characters it stands for.


### url

Layer 2, named `use <rebel>/url`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/url/).

A URL parsed, built and escaped, by RFC 3986 and touching no network: this module reads a text into the parts of a `Url`, writes the parts back, resolves a reference against a base, escapes and unescapes what a part holds, and reads a query as its keys and values in their order.

- `constant INVALID: str`, value `"invalid"`: The code of a text that is not what the function reads; the message says where and why.
- `constant NOT_TEXT: str`, value `"not_text"`: The code of escaped bytes that are not UTF-8, where the answer is a text.
- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `"not_found"`: The code of a key no pair holds, and of a port neither written nor known.
- `constant DOES_NOT_FIT: str`, value `"does_not_fit"`: The code of a port past 65535.
- `record Url(scheme: str, user: str, password: str, host: str, port: str, path: str, query: str, fragment: str, empty_authority: bool, empty_userinfo: bool, empty_password: bool, empty_query: bool, empty_fragment: bool)`: A URL in its parts, each a text and "" where the URL does not write it: `scheme://user:password@host:port/path?query#fragment`.
- `function parse(s: str) -> Url?`, called `url.parse(s)`: The parts of the URL `s` writes, a relative reference included: "/a?b", "../c" and "" are read too, with an empty scheme. Fails `invalid`, `not_text`.
- `function parse_loose(s: str) -> Url?`, called `url.parse_loose(s)`: The parts of the URL `s` writes, read as `parse` reads them after every byte its part may not hold is written as an escape: a space, a quote, a `[` in a query, a character above ASCII, a second "#", and a `%` that begins no escape, which becomes "%25". Fails `invalid`, `not_text`.
- `function parse_request_target(s: str) -> Url?`, called `url.parse_request_target(s)`: The parts of `s`, the target an HTTP request names: an absolute path with its query, "/a?b", or an absolute URL, "http://h/a?b" (RFC 9112 § 3.2). Fails `invalid`, `not_text`.
- `function format(u: Url) -> str`, called `url.format(u)`: The text of `u`, its parts joined by RFC 3986 § 5.3: the user, the password and the host are escaped, and in a raw part every byte the part may not hold is written as its escape, a `%` that begins no escape as "%25".
- `function redacted(u: Url) -> str`, called `url.redacted(u)`: The text of `u` with its password written "xxxxx", for a log, an empty password that is written included.
- `function request_target(u: Url) -> str`, called `url.request_target(u)`: The path and the query of `u` as the first line of an HTTP request names them: the path, "/" where it is empty and a "/" before it where it begins with none, then "?" and the query where `u` has one.
- `function is_abs(u: Url) -> bool`, called `url.is_abs(u)`: Whether `u` has a scheme, which is what tells a URL from a relative reference.
- `function without_fragment(u: Url) -> Url`, called `url.without_fragment(u)`: `u` without its fragment, an empty one included.
- `function resolve(base: Url, reference: Url) -> Url`, called `url.resolve(base: base, reference: reference)`: The URL `reference` names where it is found in `base`, by RFC 3986 § 5.2: "../g" against "http://a/b/c/d" is "http://a/b/g".
- `record HostPort(host: str, port: str)`: What `parse_host_port` answers: a host and a port told apart.
- `function parse_host_port(s: str) -> HostPort?`, called `url.parse_host_port(s)`: The host and the port of `s`, written as an authority writes them with no user before: "example.com", "example.com:8080", "[::1]:8080". Fails `invalid`, `not_text`.
- `function format_host_port(host: str, port: str) -> str`, called `url.format_host_port(host: host, port: port)`: The text "host:port" as an authority writes it: an IPv6 address in brackets, any other host escaped as a name, then ":" and `port` where `port` is not "".
- `function port_of(u: Url) -> i64?`, called `url.port_of(u)`: The port `u` is reached on, as a number: the one it writes, else the default of its scheme. Fails `not_found`, `does_not_fit`, `invalid`.
- `function default_port(scheme: str) -> i64?`, called `url.default_port(scheme)`: The port a URL of `scheme` is reached on where it writes none: 80 for "http", 443 for "https". Fails `not_found`.
- `function parse_path(path: str) -> [str]?`, called `url.parse_path(path)`: The segments of the raw path `path`, each unescaped: "/a%2Fb/c" answers ["a/b", "c"]. Fails `invalid`, `not_text`.
- `function format_path(segments: [str]) -> str`, called `url.format_path(segments)`: The raw path of `segments`, a "/" before each and each escaped as `escape_segment` does, so a "/" inside a segment stays in it: ["a/b", "c"] answers "/a%2Fb/c".
- `function add_segments(u: Url, segments: [str]) -> Url`, called `url.add_segments(u, segments)`: `u` with its path going on with `segments`, each escaped as `escape_segment` does: "http://h/v1" and ["users", "7"] answer "http://h/v1/users/7", and so does "http://h/v1/".
- `function remove_dot_segments(path: str) -> str`, called `url.remove_dot_segments(path)`: The raw path `path` without its "." and ".." segments, by RFC 3986 § 5.2.4: "/a/b/../c/./d" answers "/a/c/d".
- `function escape_segment(s: str) -> str`, called `url.escape_segment(s)`: `s` written as one segment of a path: every byte but a letter, a digit, "-", ".", "_" and "~" becomes "%" and two upper-case hexadecimal digits, the "/" included, so the segment stays one.
- `function escape_query(s: str) -> str`, called `url.escape_query(s)`: `s` written as a key or a value of a query, by the rules of a form (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`): a space becomes "+", and every other byte but a letter, a digit, "-", ".", "_" and "~" its escape.
- `function escape_fragment(s: str) -> str`, called `url.escape_fragment(s)`: `s` written as a fragment: as `escape_segment`, but "/" and "?" stay, which a fragment may hold as themselves.
- `function escape_bytes(data: [u8]) -> str`, called `url.escape_bytes(data)`: `data` written as escapes, for bytes that are no text: every byte but a letter, a digit, "-", ".", "_" and "~" becomes its escape.
- `function unescape(s: str) -> str?`, called `url.unescape(s)`: The text `s` stands for, each "%" and two hexadecimal digits read as one byte: what a path segment, a fragment or a name holds. Fails `invalid`, `not_text`.
- `function unescape_query(s: str) -> str?`, called `url.unescape_query(s)`: The text `s` stands for as a key or a value of a query: as `unescape`, and a "+" is a space. Fails as `unescape` does.
- `function unescape_bytes(s: str) -> [u8]?`, called `url.unescape_bytes(s)`: The bytes `s` stands for, each "%" and two hexadecimal digits read as one byte and every other byte as itself, text or not. Fails `invalid`.
- `record Pair(key: str, value: str)`: A key of a query and its value, both unescaped.
- `function parse_query(query: str) -> [Pair]?`, called `url.parse_query(query)`: The keys and values of the raw query `query`, in the order it writes them, a key held more than once kept each time: "a=1&b=2&a=3" answers three pairs. Fails `invalid`, `not_text`.
- `function format_query(pairs: [Pair]) -> str`, called `url.format_query(pairs)`: The raw query of `pairs`, in their order: each key and value escaped as `escape_query` does, "=" between the two and "&" between pairs.
- `function value_of(pairs: [Pair], key: str) -> str?`, called `url.value_of(pairs, key)`: The value of the first pair of `pairs` whose key is `key`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function values_of(pairs: [Pair], key: str) -> [str]`, called `url.values_of(pairs, key)`: The values of every pair of `pairs` whose key is `key`, in their order; none where no pair has it.
- `function has_key(pairs: [Pair], key: str) -> bool`, called `url.has_key(pairs, key)`: Whether a pair of `pairs` has the key `key`.
- `function with_value(pairs: [Pair], key: str, value: str) -> [Pair]`, called `url.with_value(pairs, key: key, value: value)`: `pairs` with `key` holding `value` alone: the first pair with that key takes the value where it stands, every later one is left out, and where no pair has the key one is added at the end.
- `function without_key(pairs: [Pair], key: str) -> [Pair]`, called `url.without_key(pairs, key)`: `pairs` without the pairs whose key is `key`, the others in their order.


### crypto

Layer 2, named `use <rebel>/crypto`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/crypto/).

Cryptographic digests, the MACs and key derivations over them, password hashing, and the comparison of two byte lists in constant time: MD5, SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256 (FIPS 180-4 and RFC 1321) and SHA3-224 to SHA3-512 (FIPS 202), all at once or in steps; SHAKE128, SHAKE256 and cSHAKE read to any length (FIPS 202, SP 800-185); BLAKE2b and BLAKE2s keyed or not (RFC 7693) and BLAKE3 in its three modes; HMAC (RFC 2104); HKDF (RFC 5869); PBKDF2 (RFC 8018) and scrypt (RFC 7914); Argon2 (RFC 9106) and bcrypt, with the PHC and modular crypt strings a password's hash is stored in; one-time passwords, HOTP (RFC 4226) and TOTP (RFC 6238), with the otpauth URI that hands their key to an authenticator app.

- `constant INVALID: str`, value `"invalid"`: The code a function fails with where its input is not what it reads: a length or a count `hkdf_expand`, `hkdf`, `pbkdf2`, `shake128`, `blake2b`, `blake3_derive_key` or `scrypt` cannot make, a cost `argon2` or `hash_bcrypt` refuses, a stored hash `verify_argon2` or `verify_bcrypt` cannot read, or a name `parse_algorithm` does not know.
- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `"not_found"`: The code `verify_hotp` and `verify_totp` fail with where no counter they try makes the code given.
- `constant MAX_OTP_WINDOW: i64`, value `1000`: The most counters `verify_hotp` tries after the one it expects, and the most steps `verify_totp` tries on either side of the time's own, so that a window read from a setting cannot make a check take the time without bound: each counter tried costs one HMAC.
- `constant MAX_MEMORY: i64`, value `2147483648`: The most memory, in bytes, that `scrypt` and `argon2` may be asked to fill: 2 GiB, which admits RFC 9106's first recommendation (Argon2id over 2 GiB) and RFC 7914's largest vector (1 GiB).
- `variant Algorithm = .md5 | .sha1 | .sha224 | .sha256 | .sha384 | .sha512 | .sha512_224 | .sha512_256 | .sha3_224 | .sha3_256 | .sha3_384 | .sha3_512`: Which digest a function computes.
- `function digest_size(algorithm: Algorithm) -> i64`, called `crypto.digest_size(algorithm)`: The length of a digest by `algorithm`, in bytes: Python's `digest_size`.
- `function block_size(algorithm: Algorithm) -> i64`, called `crypto.block_size(algorithm)`: The length of the blocks `algorithm` digests, in bytes: 64 for MD5, SHA-1, SHA-224 and SHA-256, 128 for the other SHA-2 digests, and for SHA-3 its rate, 144, 136, 104 and 72 bytes from SHA3-224 to SHA3-512, as Python's `block_size` answers.
- `function format_algorithm(algorithm: Algorithm) -> str`, called `crypto.format_algorithm(algorithm)`: The name of `algorithm` as Python's `hashlib` writes it: `md5`, `sha1`, `sha224`, `sha256`, `sha384`, `sha512`, `sha512_224`, `sha512_256`, `sha3_224`, `sha3_256`, `sha3_384` or `sha3_512`.
- `function parse_algorithm(s: str) -> Algorithm?`, called `crypto.parse_algorithm(s)`: The algorithm `s` names, as `format_algorithm` writes it. Fails `invalid`.
- `function md5(data: [u8]) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.md5(data)`: The MD5 digest of `data`, 16 bytes.
- `function md5_text(s: str) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.md5_text(s)`: The MD5 digest of the bytes of `s`, what `md5` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function sha1(data: [u8]) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha1(data)`: The SHA-1 digest of `data`, 20 bytes.
- `function sha1_text(s: str) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha1_text(s)`: The SHA-1 digest of the bytes of `s`, what `sha1` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function sha224(data: [u8]) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha224(data)`: The SHA-224 digest of `data`, 28 bytes.
- `function sha224_text(s: str) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha224_text(s)`: The SHA-224 digest of the bytes of `s`, what `sha224` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function sha256(data: [u8]) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha256(data)`: The SHA-256 digest of `data`, 32 bytes.
- `function sha256_text(s: str) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha256_text(s)`: The SHA-256 digest of the bytes of `s`, what `sha256` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function sha384(data: [u8]) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha384(data)`: The SHA-384 digest of `data`, 48 bytes.
- `function sha384_text(s: str) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha384_text(s)`: The SHA-384 digest of the bytes of `s`, what `sha384` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function sha512(data: [u8]) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha512(data)`: The SHA-512 digest of `data`, 64 bytes.
- `function sha512_text(s: str) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha512_text(s)`: The SHA-512 digest of the bytes of `s`, what `sha512` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function sha512_224(data: [u8]) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha512_224(data)`: The SHA-512/224 digest of `data`, 28 bytes: SHA-512's work from its own starting words, so not SHA-512's digest cut short.
- `function sha512_224_text(s: str) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha512_224_text(s)`: The SHA-512/224 digest of the bytes of `s`, what `sha512_224` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function sha512_256(data: [u8]) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha512_256(data)`: The SHA-512/256 digest of `data`, 32 bytes: SHA-512's work from its own starting words, so not SHA-512's digest cut short.
- `function sha512_256_text(s: str) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha512_256_text(s)`: The SHA-512/256 digest of the bytes of `s`, what `sha512_256` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function sha3_224(data: [u8]) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha3_224(data)`: The SHA3-224 digest of `data`, 28 bytes.
- `function sha3_224_text(s: str) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha3_224_text(s)`: The SHA3-224 digest of the bytes of `s`, what `sha3_224` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function sha3_256(data: [u8]) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha3_256(data)`: The SHA3-256 digest of `data`, 32 bytes.
- `function sha3_256_text(s: str) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha3_256_text(s)`: The SHA3-256 digest of the bytes of `s`, what `sha3_256` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function sha3_384(data: [u8]) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha3_384(data)`: The SHA3-384 digest of `data`, 48 bytes.
- `function sha3_384_text(s: str) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha3_384_text(s)`: The SHA3-384 digest of the bytes of `s`, what `sha3_384` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function sha3_512(data: [u8]) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha3_512(data)`: The SHA3-512 digest of `data`, 64 bytes.
- `function sha3_512_text(s: str) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.sha3_512_text(s)`: The SHA3-512 digest of the bytes of `s`, what `sha3_512` answers for its UTF-8.
- `record State(algorithm: Algorithm, run: engine.Run)`: A digest or an HMAC computed in steps: the caller holds it, feeds it piece by piece with `update` and `update_text`, and reads `digest` whenever it wants, which answers what feeding all the pieces at once would.
- `function start(algorithm: Algorithm) -> State`, called `crypto.start(algorithm)`: A state of `algorithm` that has been fed nothing.
- `function start_hmac(algorithm: Algorithm, key: [u8]) -> State`, called `crypto.start_hmac(algorithm, key)`: A state of the HMAC of `algorithm` under `key` that has been fed nothing of the message: `digest` answers the tag.
- `function update(@state: State, data: [u8])`, called `crypto.update(@state, data)`: Feeds `data` to `state`, whose digest then covers what it was fed before and then `data`.
- `function update_text(@state: State, s: str)`, called `crypto.update_text(@state, s)`: Feeds the bytes of `s` to `state`, as `update` feeds its UTF-8.
- `function digest(state: State) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.digest(state)`: The digest of every byte `state` was fed, or for an HMAC its tag: `digest_size` bytes.
- `function hmac(algorithm: Algorithm, key: [u8], data: [u8]) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.hmac(algorithm, key: key, data: data)`: The HMAC of `data` under `key` by `algorithm` (RFC 2104): a tag of `digest_size` bytes that only a holder of the key can make.
- `function hmac_text(algorithm: Algorithm, key: [u8], s: str) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.hmac_text(algorithm, key, s)`: The HMAC of the bytes of `s` under `key` by `algorithm`, what `hmac` answers for its UTF-8.
- `function equals_constant_time(a: [u8], b: [u8]) -> bool`, called `crypto.equals_constant_time(a: a, b: b)`: Whether `a` and `b` are the same bytes, in a time their contents do not decide: every byte pair is visited and no branch of the code depends on a byte's value.
- `variant Shake = .shake128 | .shake256`: Which of FIPS 202's extendable-output functions a `ShakeState` computes: its output is as long as the caller asks.
- `record ShakeState(shake: Shake, run: engine.Run)`: SHAKE or cSHAKE computed in steps: fed with `update_shake`, and read with `digest_shake` to any length, which answers the first bytes of one endless output, so a longer read begins with a shorter one.
- `function shake128(data: [u8], length: i64) -> [u8]?`, called `crypto.shake128(data, length)`: The first `length` bytes of SHAKE128 over `data` (FIPS 202 6.2): an output of any length, 32 bytes giving its full strength. Fails `invalid`.
- `function shake256(data: [u8], length: i64) -> [u8]?`, called `crypto.shake256(data, length)`: The first `length` bytes of SHAKE256 over `data` (FIPS 202 6.2), 64 bytes giving its full strength. Fails `invalid`.
- `function start_shake(shake: Shake) -> ShakeState`, called `crypto.start_shake(shake)`: A state of `shake` that has been fed nothing.
- `function start_cshake(shake: Shake, name: [u8], custom: [u8]) -> ShakeState`, called `crypto.start_cshake(shake, name: name, custom: custom)`: A state of cSHAKE (SP 800-185 3) that has been fed nothing: SHAKE kept apart from every other use by a function's name and a customization, so two uses of one input answer unrelated bytes.
- `function update_shake(@state: ShakeState, data: [u8])`, called `crypto.update_shake(@state, data)`: Feeds `data` to `state`, whose output then covers what it was fed before and then `data`.
- `function digest_shake(state: ShakeState, length: i64) -> [u8]?`, called `crypto.digest_shake(state, length)`: The first `length` bytes of the output of every byte `state` was fed. Fails `invalid`.
- `variant Blake2 = .blake2b | .blake2s`: Which BLAKE2 (RFC 7693) a `Blake2State` computes.
- `record Blake2State(blake2: Blake2, run: blake2_work.Run)`: A BLAKE2 digest computed in steps: fed with `update_blake2`, read with `digest_blake2` at any moment.
- `function blake2b(key: [u8], data: [u8], length: i64) -> [u8]?`, called `crypto.blake2b(key: key, data: data, length)`: The BLAKE2b digest of `data`, `length` bytes, under `key` when it is not empty: a digest at least as strong as SHA-3, faster, and a MAC of its own when keyed, with no HMAC around it. Fails `invalid`.
- `function blake2s(key: [u8], data: [u8], length: i64) -> [u8]?`, called `crypto.blake2s(key: key, data: data, length)`: The BLAKE2s digest of `data`, `length` bytes, under `key` when it is not empty: BLAKE2 for machines of 32 bits and for small digests. Fails `invalid`.
- `function start_blake2(blake2: Blake2, key: [u8], salt: [u8], person: [u8], length: i64) -> Blake2State?`, called `crypto.start_blake2(blake2, key: key, salt: salt, person: person, length)`: A state of `blake2` that has been fed nothing, with every parameter of the sequential mode Python's `hashlib` takes. Fails `invalid`.
- `function update_blake2(@state: Blake2State, data: [u8])`, called `crypto.update_blake2(@state, data)`: Feeds `data` to `state`, whose digest then covers what it was fed before and then `data`.
- `function digest_blake2(state: Blake2State) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.digest_blake2(state)`: The digest of every byte `state` was fed, of the size it was started with.
- `function format_blake2(blake2: Blake2) -> str`, called `crypto.format_blake2(blake2)`: The name of `blake2`, `blake2b` or `blake2s`, as Python's `hashlib` writes it.
- `record Blake3State(run: blake3_work.Run)`: A BLAKE3 hash computed in steps, in one of its three modes: a plain hash, a keyed hash, or a key derived under a context.
- `function blake3(data: [u8]) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.blake3(data)`: The BLAKE3 hash of `data`, 32 bytes: a digest as strong as SHA-3 and much faster, its input cut in chunks joined by a tree.
- `function blake3_keyed(key: [u8], data: [u8]) -> [u8]?`, called `crypto.blake3_keyed(key: key, data: data)`: The BLAKE3 keyed hash of `data` under `key`, 32 bytes: a MAC with no HMAC around it. Fails `invalid`.
- `function blake3_derive_key(context: str, material: [u8], length: i64) -> [u8]?`, called `crypto.blake3_derive_key(context, material, length)`: `length` bytes of key derived by BLAKE3 from `material` under `context`: the context names the use, so one material gives unrelated keys to two uses. Fails `invalid`.
- `function start_blake3() -> Blake3State`, called `crypto.start_blake3()`: A state of the plain BLAKE3 hash that has been fed nothing.
- `function start_blake3_keyed(key: [u8]) -> Blake3State?`, called `crypto.start_blake3_keyed(key)`: A state of the BLAKE3 keyed hash under `key` that has been fed nothing. Fails `invalid`.
- `function start_blake3_derive_key(context: str) -> Blake3State`, called `crypto.start_blake3_derive_key(context)`: A state of BLAKE3's key derivation under `context` that has been fed none of the key material.
- `function update_blake3(@state: Blake3State, data: [u8])`, called `crypto.update_blake3(@state, data)`: Feeds `data` to `state`, whose output then covers what it was fed before and then `data`.
- `function digest_blake3(state: Blake3State, length: i64) -> [u8]?`, called `crypto.digest_blake3(state, length)`: The first `length` bytes of the output of every byte `state` was fed; 32 bytes are the hash. Fails `invalid`.
- `function digest_blake3_from(state: Blake3State, offset: i64, length: i64) -> [u8]?`, called `crypto.digest_blake3_from(state, offset: offset, length: length)`: `length` bytes of the output of every byte `state` was fed, from the byte `offset` of it: the output is computed from there, not from its start, as Python's `seek` and Rust's `set_position` read it. Fails `invalid`.
- `function hkdf_extract(algorithm: Algorithm, secret: [u8], salt: [u8]) -> [u8]`, called `crypto.hkdf_extract(algorithm, secret: secret, salt: salt)`: HKDF's extraction (RFC 5869 2.2): a pseudorandom key of `digest_size` bytes made from `secret`, which may be unevenly random, the HMAC of `secret` under `salt`.
- `function hkdf_expand(algorithm: Algorithm, key: [u8], info: [u8], length: i64) -> [u8]?`, called `crypto.hkdf_expand(algorithm, key: key, info: info, length)`: HKDF's expansion (RFC 5869 2.3): `length` bytes of keying material made from `key`, bound to `info`. Fails `invalid`.
- `function hkdf(algorithm: Algorithm, secret: [u8], salt: [u8], info: [u8], length: i64) -> [u8]?`, called `crypto.hkdf(algorithm, secret: secret, salt: salt, info: info, length)`: HKDF whole (RFC 5869): `length` bytes of keying material made from `secret`, extracted with `salt` and expanded with `info`. Fails `invalid`.
- `function pbkdf2(algorithm: Algorithm, password: [u8], salt: [u8], iterations: i64, length: i64) -> [u8]?`, called `crypto.pbkdf2(algorithm, password: password, salt: salt, iterations: iterations, length: length)`: PBKDF2 (RFC 8018 5.2) with the HMAC of `algorithm`: `length` bytes of key made from a password, slowed by `iterations` so that each guess of it costs as much. Fails `invalid`.
- `function scrypt(password: [u8], salt: [u8], n: i64, r: i64, p: i64, length: i64) -> [u8]?`, called `crypto.scrypt(password: password, salt: salt, n: n, r: r, p: p, length: length)`: scrypt (RFC 7914): `length` bytes of key made from a password, each guess costing 128 × `r` × `n` bytes of memory and as many steps, so that a guesser's hardware buys little over the program's. Fails `invalid`.
- `variant Argon2 = .argon2d | .argon2i | .argon2id`: Which Argon2 (RFC 9106) a function computes.
- `record Argon2Params(argon2: Argon2, passes: i64, memory: i64, lanes: i64, length: i64)`: What an Argon2 hash costs and makes.
- `function argon2_low_memory() -> Argon2Params`, called `crypto.argon2_low_memory()`: RFC 9106 4's second recommendation, for a machine short of memory: Argon2id, 3 passes over 64 MiB in 4 lanes, a tag of 32 bytes, to be used with a salt of 16 bytes; Python's `argon2.profiles.RFC_9106_LOW_MEMORY`.
- `function argon2_high_memory() -> Argon2Params`, called `crypto.argon2_high_memory()`: RFC 9106 4's first recommendation: Argon2id, 1 pass over 2 GiB in 4 lanes, a tag of 32 bytes, to be used with a salt of 16 bytes; Python's `argon2.profiles.RFC_9106_HIGH_MEMORY`.
- `function argon2(params: Argon2Params, password: [u8], salt: [u8], secret: [u8], data: [u8]) -> [u8]?`, called `crypto.argon2(params, password: password, salt: salt, secret: secret, data: data)`: The Argon2 tag of `password` (RFC 9106): `params.length` bytes that cost `params.memory` KiB and `params.passes` passes to make, as a password's hash or as a key. Fails `invalid`.
- `function hash_argon2(params: Argon2Params, password: [u8], salt: [u8]) -> str?`, called `crypto.hash_argon2(params, password: password, salt: salt)`: The PHC string of `password`'s Argon2 hash, the form a password is stored in: `$argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$` and the salt and the tag in base 64 with no padding. Fails `invalid`.
- `function verify_argon2(password: [u8], hash: str) -> bool?`, called `crypto.verify_argon2(password, hash)`: Whether `password` is the one `hash`, a PHC string of Argon2, was made from: the tag computed again with the string's type, version, costs and salt, and compared in constant time. Fails `invalid`.
- `function parse_argon2(hash: str) -> Argon2Params?`, called `crypto.parse_argon2(hash)`: The type and the costs a PHC string of Argon2 was made with, to tell a hash stored with costs now too low, which the program then hashes again. Fails `invalid`.
- `function hash_bcrypt(password: [u8], salt: [u8], cost: i64) -> str?`, called `crypto.hash_bcrypt(password: password, salt: salt, cost)`: The string of `password`'s bcrypt hash, `$2b$`, the cost in two digits, `$`, the salt and the hash in bcrypt's own base 64, 60 characters: OpenBSD's form, which every bcrypt reads. Fails `invalid`.
- `function verify_bcrypt(password: [u8], hash: str) -> bool?`, called `crypto.verify_bcrypt(password, hash)`: Whether `password` is the one `hash`, a bcrypt string, was made from: the string made again with its own salt and cost and compared whole, in constant time, as OpenBSD's does. Fails `invalid`.
- `function parse_bcrypt_cost(hash: str) -> i64?`, called `crypto.parse_bcrypt_cost(hash)`: The cost a bcrypt string was made with, 4 to 31, to tell a hash stored with a cost now too low: Go's `bcrypt.Cost`. Fails `invalid`.
- `record Otp(algorithm: Algorithm, key: [u8], digits: i64, period: i64)`: What a one-time password is made with, HOTP's (RFC 4226) and TOTP's (RFC 6238) alike: the digest of its HMAC, the key shared with the authenticator, the length of a code, and the seconds a TOTP code lasts.
- `function new_otp(key: [u8]) -> Otp`, called `crypto.new_otp(key)`: The settings of a one-time password under `key` with the defaults of RFC 6238 and of the authenticator apps: SHA-1, 6 digits and 30 seconds.
- `function hotp(otp: Otp, counter: u64) -> str?`, called `crypto.hotp(otp, counter)`: The HOTP code of `counter` (RFC 4226): the HMAC of the counter as eight bytes, the highest first, cut by the RFC's dynamic truncation to 31 bits and written as its last `otp.digits` decimal digits, zeros in front. Fails `invalid`.
- `function totp(otp: Otp, seconds: i64) -> str?`, called `crypto.totp(otp, seconds)`: The TOTP code of the time `seconds` (RFC 6238): the HOTP code of its time step, `seconds` divided by `otp.period`, so that one code lasts from one multiple of the period to the next. Fails `invalid`.
- `function verify_hotp(otp: Otp, code: str, counter: u64, window: i64) -> u64?`, called `crypto.verify_hotp(otp, code, counter, window)`: The counter whose HOTP code `code` is: `counter`, or one of the `window` counters after it, RFC 4226's look-ahead, so that a code made by a device that counted on without the server is still taken. Fails `not_found`, `invalid`.
- `function verify_totp(otp: Otp, code: str, seconds: i64, window: i64) -> u64?`, called `crypto.verify_totp(otp, code, seconds: seconds, window: window)`: The time step whose TOTP code `code` is: the step of `seconds`, or one within `window` steps before or after it, for a clock that runs early or late, the nearest first. Fails `not_found`, `invalid`.
- `function format_hotp_uri(otp: Otp, account: str, issuer: str, counter: u64) -> str?`, called `crypto.format_hotp_uri(otp, account: account, issuer: issuer, counter)`: The otpauth URI that hands `otp`'s HOTP settings and the next counter to an authenticator app, in Google Authenticator's Key Uri Format, often shown as a QR code: `otpauth://hotp/`, the issuer, a colon and the account as its label, then the key in base 32 with no padding (`bytes.format_base32_unpadded`, which `bytes.parse_base32_unpadded` reads back), the issuer, the digest's name, the digits and the counter. Fails `invalid`.
- `function format_totp_uri(otp: Otp, account: str, issuer: str) -> str?`, called `crypto.format_totp_uri(otp, account: account, issuer: issuer)`: The otpauth URI that hands `otp`'s TOTP settings to an authenticator app, in Google Authenticator's Key Uri Format: what `format_hotp_uri` writes, `totp` for `hotp`, with the period in place of the counter. Fails `invalid`.


### big

Layer 2, named `use <rebel>/big`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/big/).

Numbers of any size, held exactly: integers, decimals and fractions, their arithmetic, and their text in any base.

- `constant INVALID: str`, value `"invalid"`: The code of a text that is not a number of the form the function reads, and of an inverse that does not exist: `parse`, `parse_base`, `parse_literal`, `parse_decimal`, `parse_fraction`, `power_mod`, `inverse_mod`, `sqrt_mod`, and the conversions from a float given NaN.
- `constant DOES_NOT_FIT: str`, value `"does_not_fit"`: The code of a number outside the type asked for, the language's own code: `int_of`, `u64_of`, `to_bytes`, `to_bytes_width`, `to_bytes_signed_width`, `exact_scale`, an exponent past `MAX_EXPONENT` in a text, and the conversions from a float given an infinity.
- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `"not_found"`: The code of a square root modulo a prime that does not exist: `sqrt_mod`.
- `constant MAX_EXPONENT: i64`, value `999999`: The largest exponent `parse_decimal` and `parse_fraction` read after an `e`, either sign: Python's `decimal` holds the same bound in its default context.
- `record Integer(value: signed.Signed)`: An integer of any size.
- `record Decimal(unscaled: Integer, scale: i64)`: A decimal number: `unscaled` divided by ten to the power `scale`, so 1.50 is 150 with a scale of 2 and 1500 is 15 with a scale of -2.
- `record Fraction(numerator: Integer, denominator: Integer)`: A fraction in lowest terms.
- `record Division(quotient: Integer, remainder: Integer)`: What `divide` and `divide_euclidean` answer: `n` equals `quotient` times `by`, plus `remainder`.
- `record DecimalDivision(quotient: Integer, remainder: Decimal)`: What `divide_decimal_whole` answers: `n` equals `quotient` times `by`, plus `remainder`.
- `record Bezout(gcd: Integer, x: Integer, y: Integer)`: What `gcd_with_coefficients` answers: `gcd` equals `a` times `x` plus `b` times `y`.
- `variant Rounding = .toward_zero | .away_from_zero | .floor | .ceiling | .half_even | .half_away_from_zero | .half_toward_zero | .away_if_zero_or_five`: How a result that falls between two numbers is rounded to one of them.
- `variant ByteOrder = .big_endian | .little_endian`: The order of an integer's bytes.
- `function from_int(n: i64) -> Integer`, called `big.from_int(n)`: The integer `n`.
- `function from_u64(n: u64) -> Integer`, called `big.from_u64(n)`: The integer `n`.
- `function int_of(n: Integer) -> i64?`, called `big.int_of(n)`: `n` as an `i64`. Fails `does_not_fit`.
- `function u64_of(n: Integer) -> u64?`, called `big.u64_of(n)`: `n` as a `u64`. Fails `does_not_fit`.
- `function float_of(n: Integer) -> f64`, called `big.float_of(n)`: The `f64` nearest `n`, a tie going to the one whose last bit is zero.
- `function from_float(x: f64) -> Integer?`, called `big.from_float(x)`: The integer part of `x`, its fraction dropped toward zero, exactly: 1e300 answers all of its 301 digits. Fails `invalid`, `does_not_fit`.
- `function parse(s: str) -> Integer?`, called `big.parse(s)`: The integer `s` spells in base ten: an optional `+` or `-`, then one digit or more, and nothing else. Fails `invalid`.
- `function parse_base(s: str, base: i64) -> Integer?`, called `big.parse_base(s, base)`: The integer `s` spells in `base`: an optional `+` or `-`, then one digit of `base` or more, with no prefix. Fails `invalid`.
- `function parse_literal(s: str) -> Integer?`, called `big.parse_literal(s)`: The integer `s` spells as the language writes one: an optional sign, then `0x`, `0o` or `0b` and digits of base 16, 8 or 2, or digits of base ten, with a `_` allowed between two digits. Fails `invalid`.
- `function format(n: Integer) -> str`, called `big.format(n)`: `n` in base ten: a `-` where it is negative, then its digits, with no zero before them.
- `function format_base(n: Integer, base: i64) -> str`, called `big.format_base(n, base)`: `n` in `base`: a `-` where it is negative, then its digits with no prefix and no zero before them.
- `function from_bytes(b: [u8], order: ByteOrder) -> Integer`, called `big.from_bytes(b, order)`: The integer that the bytes `b` spell as an unsigned number.
- `function from_bytes_signed(b: [u8], order: ByteOrder) -> Integer`, called `big.from_bytes_signed(b, order)`: The integer that the bytes `b` spell in two's complement, the top bit of the most significant byte being the sign.
- `function to_bytes(n: Integer, order: ByteOrder) -> [u8]?`, called `big.to_bytes(n, order)`: `n` as the fewest bytes that spell it as an unsigned number. Fails `does_not_fit`.
- `function to_bytes_signed(n: Integer, order: ByteOrder) -> [u8]`, called `big.to_bytes_signed(n, order)`: `n` as the fewest bytes that spell it in two's complement.
- `function to_bytes_width(n: Integer, width: i64, order: ByteOrder) -> [u8]?`, called `big.to_bytes_width(n, width, order)`: `n` as exactly `width` bytes spelling it as an unsigned number, zeros filling the most significant ones. Fails `does_not_fit`.
- `function to_bytes_signed_width(n: Integer, width: i64, order: ByteOrder) -> [u8]?`, called `big.to_bytes_signed_width(n, width, order)`: `n` as exactly `width` bytes in two's complement, the sign filling the most significant ones. Fails `does_not_fit`.
- `function sign(n: Integer) -> i64`, called `big.sign(n)`: -1, 0 or 1 as `n` is below zero, zero, or above it.
- `function abs(n: Integer) -> Integer`, called `big.abs(n)`: `n` without its sign.
- `function negate(n: Integer) -> Integer`, called `big.negate(n)`: `n` with its sign turned; zero stays zero.
- `function compare(a: Integer, b: Integer) -> i64`, called `big.compare(a: a, b: b)`: -1, 0 or 1 as `a` is below `b`, equal to it, or above it.
- `function compare_abs(a: Integer, b: Integer) -> i64`, called `big.compare_abs(a: a, b: b)`: -1, 0 or 1 as the absolute value of `a` is below that of `b`, equal to it, or above it.
- `function add(a: Integer, b: Integer) -> Integer`, called `big.add(a: a, b: b)`: `a` plus `b`.
- `function subtract(a: Integer, b: Integer) -> Integer`, called `big.subtract(a: a, b: b)`: `a` less `b`.
- `function multiply(a: Integer, b: Integer) -> Integer`, called `big.multiply(a: a, b: b)`: `a` times `b`.
- `function divide(n: Integer, by: Integer, rounding: Rounding) -> Division`, called `big.divide(n: n, by: by, rounding)`: The quotient of `n` by `by` rounded as `rounding` says, and what remains.
- `function divide_euclidean(n: Integer, by: Integer) -> Division`, called `big.divide_euclidean(n: n, by: by)`: The quotient of `n` by `by` whose remainder is never negative, and the remainder, from 0 to the absolute value of `by` less one.
- `function power(base: Integer, exponent: i64) -> Integer`, called `big.power(base, exponent)`: `base` raised to the power `exponent`.
- `function power_mod(base: Integer, exponent: Integer, modulus: Integer) -> Integer?`, called `big.power_mod(base: base, exponent: exponent, modulus: modulus)`: `base` raised to the power `exponent`, modulo `modulus`: from 0 to the absolute value of `modulus` less one, whatever the signs. Fails `invalid`.
- `function inverse_mod(n: Integer, modulus: Integer) -> Integer?`, called `big.inverse_mod(n: n, modulus: modulus)`: The inverse of `n` modulo `modulus`: the integer from 0 to the absolute value of `modulus` less one that times `n` leaves 1. Fails `invalid`.
- `function sqrt_mod(n: Integer, prime: Integer) -> Integer?`, called `big.sqrt_mod(n: n, prime: prime)`: A square root of `n` modulo the odd prime `prime`: an integer from 0 to `prime` less one whose square leaves `n`, the one Go's `ModSqrt` answers. Fails `not_found`, `invalid`.
- `function jacobi(a: Integer, b: Integer) -> i64`, called `big.jacobi(a: a, b: b)`: The Jacobi symbol of `a` over `b`: -1, 0 or 1.
- `function is_probable_prime(n: Integer, rounds: i64) -> bool`, called `big.is_probable_prime(n, rounds)`: Whether `n` is prime, by the Baillie-PSW test and `rounds` more rounds of Miller-Rabin.
- `function gcd(a: Integer, b: Integer) -> Integer`, called `big.gcd(a: a, b: b)`: The greatest common divisor of `a` and `b`, never negative.
- `function lcm(a: Integer, b: Integer) -> Integer`, called `big.lcm(a: a, b: b)`: The least common multiple of `a` and `b`, never negative.
- `function gcd_with_coefficients(a: Integer, b: Integer) -> Bezout`, called `big.gcd_with_coefficients(a: a, b: b)`: The greatest common divisor of `a` and `b`, with the coefficients `x` and `y` that make it `a` times `x` plus `b` times `y`.
- `function sqrt(n: Integer) -> Integer`, called `big.sqrt(n)`: The square root of `n`, rounded down: the largest integer whose square is not above `n`.
- `function factorial(n: i64) -> Integer`, called `big.factorial(n)`: `n` factorial: the product of the integers from 1 to `n`.
- `function binomial(n: i64, k: i64) -> Integer`, called `big.binomial(n: n, k: k)`: The count of ways to choose `k` things of `n`.
- `function product_of_range(from: i64, to: i64) -> Integer`, called `big.product_of_range(from: from, to: to)`: The product of the integers from `from` to `to`, `to` left out as the built-in `range` leaves it.
- `function bit_len(n: Integer) -> i64`, called `big.bit_len(n)`: How many bits the absolute value of `n` needs: 0 for zero.
- `function bit_count(n: Integer) -> i64`, called `big.bit_count(n)`: How many bits of the absolute value of `n` are 1.
- `function trailing_zero_bits(n: Integer) -> i64`, called `big.trailing_zero_bits(n)`: How many zero bits end the absolute value of `n`: 0 for zero.
- `function bit(n: Integer, index: i64) -> bool`, called `big.bit(n, index)`: Whether the bit `index` of `n` is 1, a negative `n` read in two's complement of infinite width.
- `function with_bit(n: Integer, index: i64, value: bool) -> Integer`, called `big.with_bit(n, index, value)`: `n` with its bit `index` set to 1 where `value` is true and to 0 where it is false, a negative `n` read in two's complement of infinite width.
- `function bit_and(a: Integer, b: Integer) -> Integer`, called `big.bit_and(a: a, b: b)`: The bits that are 1 in both `a` and `b`, as two's complement of infinite width reads a negative integer.
- `function bit_or(a: Integer, b: Integer) -> Integer`, called `big.bit_or(a: a, b: b)`: The bits that are 1 in `a` or `b`, as two's complement of infinite width reads a negative integer.
- `function bit_xor(a: Integer, b: Integer) -> Integer`, called `big.bit_xor(a: a, b: b)`: The bits that are 1 in one of `a` and `b` and not both, as two's complement of infinite width reads a negative integer.
- `function bit_and_not(a: Integer, b: Integer) -> Integer`, called `big.bit_and_not(a: a, b: b)`: The bits that are 1 in `a` and 0 in `b`, as two's complement of infinite width reads a negative integer.
- `function bit_not(n: Integer) -> Integer`, called `big.bit_not(n)`: Every bit of `n` turned, which is -1 less `n`.
- `function shift_left(n: Integer, count: i64) -> Integer`, called `big.shift_left(n, count)`: `n` times 2 to the power `count`.
- `function shift_right(n: Integer, count: i64) -> Integer`, called `big.shift_right(n, count)`: `n` divided by 2 to the power `count`, rounded toward the floor, as two's complement shifts: -1 shifted right stays -1.
- `function random_below(@generator: random.Generator, n: Integer) -> Integer`, called `big.random_below(@generator, n)`: An integer from 0 to `n` less one, every one as likely.
- `function random_below_chacha8(@generator: random.ChaCha8, n: Integer) -> Integer`, called `big.random_below_chacha8(@generator, n)`: An integer from 0 to `n` less one, every one as likely, drawn from a ChaCha8, whose numbers nobody who has not its seed can tell: the draw a key or a secret exponent is made by, from a generator `random.from_system_chacha8` seeded.
- `function digit_count(n: Integer) -> i64`, called `big.digit_count(n)`: How many decimal digits the absolute value of `n` has: zero has one.
- `function parse_decimal(s: str) -> Decimal?`, called `big.parse_decimal(s)`: The decimal `s` spells: an optional `+` or `-`, digits with at most one `.` among them or at either end, at least one digit, then optionally `e` or `E`, an optional sign and the digits of a power of ten. Fails `invalid`, `does_not_fit`.
- `function format_decimal(d: Decimal) -> str`, called `big.format_decimal(d)`: `d` written with a point and no exponent: as many digits after the point as its scale, none where the scale is 0 or less.
- `function format_decimal_scientific(d: Decimal) -> str`, called `big.format_decimal_scientific(d)`: `d` written as the General Decimal Arithmetic writes it, which is Python's `str` of a `Decimal`: with a point and no exponent where the exponent is 0 or less and the number is not below one millionth, else one digit, the rest after a point, and `E` with its sign.
- `function format_decimal_engineering(d: Decimal) -> str`, called `big.format_decimal_engineering(d)`: `d` written as `format_decimal_scientific` writes it, but with an exponent that is a multiple of three, as Python's `to_eng_string` writes it.
- `function add_decimal(a: Decimal, b: Decimal) -> Decimal`, called `big.add_decimal(a: a, b: b)`: `a` plus `b`, exactly, at the larger of their scales.
- `function subtract_decimal(a: Decimal, b: Decimal) -> Decimal`, called `big.subtract_decimal(a: a, b: b)`: `a` less `b`, exactly, at the larger of their scales.
- `function multiply_decimal(a: Decimal, b: Decimal) -> Decimal`, called `big.multiply_decimal(a: a, b: b)`: `a` times `b`, exactly, at the sum of their scales.
- `function divide_decimal(n: Decimal, by: Decimal, scale: i64, rounding: Rounding) -> Decimal`, called `big.divide_decimal(n: n, by: by, scale, rounding)`: `n` divided by `by`, rounded to `scale` digits after the point as `rounding` says.
- `function divide_decimal_whole(n: Decimal, by: Decimal, rounding: Rounding) -> DecimalDivision`, called `big.divide_decimal_whole(n: n, by: by, rounding)`: The whole quotient of `n` by `by` rounded as `rounding` says, and what remains.
- `function with_scale(d: Decimal, scale: i64, rounding: Rounding) -> Decimal`, called `big.with_scale(d, scale, rounding)`: `d` rounded to `scale` digits after the point as `rounding` says: Python's `quantize`.
- `function with_precision(d: Decimal, digits: i64, rounding: Rounding) -> Decimal`, called `big.with_precision(d, digits, rounding)`: `d` rounded to `digits` significant digits as `rounding` says, as Python's `decimal` rounds a result to its context's precision.
- `function trim_zeros(d: Decimal) -> Decimal`, called `big.trim_zeros(d)`: `d` with the zeros that end its digits taken off and its scale lowered by as many, so 1.500 is 1.5 and 1500 is 15 at scale -2: Python's `normalize`.
- `function compare_decimal(a: Decimal, b: Decimal) -> i64`, called `big.compare_decimal(a: a, b: b)`: -1, 0 or 1 as the value of `a` is below that of `b`, equal to it, or above it, whatever their scales.
- `function sqrt_decimal(d: Decimal, scale: i64, rounding: Rounding) -> Decimal`, called `big.sqrt_decimal(d, scale, rounding)`: The square root of `d`, rounded to `scale` digits after the point as `rounding` says.
- `function power_decimal(d: Decimal, exponent: i64) -> Decimal`, called `big.power_decimal(d, exponent)`: `d` raised to the power `exponent`, exactly, at `exponent` times its scale.
- `function decimal_of_float(x: f64) -> Decimal?`, called `big.decimal_of_float(x)`: The exact value of `x` as a decimal, with the fewest digits that hold it, as Python's `Decimal.from_float` answers: 0.1 is 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625. Fails `invalid`, `does_not_fit`.
- `function float_of_decimal(d: Decimal) -> f64`, called `big.float_of_decimal(d)`: The `f64` nearest the value of `d`, a tie going to the one whose last bit is zero.
- `function fraction(numerator: Integer, denominator: Integer) -> Fraction`, called `big.fraction(numerator: numerator, denominator: denominator)`: The fraction `numerator` over `denominator`, in lowest terms with the sign on the numerator.
- `function add_fraction(a: Fraction, b: Fraction) -> Fraction`, called `big.add_fraction(a: a, b: b)`: `a` plus `b`.
- `function subtract_fraction(a: Fraction, b: Fraction) -> Fraction`, called `big.subtract_fraction(a: a, b: b)`: `a` less `b`.
- `function multiply_fraction(a: Fraction, b: Fraction) -> Fraction`, called `big.multiply_fraction(a: a, b: b)`: `a` times `b`.
- `function divide_fraction(n: Fraction, by: Fraction) -> Fraction`, called `big.divide_fraction(n: n, by: by)`: `n` divided by `by`.
- `function power_fraction(f: Fraction, exponent: i64) -> Fraction`, called `big.power_fraction(f, exponent)`: `f` raised to the power `exponent`.
- `function compare_fraction(a: Fraction, b: Fraction) -> i64`, called `big.compare_fraction(a: a, b: b)`: -1, 0 or 1 as `a` is below `b`, equal to it, or above it.
- `function round_fraction(f: Fraction, rounding: Rounding) -> Integer`, called `big.round_fraction(f, rounding)`: `f` rounded to a whole number as `rounding` says.
- `function decimal_of_fraction(f: Fraction, scale: i64, rounding: Rounding) -> Decimal`, called `big.decimal_of_fraction(f, scale, rounding)`: `f` as a decimal of `scale` digits after the point, rounded as `rounding` says.
- `function fraction_of_decimal(d: Decimal) -> Fraction`, called `big.fraction_of_decimal(d)`: The value of `d` as a fraction in lowest terms.
- `function exact_scale(f: Fraction) -> i64?`, called `big.exact_scale(f)`: The fewest digits after the point that write `f` exactly as a decimal. Fails `does_not_fit`.
- `function float_of_fraction(f: Fraction) -> f64`, called `big.float_of_fraction(f)`: The `f64` nearest `f`, a tie going to the one whose last bit is zero.
- `function float32_of_fraction(f: Fraction) -> f32`, called `big.float32_of_fraction(f)`: The `f32` nearest `f`, rounded once, a tie going to the one whose last bit is zero.
- `function fraction_of_float(x: f64) -> Fraction?`, called `big.fraction_of_float(x)`: The exact value of `x` as a fraction: 0.1 is 3602879701896397/36028797018963968. Fails `invalid`, `does_not_fit`.
- `function approximate(f: Fraction, max_denominator: Integer) -> Fraction`, called `big.approximate(f, max_denominator)`: The fraction nearest `f` whose denominator is at most `max_denominator`, as Python's `limit_denominator` answers it.
- `function parse_fraction(s: str) -> Fraction?`, called `big.parse_fraction(s)`: The fraction `s` spells: an integer as `parse` reads one, a `/` and a denominator of digits alone, or a decimal as `parse_decimal` reads one. Fails `invalid`, `does_not_fit`.
- `function format_fraction(f: Fraction) -> str`, called `big.format_fraction(f)`: `f` written as its numerator, a `/` and its denominator, or as the numerator alone where the denominator is 1, as Python's `str` writes a `Fraction`.


### flags

Layer 2, named `use <rebel>/flags`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/flags/).

The arguments of a program read against a declaration: options long and short, with a value and without, given once or many times, positionals, subcommands, defaults, and a help page made from the declaration itself.

- `constant INVALID: str`, value `"invalid"`: The code of arguments the declaration does not read, and of a value that is not of its kind: `parse` and the functions that read a value as a number.
- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `"not_found"`: The code of a value asked for that was neither given nor declared with a default: `value_of`, `int_of`, `float_of`, `subcommand`.
- `constant NOT_TEXT: str`, value `"not_text"`: The code of an argument of the program that is not UTF-8: `parse_args`.
- `record Command(spec: decl.Spec)`: A command: its name, what it says of itself, the arguments it takes and its subcommands.
- `record Argument(want: decl.Want)`: One argument a command takes: a flag, an option with a value, or a positional.
- `variant Kind = .text | .integer | .float | .choice(among: [str])`: What an option's or a positional's values are read as; `parse` refuses a value that is not one.
- `variant Arity = .one | .optional | .many | .at_least_one`: How many values a positional takes.
- `function command(name: str, about: str) -> Command`, called `flags.command(name: name, about: about)`: A command named `name`, taking nothing yet, that answers `-h` and `--help` with its help.
- `function flag(long: str, short: str, help: str) -> Argument`, called `flags.flag(long: long, short: short, help: help)`: An option of no value: `--verbose`, `-v`.
- `function option(long: str, short: str, value_name: str, help: str) -> Argument`, called `flags.option(long: long, short: short, value_name: value_name, help: help)`: An option taking one value each time it is given: `--max 5`, `--max=5`, `-m 5`, `-m5`.
- `function positional(name: str, help: str) -> Argument`, called `flags.positional(name: name, help: help)`: A positional named `name`, taking exactly one value.
- `function with_kind(a: Argument, kind: Kind) -> Argument`, called `flags.with_kind(a, kind)`: A copy of `a` whose values are read as `kind`.
- `function with_default(a: Argument, value: str) -> Argument`, called `flags.with_default(a, value)`: A copy of `a` whose value, where none is given, is `value`.
- `function with_required(a: Argument) -> Argument`, called `flags.with_required(a)`: A copy of `a` that a parse refuses to go without.
- `function with_arity(a: Argument, arity: Arity) -> Argument`, called `flags.with_arity(a, arity)`: A copy of the positional `a` taking as many values as `arity` says.
- `function with_negation(a: Argument) -> Argument`, called `flags.with_negation(a)`: A copy of the flag `a` that `--no-` and its long name turn off again: `--color` and `--no-color`, the last given winning.
- `function with_section(a: Argument, title: str) -> Argument`, called `flags.with_section(a, title)`: A copy of the option `a` that the help lists under a heading of its own.
- `function with_hidden(a: Argument) -> Argument`, called `flags.with_hidden(a)`: A copy of `a` that the help and the usage leave out; a parse reads it all the same.
- `function add(@c: Command, a: Argument)`, called `flags.add(@c, a)`: Adds `a` to `c`, after the arguments it takes already.
- `function add_command(@c: Command, sub: Command)`, called `flags.add_command(c: @c, sub: sub)`: Adds `sub` to `c` as a subcommand: the first positional of the arguments then names one, and every argument after it is `sub`'s.
- `function add_exclusive(@c: Command, names: [str], required: bool)`, called `flags.add_exclusive(@c, names, required)`: Adds to `c` a group of options of which at most one may be given.
- `function with_options_first(c: Command) -> Command`, called `flags.with_options_first(c)`: A copy of `c` where every argument from the first positional on is a positional, options included: a command that runs another, `nice CMD -x`.
- `function without_help(c: Command) -> Command`, called `flags.without_help(c)`: A copy of `c` that does not answer `-h` and `--help`, so that a program may give the names to options of its own.
- `function with_epilog(c: Command, text: str) -> Command`, called `flags.with_epilog(c, text)`: A copy of `c` whose help ends with `text`.
- `function with_env(a: Argument, name: str) -> Argument`, called `flags.with_env(a, name)`: A copy of `a` that takes its value from the environment variable `name` where the command line does not give it, which `parse_with_env` reads.
- `function with_alias(a: Argument, name: str) -> Argument`, called `flags.with_alias(a, name)`: A copy of the option `a` that `--` and `name` name as well: `--colour` for `--color`.
- `function with_missing_value(a: Argument, value: str) -> Argument`, called `flags.with_missing_value(a, value)`: A copy of the option `a` that, given with no value after `=`, takes `value` and leaves the next argument alone: `--color` alone is `--color=always`.
- `function with_delimiter(a: Argument, delimiter: str) -> Argument`, called `flags.with_delimiter(a, delimiter)`: A copy of `a` whose every value is split at `delimiter` into several: `--tag a,b` gives `a` and `b`.
- `function with_range(a: Argument, lowest: i64, highest: i64) -> Argument`, called `flags.with_range(a, lowest: lowest, highest: highest)`: A copy of the integer argument `a` whose values must lie from `lowest` to `highest`, both included.
- `function with_version(c: Command, version: str) -> Command`, called `flags.with_version(c, version)`: A copy of `c` that answers `-V` and `--version` with `version`: the parse stops there, as at `-h`, and `is_version` says so.
- `function with_short_alias(a: Argument, short: str) -> Argument`, called `flags.with_short_alias(a, short)`: A copy of the option `a` that `-` and `short` name as well.
- `function with_command_hidden(c: Command) -> Command`, called `flags.with_command_hidden(c)`: A copy of the subcommand `c` that its parent's help and completions leave out; its parent's arguments choose it all the same.
- `function with_command_alias(c: Command, name: str) -> Command`, called `flags.with_command_alias(c, name)`: A copy of the subcommand `c` that its parent's arguments may choose by `name` too.
- `function with_help_on_empty(c: Command) -> Command`, called `flags.with_help_on_empty(c)`: A copy of `c` whose parse given no argument at all answers `is_help`, as where `-h` was given.
- `function with_external_commands(c: Command) -> Command`, called `flags.with_external_commands(c)`: A copy of `c` that takes a word naming none of its subcommands as another program's command: the word and every argument after it are kept, unread, for `external_of`.
- `function add_requirement(@c: Command, name: str, needs: str)`, called `flags.add_requirement(@c, name: name, needs: needs)`: Adds to `c` that the argument `name` needs `needs` given with it: a parse where `name` is given and `needs` is not fails `invalid`.
- `record Found(got: scan.Got)`: What a parse found: a value read only through the functions below.
- `function parse(c: Command, arguments: [str]) -> Found?`, called `flags.parse(c, arguments)`: What `arguments` give the command `c`. Fails `invalid`.
- `function parse_known(c: Command, arguments: [str]) -> Found?`, called `flags.parse_known(c, arguments)`: What `arguments` give `c`, the options it does not declare kept rather than refused: each as written, in `unknown_of`. Fails `invalid`.
- `function parse_args(c: Command) -> Found?`, called `flags.parse_args(c)`: What the program's own arguments give `c`. Fails `not_text`.
- `function parse_with_env(c: Command, arguments: [str], env: {str: str}) -> Found?`, called `flags.parse_with_env(c, arguments, env)`: What `arguments` and the environment `env` give the command `c`: an argument declared `with_env` and not given takes its variable's value. Fails `invalid`.
- `function parse_args_with_env(c: Command, env: {str: str}) -> Found?`, called `flags.parse_args_with_env(c, env)`: What the program's own arguments and the environment `env` give `c`. Fails `not_text`.
- `function is_help(f: Found) -> bool`, called `flags.is_help(f)`: Whether `-h` or `--help` was given, to the command of `f` or to a subcommand chosen under it.
- `function help_text(f: Found) -> str`, called `flags.help_text(f)`: The help page of the deepest command chosen in `f`: the one `-h` was given to, where `is_help` says so.
- `function name_of(f: Found) -> str`, called `flags.name_of(f)`: The name of the command `f` answers for.
- `function subcommand(f: Found) -> Found?`, called `flags.subcommand(f)`: What was found for the subcommand chosen. Fails `not_found`.
- `function is_given(f: Found, name: str) -> bool`, called `flags.is_given(f, name)`: Whether the argument `name` was given, as a flag, an option, its negation or a positional; a default is not given.
- `function is_on(f: Found, name: str) -> bool`, called `flags.is_on(f, name)`: Whether the flag `name` was given and not turned off after by its negation.
- `function count_of(f: Found, name: str) -> i64`, called `flags.count_of(f, name)`: How many times the argument `name` was given: `-vvv` gives `v` 3.
- `function value_of(f: Found, name: str) -> str?`, called `flags.value_of(f, name)`: The last value given to `name`, else its default. Fails `not_found`.
- `function values_of(f: Found, name: str) -> [str]`, called `flags.values_of(f, name)`: Every value given to `name`, in the order given, else its default; empty where neither stands.
- `function int_of(f: Found, name: str) -> i64?`, called `flags.int_of(f, name)`: The value of `name` read as an integer as the language writes one. Fails `not_found`, `invalid`.
- `function float_of(f: Found, name: str) -> f64?`, called `flags.float_of(f, name)`: The value of `name` read as a decimal number. Fails `not_found`, `invalid`.
- `function unknown_of(f: Found) -> [str]`, called `flags.unknown_of(f)`: The options `parse_known` kept because the command of `f` does not declare them, as written, in order; empty after `parse`.
- `function is_version(f: Found) -> bool`, called `flags.is_version(f)`: Whether `-V` or `--version` was given, to the command of `f` or to a subcommand chosen under it.
- `function version_text(f: Found) -> str`, called `flags.version_text(f)`: The version line of the deepest command chosen in `f`: its name and its parents', a space and its version, `tool 1.4.2`.
- `variant Source = .command_line | .environment | .fallback | .absent`: Where an argument's values came from.
- `function source_of(f: Found, name: str) -> Source`, called `flags.source_of(f, name)`: Where the values of the argument `name` came from.
- `function external_of(f: Found) -> [str]`, called `flags.external_of(f)`: The word naming another program's command and every argument after it, where the command of `f` was declared `with_external_commands`; empty otherwise.
- `function help_of(c: Command) -> str`, called `flags.help_of(c)`: The help page of `c`: its usage, what it says of itself, its positionals, its options under their headings with their defaults and the words they take, its subcommands and its epilog, a blank line between each two and no line break at the end.
- `function usage_of(c: Command) -> str`, called `flags.usage_of(c)`: The usage of `c`: `usage: `, its name, then each argument it takes as a user writes it, `[-v]`, `[-m NUM]`, `FILE...`, wrapped before column 80.
- `variant Shell = .bash | .zsh | .fish`: A shell that `completion_of` writes a script for.
- `function completion_of(c: Command, shell: Shell) -> str`, called `flags.completion_of(c, shell)`: A script that completes the command `c` in `shell`, made from its declaration: at any depth of subcommands it offers the options, the subcommands, the words of a choice, or the names of files where a value is text, and skips each option's value while finding the subcommand.


### ini

Layer 2, named `use <rebel>/ini`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/ini/).

INI read and written: sections in brackets, each holding keys and their values, in the order they were written, as Python's `configparser` reads them.

- `constant INVALID: str`, value `"invalid"`: The code of a text that is not INI as the options read it, of a document that would not read back, and of a value that is not a boolean.
- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `"not_found"`: The code of a section or a key looked up that is not there: `value_of`, `bool_of`, `section_of`, `remove_section`, `remove_key`.
- `constant EXISTS: str`, value `"exists"`: The code of a section added that is there already: `add_section`.
- `constant DEFAULT_SECTION: str`, value `"DEFAULT"`: The name of the section whose keys every other section holds where it does not hold its own: Python's `DEFAULTSECT`.
- `record Entry(key: str, value: str, bare: bool, comments: [str])`: A key and its value.
- `record Section(name: str, comments: [str], entries: [Entry])`: A section: a header and the keys under it.
- `record Document(sections: [Section], closing: [str])`: An INI document: its sections in the order first written, each name once.
- `record ReadOptions(delimiters: [str], comment_prefixes: [str], inline_comment_prefixes: [str], duplicates: bool, lower_keys: bool, bare_keys: bool, unnamed_section: bool, keep_comments: bool, empty_lines_in_values: bool)`: How a text is read.
- `function strict_read_options() -> ReadOptions`, called `ini.strict_read_options()`: Python's defaults, but keys kept as written: `=` and `:`, `#` and `;` comment lines and no inline ones, nothing given twice, no bare key, no key before a header, comments dropped, empty lines kept inside a value.
- `function parse(text: str) -> Document?`, called `ini.parse(text)`: The document `text` holds, read as `strict_read_options` reads. Fails `invalid`.
- `function parse_with(text: str, options: ReadOptions) -> Document?`, called `ini.parse_with(text, options)`: The document `text` holds, read as `options` say. Fails `invalid`.
- `function from_map(sections: {str: {str: str}}) -> Document`, called `ini.from_map(sections)`: A document of the sections of `sections`, in the map's order, each holding its keys in the map's order.
- `function sections_of(doc: Document) -> [str]`, called `ini.sections_of(doc)`: The names of the sections of `doc`, in order, `DEFAULT_SECTION` left out as Python leaves it out.
- `function has_section(doc: Document, name: str) -> bool`, called `ini.has_section(doc, name)`: Whether `doc` holds a section named `name`.
- `function has_key(doc: Document, section: str, key: str) -> bool`, called `ini.has_key(doc, section: section, key: key)`: Whether `key` has a value in the section `section` of `doc`, its own or `DEFAULT_SECTION`'s.
- `function value_of(doc: Document, section: str, key: str) -> str?`, called `ini.value_of(doc, section: section, key: key)`: The value of `key` in the section `section` of `doc`, else in `DEFAULT_SECTION`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function bool_of(doc: Document, section: str, key: str) -> bool?`, called `ini.bool_of(doc, section: section, key: key)`: The value of `key` in `section` read as a boolean, as Python reads one: `1`, `yes`, `true` and `on` are true, `0`, `no`, `false` and `off` false, in any case. Fails `not_found`, `invalid`.
- `function section_of(doc: Document, name: str) -> {str: str}?`, called `ini.section_of(doc, name)`: The keys and values of the section `name`, its own in order, then those of `DEFAULT_SECTION` it does not hold. Fails `not_found`.
- `function set_value(@doc: Document, section: str, key: str, value: str)`, called `ini.set_value(@doc, section: section, key: key, value: value)`: Gives `key` the value `value` in the section `section`: in its place where the section holds it, at the end otherwise, the section added at the end where `doc` has none of that name.
- `function add_section(@doc: Document, name: str) -> ()?`, called `ini.add_section(@doc, name)`: Adds an empty section `name` at the end of `doc`. Fails `exists`.
- `function remove_section(@doc: Document, name: str) -> ()?`, called `ini.remove_section(@doc, name)`: Removes the section `name` and every key in it. Fails `not_found`.
- `function remove_key(@doc: Document, section: str, key: str) -> ()?`, called `ini.remove_key(@doc, section: section, key: key)`: Removes `key` from the section `section`. Fails `not_found`.
- `record WriteOptions(delimiter: str, spaced: bool)`: How a document is written.
- `function spaced_write_options() -> WriteOptions`, called `ini.spaced_write_options()`: Python's layout: `key = value`.
- `function format(doc: Document) -> str?`, called `ini.format(doc)`: `doc` written as `spaced_write_options` writes it. Fails `invalid`.
- `function format_with(doc: Document, options: WriteOptions) -> str?`, called `ini.format_with(doc, options)`: `doc` written as `options` say. Fails `invalid`.


### java_properties

Layer 2, named `use <rebel>/java_properties`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/java_properties/).

Java's properties files read and written as `java.util.Properties` reads and writes them: Spring Boot's `application.properties`, a resource bundle, Gradle's and Maven's settings.

- `constant INVALID: str`, value `"invalid"`: The code of a text that is not a properties file, `parse` and `decode` failing with it at a `\u` not followed by four hexadecimal digits or writing half of a surrogate pair no other half completes, and of entries `format` would not write so that they read back: a key twice.
- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `"not_found"`: The code of a key looked up that is not there: `value_of`, `remove_key`.
- `record Entry(key: str, value: str)`: A key and its value.
- `function parse(text: str) -> [Entry]?`, called `java_properties.parse(text)`: The entries `text` writes, as `Properties.load(Reader)` reads it: each key once, in the order the text first names it, with the last value the text gives it. Fails `invalid`.
- `function decode(data: [u8]) -> [Entry]?`, called `java_properties.decode(data)`: The entries the bytes `data` write, read as Java 9 and later read a resource bundle (`PropertyResourceBundle`): as UTF-8, and where any byte is not, the whole file again as ISO 8859-1, each byte the character of its number. Fails as `parse` does.
- `function decode_latin1(data: [u8]) -> [Entry]?`, called `java_properties.decode_latin1(data)`: The entries the bytes `data` write, read as ISO 8859-1, each byte the character of its number, as `Properties.load(InputStream)` reads them: a character outside ISO 8859-1 stands in such a file as `\uXXXX`. Fails as `parse` does.
- `function value_of(entries: [Entry], key: str) -> str?`, called `java_properties.value_of(entries, key)`: The value of `key` in `entries`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function has_key(entries: [Entry], key: str) -> bool`, called `java_properties.has_key(entries, key)`: Whether an entry of `entries` has `key`.
- `function set_value(@entries: [Entry], key: str, value: str)`, called `java_properties.set_value(@entries, key: key, value: value)`: Sets the value of `key`: the first entry that has it takes `value`, or an entry is added at the end where none has it.
- `function remove_key(@entries: [Entry], key: str) -> ()?`, called `java_properties.remove_key(@entries, key)`: Removes every entry that has `key`. Fails `not_found`.
- `record WriteOptions(comments: str, ascii: bool)`: How `format_with` writes a file.
- `function default_write_options() -> WriteOptions`, called `java_properties.default_write_options()`: The options `format` writes with: no comment, every character as it is.
- `function ascii_write_options() -> WriteOptions`, called `java_properties.ascii_write_options()`: The options of a file that ASCII alone writes, for a reader of ISO 8859-1 as well as of UTF-8: no comment, every character outside space to `~` as `\uXXXX`.
- `function format(entries: [Entry]) -> str?`, called `java_properties.format(entries)`: `entries` as the text of a properties file, as `Properties.store(Writer)` writes them but for its line of the date: `key=value` and a line feed for each, in the order of `entries`, escaped so that `parse` reads them back. Fails `invalid`.
- `function format_with(entries: [Entry], options: WriteOptions) -> str?`, called `java_properties.format_with(entries, options)`: `entries` as the text of a properties file, written as `options` say. Fails as `format` does.


### semver

Layer 2, named `use <rebel>/semver`, [its reference](https://heroes-lang.org/rebel/semver/).

Versions by Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 (semver.org), read, written and ordered, and ranges of versions as Cargo reads them: which versions a requirement such as `^1.2`, `~1.4.3` or `>=1.2, <1.5` admits, and the highest of a list it admits.

- `constant INVALID: str`, value `"invalid"`: The code of a text that is not a version, a range, or the identifiers asked: `parse`, `parse_range`, `with_pre`, `with_build`.
- `constant DOES_NOT_FIT: str`, value `"does_not_fit"`: The code of a number past 18446744073709551615: `parse`, `parse_range`, `next_major`, `next_minor`, `next_patch`.
- `constant NOT_FOUND: str`, value `"not_found"`: The code of a search that admits nothing: `highest`, `highest_admitted`, `lowest_admitted`, `lowest_possible`.
- `constant MAX_COMPARATORS: i64`, value `32`: The most comparators a set of a range may hold, as Cargo's crate allows: `parse_range` refuses more.
- `record Version(major: u64, minor: u64, patch: u64, pre: [str], build: [str])`: A version: three numbers, a pre-release and build metadata.
- `function parse(text: str) -> Version?`, called `semver.parse(text)`: The version `text` holds, by SemVer 2.0.0's grammar. Fails `invalid`, `does_not_fit`.
- `function is_valid(text: str) -> bool`, called `semver.is_valid(text)`: Whether `text` is a version that `parse` reads.
- `function new(major: u64, minor: u64, patch: u64) -> Version`, called `semver.new(major: major, minor: minor, patch: patch)`: The release `major.minor.patch`, with no pre-release and no metadata.
- `function format(v: Version) -> str`, called `semver.format(v)`: `v` written as SemVer writes it: `1.2.3-alpha.1+build.5`, the build metadata kept.
- `function with_pre(v: Version, pre: str) -> Version?`, called `semver.with_pre(v, pre)`: `v` with the pre-release `pre`. Fails `invalid`.
- `function with_build(v: Version, build: str) -> Version?`, called `semver.with_build(v, build)`: `v` with the build metadata `build`. Fails `invalid`.
- `function is_prerelease(v: Version) -> bool`, called `semver.is_prerelease(v)`: Whether `v` is a pre-release: whether it has pre-release identifiers.
- `function compare(a: Version, b: Version) -> i64`, called `semver.compare(a: a, b: b)`: Which of `a` and `b` has the higher precedence by SemVer 2.0.0: -1 where `a` is lower, 1 where it is higher, 0 where they have the same.
- `function compare_build(a: Version, b: Version) -> i64`, called `semver.compare_build(a: a, b: b)`: Which of `a` and `b` orders first in a total order that agrees with `==`: precedence first, as `compare`, then build metadata, as Cargo's crate orders it.
- `function is_before(a: Version, b: Version) -> bool`, called `semver.is_before(a: a, b: b)`: Whether `a` orders before `b` by `compare_build`: the order to give `lists.sort_by`, which then sorts versions from the lowest.
- `function highest(versions: [Version]) -> Version?`, called `semver.highest(versions)`: The highest of `versions` by `compare_build`. Fails `not_found`.
- `function next_major(v: Version) -> Version?`, called `semver.next_major(v)`: The next major release after `v`: `1.4.2` gives `2.0.0`, and a pre-release of a major release, `2.0.0-rc.1`, gives that release, `2.0.0`, as npm's `inc` answers. Fails `does_not_fit`.
- `function next_minor(v: Version) -> Version?`, called `semver.next_minor(v)`: The next minor release after `v`: `1.4.2` gives `1.5.0`, and a pre-release of a minor release, `1.5.0-rc.1`, gives `1.5.0`, as npm's `inc` answers. Fails `does_not_fit`.
- `function next_patch(v: Version) -> Version?`, called `semver.next_patch(v)`: The next patch release after `v`: `1.4.2` gives `1.4.3`, and a pre-release, `1.4.3-rc.1`, gives its release, `1.4.3`, as npm's `inc` answers. Fails `does_not_fit`.
- `variant Op = .exact | .greater | .greater_eq | .less | .less_eq | .tilde | .caret | .wildcard`: What a comparator compares a version with.
- `record Comparator(op: Op, major: u64, minor: u64, patch: u64, written: i64, pre: [str])`: One comparison a range makes: an operator and a version, partial or whole.
- `record Range(sets: [[model.Cmp]])`: A range of versions: sets of comparators, a version admitted where every comparator of one set admits it.
- `function parse_range(text: str) -> Range?`, called `semver.parse_range(text)`: The range `text` holds, by Cargo's grammar and npm's `||`. Fails `invalid`, `does_not_fit`.
- `function from_comparators(sets: [[Comparator]]) -> Range`, called `semver.from_comparators(sets)`: The range of the sets of comparators `sets`, a version admitted where every comparator of one set admits it.
- `function comparators_of(r: Range) -> [[Comparator]]`, called `semver.comparators_of(r)`: The sets of comparators of `r`, in the order written: what `parse_range` read, a bare version as `caret`.
- `function format_range(r: Range) -> str`, called `semver.format_range(r)`: `r` written as Cargo writes a requirement: each comparator with its operator, a bare version as `^`, comparators joined by `, ` and sets by ` || `.
- `function admits(r: Range, v: Version) -> bool`, called `semver.admits(r, v)`: Whether `r` admits `v`, by Cargo's rule.
- `function admitted_of(r: Range, versions: [Version]) -> [Version]`, called `semver.admitted_of(r, versions)`: The versions of `versions` that `r` admits, in their order.
